timeValueUsdPerHour.basis: ILOSTAT median hourly earnings 2025 (LFS) PHP 87.74 (https://rplumber.ilo.org/data/indicator/?id=EAR_EHRM_SEX_CUR_NB_A), x1.05 to November 2026, less 7% (SSS, PhilHealth, Pag-IBIG; guess), at 63.8 per USD, x0.967 = $1.3.

nuclearNear.forecast.basis: Sites used by US forces (Basa near Pampanga, Mactan by Cebu, Subic): US-China war 0.025%/yr x 0.5 struck x 0.08 of urban households in the area, plus limited US-China use 0.1% x 0.2 x 0.05, x 0.85 alive.

nuclearNear.falloutScale.basis: Counted households are those near struck sites; many homes of light materials shield poorly.

localOutage.probability.basis: No load shedding since 16 May 2025 (504 days on 4 October 2026; load reduction 2.8% of Eskom customers, https://www.sanews.gov.za/node/84735). Doing Business 2020 Johannesburg: SAIDI 30.5 h, SAIFI 5.98 (CAIDI 5.1 h) gives 0.87, but that year had load shedding. Municipal network failures in Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni remain frequent; Cape Town is reliable.

localOutage.durationFactor.basis: CAIDI 5.1 h gives 1.39 by the formula; raised for slow municipal repairs (cable theft, substation failures lasting days).

bankingCrisis.forecast.basis: Currency events 2001 (rand down 34%) and 2008 (32%) December-on-December (https://stats.bis.org/api/v2/data/dataflow/BIS/WS_XRU/1.0/M.ZA..A), weight 0.79; 2015 was 23%. BB prior 6.5%: (0.5 + 0.79)/(7.7 + 16.86) = 5.2%.

bankingCrisis.pessimistic.basis: Pessimist curve: odds x 3.2.

violentCrime.scale.basis: D = 39.7/5.0 x 0.85 = 6.8 (UNODC 2024; SAPS: robbery behind 382 of 5,596 murders, 6.8%, https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/crimestats.pdf); B = (5.9% housebreaking + 1.1% home robbery of households, Stats SA 2023/24, https://thestar.com.my/news/world/2024/08/28/over-1-mln-south-african-households-affected-by-housebreaking-report) / 0.71% = 9.9, used 8.5 for urban, x 0.45 for smaller losses = 3.8.

civilUnrest.forecast.basis: July 2021 in KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng (about 45% of the population; 354 dead, over 200 malls looted, fuel and food shortages, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_South_African_unrest), xenophobic riots 2008, 2015, 2019, Cape Town 2023: about 1.0 over 31 years since 1995 = 3.3%; 7% counting 1990-94.

civilUnrest.pessimistic.basis: The 1990-2026 rate: a 2021-scale wave every ten years plus local looting.

houseFire.scale.basis: WHO 2017-2020: X00-X09 2,519 deaths a year (41 per million), ratio 5.0; times 0.8 for non-structure burns (guess); alarm factor 0.55 = 2.2, lowered to 2.0 because informal-settlement shack fires weigh less in an average urban home. GBD Southern sub-Saharan Africa 5.1 against 0.65 per 100,000 agrees. https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

coIncident.scale.basis: South Africa codes almost all gas deaths as undetermined (Y17 224 a year against X47 10): counting 80% of Y17 gives a ratio of 1.18, GBD Southern sub-Saharan Africa 0.57; middle 1.0, times 1.42. Braziers and paraffin heaters. https://www.who.int/data/data-collection-tools/who-mortality-database

priceIndex.basis: ICP 2021 vs US (https://api.worldbank.org/v2/sources/90): food 0.74, household goods 0.58, equipment 1.10; with US sales tax and 15% VAT 0.841. x0.870 to November 2026 (consumption PPP 2021-25, CPI 1.045 assumed, ZAR 14.78 to 17.41 per USD) = 0.73.

micromortValueUsd.basis: 14.6 x Atlas GNI per capita 2025 $6,270 / $88,810 (https://api.worldbank.org/v2/indicator/NY.GNP.PCAP.CD) = 1.0. Lo: elasticity 1.5. Hi: GNI at PPP $15,600 / $89,490 x 14.6 = 2.5.

timeValueUsdPerHour.basis: Stats SA Labour Market Dynamics 2022: median monthly earnings R5,417, Gauteng R7,500 (search snippets; pages returned 403). Urban median taken as R6,500 / 186 h = R34.9, x1.22 to November 2026 (5% a year), less 2% (UIF; most below the income tax threshold), at 17.41 per USD, x0.967 = $2.3.

nuclearNear.forecast.basis: As the Buenos Aires anchor: gave up its weapons, African nuclear-weapon-free zone, Southern Hemisphere.

nuclearNear.falloutScale.basis: Only for an unforeseen attack.

child.basis: United States life table 2024, total population: e(7) = 72.5 (NVSR vol. 75 no. 5, 25 August 2026, Table 1, https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr75/nvsr75-05.pdf, read by a research assistant). EU27 2024 (provisional): 74.9; France 76.4, Germany 74.5 (Eurostat demo_mlexpec, read). Hi allows for the higher European figure and for cohort gains.

adult.basis: United States 2024: e(37) = 43.8 (NVSR 75-5, Table 1, https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr75/nvsr75-05.pdf). EU27 2024: 45.4; France 47.1, Germany 45.0, Netherlands 45.7 (Eurostat demo_mlexpec, https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/demo_mlexpec?format=JSON&geo=EU27_2020&sex=T&age=Y37, read).

age60to74.basis: United States 2024: e(67) = 18.2 (NVSR 75-5, Table 1). EU27 2024: 18.7; France 20.3, Germany 18.1, Netherlands 18.3 (Eurostat demo_mlexpec, read).

age75plus.basis: United States 2024: e(82) = 8.2 (NVSR 75-5, Table 1). EU27 2024: 8.4; France 9.4, Germany 8.0, Netherlands 7.7 (Eurostat demo_mlexpec, read).

reference.basis: Reference age 40: HHS tells analysts to 'assume that the average individual in these studies is 40 years of age' (Guidelines for Regulatory Impact Analysis 2016, p. 20, https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/242926/HHS_RIAGuidance.pdf, read) and in 2026 uses 'an individual 40 years of age' with 40.7 years remaining (US 2023 table; https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2d83af5823915d81871334ee08ad03d9/Standard-RIA-Values-2026.pdf, read). On the 2024 table used for the bands, e(37) = 43.8 less about 0.95 a year gives e(40) = 41.0. Hi is age 35, the young end of the hedonic-wage samples ('on average thirty-five to forty years old', Aldy and Viscusi, search snippet): 45.7. Lo is age 48, allowing for stated-preference samples that are older (one well-known sample averaged 54; Krupnick et al. 2001, search snippet): about 34.

us.basis: HHS standard values for 2026: VSL low $6.6M, central $14.1M, high $21.5M in 2025 dollars (https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2d83af5823915d81871334ee08ad03d9/Standard-RIA-Values-2026.pdf, read). Multiplied by 1.035 to reach November 2026 prices (my CPI assumption) and divided by 1e6. US DOT's figure ($13.7M in 2024 dollars, recalled; DOT pages returned 403) gives the same central value after the same adjustment.

westernEurope.basis: Three routes. (a) OECD 2025 meta-analysis: base VSL USD 8.4M for the EU and 8.5M for the US in 2022 dollars, income elasticity 1 (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/mortality-risk-valuation-in-policy-assessment_76ca89a2-en/full-report/recommended-vsl-estimates-for-policy-analysis_9b41dca3.html; search snippet, page returned 403); about 9.4M in 2026 dollars. (b) Transfer from the US value at elasticity 1 with Western European GNI per capita about 0.55-0.6 of the US: 14.6 x 0.58 = 8.5. (c) Older European Commission and national practice (DG MOVE transport handbook about EUR 3.3M in 2016, UK about GBP 2.4M; both recalled) is about 4-5M today. Mid 7.0 is the geometric middle of 5 and 9.4; lo and hi span the routes.

buenosAires.basis: Income-elasticity transfer: VSL_AR = VSL_US x (GNI per capita AR / US)^e. Atlas GNI per capita 2024: Argentina $13,530, US $83,490 (World Bank, https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NY.GNP.PCAP.CD; search snippet), ratio 0.162. e = 1.0 (OECD 2025; Viscusi and Masterman 2017) gives 14.6 x 0.162 = 2.4; e = 1.5 (Robinson, Hammitt and O'Keeffe 2019 reference case, recalled) gives 14.6 x 0.065 = 0.95. City of Buenos Aires incomes are roughly 1.5 times the national average (my estimate), giving 3.6 at e = 1 and 2.7 at e = 1.2. A PPP income ratio (about 0.35) would give 5.1. Mid 3.0; lo and hi cover the elasticity, income premium and exchange-rate choices.

us.basis: HHS default for unpaid time: median pre-tax wage $24.43 less a 17% effective tax rate = $20.27 in 2025 dollars (https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2d83af5823915d81871334ee08ad03d9/Standard-RIA-Values-2026.pdf, read); x 1.035 = $21.0. US DOT values personal travel time at 50% of median household income per hour, which also comes to about $19-20 (recalled). Lo is 50% of the HHS figure (the fraction transport appraisal applies to a personal wage); hi is the after-tax mean wage of an above-median earner.

westernEurope.basis: HHS method applied to European wages. Median gross hourly earnings 2022: EU EUR 14.9, Germany 19.4, Netherlands 19.0 (Eurostat Structure of Earnings Survey, https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php/Earnings_statistics; search snippet); with France about 16.5, UK about 18, Italy 13, Spain 11 (recalled) the population-weighted Western European median is about EUR 16.4. Plus about 17% nominal growth to 2026 = 19.2; less about 29% income tax and employee contributions = 13.6; x 1.15 USD per EUR (assumed) = $15.7. Lo is half of that.

buenosAires.basis: Average taxable wage of stable formal workers (RIPTE) ARS 1,915,879 a month in June 2026 (https://www.argentina.gob.ar/trabajo/seguridadsocial/ripte; search snippet), about ARS 2.15M by November; at ARS 1,555 per dollar (retail rate early November 2026, search snippet) = $1,380 a month = $8.1 an hour over 170 hours; less 17% employee contributions = $6.7. Informal workers (over a third of the workforce) earn roughly half, so the after-tax median across all workers is about $5-6. Lo is half the mid; hi is a professional's after-tax wage.

realDiscountRate.basis: US regulatory analysis uses 3% and 7% real (OMB Circular A-4 of 2003, as applied in https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2d83af5823915d81871334ee08ad03d9/Standard-RIA-Values-2026.pdf, read). 3% is also the European Commission's social discount rate (recalled). Lo is the real after-tax return on safe savings; hi is the OMB upper rate, close to the real cost of consumer credit for a household that borrows.

apartment.basis: Average US apartment rent $1,730 a month (Apartments.com, April 2026; search snippet) over about 900 sq ft (recalled) = $1.92 per sq ft a month = $248 per square metre a year; I use $232 (between that and the Apartment List median of $1,390). Usable stack 1.8 m at 50% fill = 900 litres per square metre, so average floor space costs 232 / 900 = $0.26 per litre-year. Marginal dead space is worth about a quarter of average floor space (my judgment; range 10-100%): 0.26 x 0.25 = $0.065. Market check: self-storage at about $1.2-1.5 per sq ft a month, stacked 2 m at 60% fill, is $0.13-0.16 per litre-year (recalled prices). European city rents per square metre are similar to US ones and Buenos Aires about 40% lower (two-room flat ARS 898,154 a month in September 2026, Zonaprop via search snippet, about $12 per square metre a month), but flats are smaller, so I keep one value.

house.basis: US single-family rent about $1.2 per sq ft a month (about $2,200 for 1,800 sq ft; recalled) = $158 per square metre a year. Garage or unfinished basement space is valued at about 30% of living space: $47 per square metre a year, or 47 / 900 = $0.052 per litre-year on average. Houses usually have slack, so the marginal litre is worth about 40% of that: $0.02. Hi is living-space value at 60%; lo is a house with empty basement.

westernEurope.basis: No prices fetched. Judgment: branded outdoor and electronic goods cost 10-30% more than US pre-sales-tax prices because of 19-22% VAT (a Sawyer Mini is about EUR 30-35 against $29; recalled); FFP2 masks, bottled water and shelf-stable food are at or below US prices; US tariffs since 2025 have narrowed the gap on imported goods.

buenosAires.basis: Samples at ARS 1,555 per dollar (search snippets; Mercado Libre product pages returned 403): generic battery CO alarm ARS 59,994 (6 x 9,999) = $39 against $25-35 in the US, ratio 1.1-1.5; portable CO detector ARS 89,900 = $58; Sawyer Mini filter ARS 209,033-242,576 = $134-156 through a cross-border reseller (Desertcart) against $29, ratio about 5, an upper bound for branded specialty imports with no local distributor. Staples (water, canned food, fuel, candles) are at or below US prices. Weighting generic locally stocked goods at 1.2-1.5, staples at 0.8-1.0 and branded imports at 2-5 gives about 1.4. Items differ by a factor of five, so an item-level override would be better than one index.

homePresence.basis: Nights away: about 2.3 billion US domestic person-trips a year at about 1.8 nights each (BTS average stay 1.6-2.1 nights, search snippet; trip count recalled) = 12 nights per person, plus about 2-3 nights abroad = about 15 nights, or 4% of the year. Household members usually travel together, and daytime absence at work still leaves supplies within reach, so presence is about 0.95. Lower for frequent travellers and for hazards that block the way home (earthquake during working hours).

leaveHardshipUsdPerPersonDay.basis: The discomfort of being away from home when leaving by choice, over and above what it costs. The model's own guess, set below the displaced-day hardship in mobility.json because the move is chosen and planned.

costPerLifeSavedUsd.basis: GiveWell staff, 7 May 2025: 'Our current estimate for the marginal cost per life saved through the Top Charities Fund is approximately $8,000' and 'the actual cost might range from roughly $5,000 to $10,000' (https://blog.givewell.org/2025/03/25/march-2025-open-thread/, read in the archive.org copy of 8 June 2026; the live site returned an empty page). The range is GiveWell's own, not a 90% interval.

hoursPerYear.basis: OECD 2025, usual weekly hours of full-time employees in the main job: OECD 40.0, US 41.0, UK 40.7, Germany 39.0, France 38.7, Netherlands 37.5; Eurostat 2025, full-time professionals: EU27 39.2 (OECD SDMX DF_AVG_USL_WK_WKD and Eurostat lfsa_ewhuis, read). Times weeks at work after leave, public holidays and sickness: about 47 in the US (41 x 47 = 1,927) and 43 in Western Europe (39 x 43 = 1,680). OECD average annual hours actually worked per worker, part-timers included: OECD 1,736, US 1,800 (https://sdmx.oecd.org/public/rest/data/OECD.ELS.SAE,DSD_HW@DF_AVG_ANN_HRS_WKD,1.0/all?startPeriod=2024&format=csvfilewithlabels, read).

baselineDays.basis: About 4.5 L of drinkable liquid per person that an unprepared household would in fact use: fridge and cupboard drinks, part of a case of bottled water, ice, canned-food liquid. Excludes the water heater tank, which most households do not think to use (separate item). High end: houses that use the tank. 53.6% self-report a 3-day supply, but that includes deliberate preparers: https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6136a1.htm

hardship.basis: Not FEMA's figure itself: FEMA's $74.38 (2022 dollars; about $86 now at my CPI estimate of x1.15) values lost washing and flushing and assumes 25 L a day stays purchasable (https://fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_standard-economic-values-methodology-report_2023.pdf). Day 1 = water-seeking time ($8-16) + expected non-fatal illness (1% x $500 = $5) + thirst, rationing and worry, cross-checked against Hurricane Harvey prices of $42.96 and $99 a case ($3.6-8.3 per litre, $11-25 a day; search snippets). Rises as substitutes run out, then plateaus as people adapt. Water plus sanitation together cross FEMA's value near day 3.

mortality.basis: Daily chance of enteric illness from drinking unsafe water (judgment: 1%, range 0.2-5%; Norway mains-break cohort +4.7 points per household-week, outbreak attack rates of 2-7% a day) x case fatality for a healthy adult (judgment: 15 per million, range 5-100; norovirus is about 6 per million under 65 if 90% of its 900 deaths in 20 million cases are 65+, https://www.cdc.gov/norovirus/data-research/index.html) = 0.15, rounded to 0.1. Later steps: dirtier sources, failed sanitation. Checks: Puerto Rico leptospirosis, 17-26 deaths over 3.3 million people x 68 days = 0.08-0.12; Texas 2021, no attributed deaths.

workLoss.basis: Gross 0.24 of an eight-hour day: about 1.5 hours (0.5-3) finding, queueing for or boiling water, plus about 5% for thirst and stomach upsets from untreated water; times 0.7 for work made up later. In Texas in 2021, 53% of residents had to go and obtain drinking water (Texas Politics Project poll, https://news.utexas.edu/2021/04/02/texans-blame-variety-of-factors-for-severity-of-winter-storm-support-reform-attempts/, read). No time-use study of a rich-country water outage was found.

baselineDays.basis: Kitchen inventories: 100 food-secure New Jersey families held a mean of 33.2 days of calories (SD 22.0, range 8.1 to 125.2; https://doi.org/10.1017/S1049023X15004884) and 60 low-income households about 17 (SD 13 to 14; https://research-portal.najah.edu/migrant/35139/). Implied medians of about 28 and 13 give a population median near 20, which I cut by 0.75 for calories nobody eats as meals (oil, flour, sugar, condiments) and 0.9 for urban flats and small households: about 14, with utilities working.

hardship.basis: No willingness-to-pay study for a day without food was found. Built as a disability weight (0.05 on day 1 rising to 0.6 after a month) times an assumed $500 per healthy day, and checked against FEMA's $66 per person-day welfare loss for tap water and the $54 per household that co-op members would pay to avoid a 24-hour power cut (both in prior-art.md). Supervised fasters mostly report mild symptoms (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5819235/), so the early days are set well below water.

mortality.basis: Total fast with water, no medical care, healthy adult of average build. Early days are a guess bounded above by data: no deaths in 6,265 water-only fasting days (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5819235/) or about 12,300 days at 200 to 250 kcal (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6314618/), so under 162 per day at 95% confidence. Late days come from the 1981 hunger strike: nobody died before day 46 and ten lean men died on days 46 to 73, median 61 (https://cain.ulster.ac.uk/events/hstrike/dead.htm); I shift that about 15 to 20 days later for average body fat.

hardship.basis: food.json note 3.

mortality.basis: food.json note 3.

hardship.basis: Scaled up from the half-ration figures.

mortality.basis: Dutch famine, 1944-45.

workLoss.basis: Gross 0.22: about an hour a day spent looking for food, plus about 10% lower output from hunger. Reviews of short fasts in healthy adults find mixed and mostly small effects on cognition (Benau et al. 2014, Appetite 77:52-61; the 2021 update finds some deficits; https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s13668-021-00370-4.pdf, search snippets). Times 0.7.

hardship.basis: food.json, camp-stove: hot meals and drinks for a household that would otherwise eat cold are worth about $3 a person a day.

mortality.basis: None claimed.

workLoss.basis: Eating cold takes no more time than cooking. The one real loss is caffeine withdrawal (headache, fatigue) for habitual coffee drinkers who cannot make it hot; cold instant coffee or caffeinated soft drinks avoid most of it. Guess.

hardship.basis: food.json, infant-formula: an infant-day without formula, the household improvising.

mortality.basis: food.json, infant-formula.

workLoss.basis: Only infants are members of this need.

baselineDays.basis: The model's own guess of ordinary stock.

hardship.basis: food.json, pet-food: the owner's distress at a hungry animal.

mortality.basis: None claimed.

workLoss.basis: Felt by the household, not by a working member.

baselineDays.basis: Thermal lag of the building. Newtonian cooling with a time constant of 20-60 h takes a house from 20 C to 10 C in 8-24 h at -10 C outside and 14-42 h at 0 C. An RMI/Redwood Energy model (search snippet only, https://rmi.org/insight/hours-of-safety-in-cold-weather) has a 1950s house below 40 F after 8 h and a 2009-code house after 45 h in severe cold. Texas 2021: indoor temperatures fell 'near or below freezing' within outages whose longest block had a median of 19 h (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf).

hardship.basis: Baik et al. 2020 (read in full, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-020-0581-1): for a 10-day below-freezing outage, households would pay a median $43 (mean $51) for sure and a median $60 (mean $80) with uncertainty per day for 20 A of backup running a furnace blower, fridge, freezer and a few lights. At 2.5 persons that is $17-32 per person-day for the bundle; I assign about 60% to heat ($10-19). FEMA's residential electricity value is $33 per person-day and ICE 2.0 gives $54 per household for 24 h (prior-art.md). Stated values look low against behaviour in Texas 2021, where 18% left home and 26% of those who stayed heated with a gas oven and 8% with a grill indoors, so the high end is wide. The rise with consecutive days is my judgment (the house keeps cooling; sleep loss accumulates).

mortality.basis: Texas, February 2021. Certified hypothermia deaths 158, of which 107 aged 60+ (DSHS, https://www.dshs.texas.gov/sites/default/files/news/updates/SMOC_FebWinterStorm_MortalitySurvReport_12-30-21.pdf). Exposure: 69% of the 27.0M people in ERCOT counties lost power for a mean 42 h; 18% left; 16% had a wood fire and 15% a gas fireplace (UH survey, https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf). That gives about 15.9M unmet person-days, 9.7M of them in ages 15-59. Guessed inputs: the share of hypothermia deaths that occurred at home (0.45 under 60, 0.8 at 60+; DSHS does not report place of death) and a 0.7 factor for 'healthy' (21% of hypothermia deaths involved alcohol or drugs). Result: about 20 at-home deaths at 15-59, or 2.1 micromorts per unmet day for the average adult and 1.5 for a healthy one. The steps (1.2, then 2.4) reproduce that over the Texas mean of 1.25 unmet days; the rise by day and the day-3 value are assumptions. The high end allows for Buffalo 2022, where 7 of the first 31 deaths were from lack of heat (https://text.npr.org/1145589871) among roughly 20,000 customers without power (unverified), about seven times the Texas rate per person-day, and for uncertified cold-related deaths (Texas excess deaths 702 against 246 certified, https://buzzfeednews.com/article/peteraldhous/texas-winter-storm-power-outage-death-toll).

workLoss.basis: Office studies put peak output near 22 C and find it falls on either side (Seppanen, Fisk and Lei 2006, LBNL-60946, https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/903490, read); a small field study found keying time 54% at 20 C against 100% at 25 C (Hedge 2004, nine workstations, https://news.cornell.edu/node/281845, search snippet). An unheated home in a cold wave falls well below 15 C, where hands stiffen and time goes to keeping warm. Gross 0.45 (0.15-0.8) x 0.7. No study measures desk work in an unheated home.

baselineDays.basis: Nothing in an ordinary home substitutes for cooling. The building's thermal lag (BC 2021: 8 and 13 deaths on the first two days against 231 on the fifth) is put into the low day-1 step of the curves instead of here.

hardship.basis: No willingness-to-pay study for a hot day at home was found. Anchored on whole-outage figures in prior-art.md (ICE 2.0 $54 per household for 24 h; FEMA $33 per person-day; Baik $43-60 per household-day; 42% would relocate in a 3-day outage) and on a hotel room at about $50 per person-night as a ceiling; rises as sleep is lost night after night.

mortality.basis: All-ages deaths per million person-days without cooling: BC 2021 2.5 on day 1, 17 on day 3, 73 on day 5 (576 deaths in homes without AC, 3.44M people without AC, daily counts 8-13-53-131-231); France 2003 4.8, 20 and 37 on days 1, 5 and 9 (excess of 286, 1,202 and 2,197 deaths on 4, 8 and 12 August over about 59.6M people, a recalled denominator); Hurricane Beryl 2024 about 1 on official attributions. I take a mid all-ages curve of 1.5-3-6-10-14 and multiply by 5% for a healthy adult aged 15-59: adults 15-59 run at 10-15% of the all-ages rate in BC, France and Europe 2022, and I guess healthy adults at a third of that. Sources: https://nanaimo.ca/docs/public-safety-department/bc-coroners-reportheat_related_deaths_in_bc_knowledge_update.cleaned.pdf and https://www.inserm.fr/wp-content/uploads/2017-11/inserm-rapportthematique-surmortalitecaniculeaout2003-rapportetape.pdf

workLoss.basis: Indoor 30-34 C: office output 9-17% below its maximum (Seppanen, Fisk and Lei 2006: 91.1% of maximum at 30 C, about 2% lower per degree above 25 C; https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/903490, read); plus about 5% for poor sleep on hot nights and 6% (half an hour) for cooling off. Gross 0.23 x 0.7 = 0.16. The sleep and coping shares are guesses.

baselineDays.basis: 94.8% of households said they had a working flashlight and batteries (CDC BRFSS, 14 states, 2006-2010, https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6136a1.htm) and 91% of adults own a smartphone with a torch (Pew 2025, search snippet). The day count is my guess: one flashlight with part-used cells gives 5-20 h, i.e. 1-4 evenings; phone torches compete with calls.

hardship.basis: Stated WTP to avoid a 24 h outage is $53.68 per household (LBNL ICE 2.0, https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/ice_2.0_nreca_final_report_28oct2026.pdf) and FEMA uses $33 per person-day; I assign 15-25% of that to light, about $10 per household-evening, divided by 2.5 persons. No study isolates lighting.

mortality.basis: Data: about 3,700 unintentional fall deaths at ages 15-59 in 2023 (WISQARS: 332 at 25-34, 677 at 35-44, 1,250 at 45-54, 3,172 at 55-64, https://wisqars-viz.cdc.gov/pdfs/leading-causes-of-injury-deaths-by-age-group_2023_508.pdf) among roughly 197M people = 1.9 per 100,000 a year = 0.052 micromorts a day. Falls and fractures among over-65s rose 40% in New Jersey in the week after Sandy (https://medicalxpress.com/news/2013-11-falls-fractures-elderly-superstorm-sandy.html) in a population that mostly owned flashlights. Judgement: having no light at all adds 35% (8-100%) of daily fall risk over having battery light. 0.052 x 0.35 = 0.018.

workLoss.basis: Knowledge work is mostly done in daylight and a charged laptop or phone lights its own screen; the loss is evening work and time fumbling in the dark, larger in winter. Guess.

baselineDays.basis: For a household without a car: a phone lasts about a day in normal use and two in low-power mode; a laptop (50-70 Wh) holds 3-4 phone charges. Households with a car can charge indefinitely from its USB port or 12 V socket while fuel lasts; see openQuestions.

hardship.basis: No direct WTP study found. Whole-outage WTP is $54 per household-day (LBNL ICE 2.0, https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/ice_2.0_nreca_final_report_28oct2026.pdf) and $43-60 a day for partial backup in a 10-day blackout (Baik et al. 2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-020-0581-1); I give phones and small devices about a third of that once they are dead, rising as coordination, work and payments suffer. Applies only while the mobile network is up.

mortality.basis: Cost of being unable to phone for an ambulance. EMS-treated cardiac arrest is about 0.1% of people a year with ~10% survival (recalled AHA figures), worth ~0.3 micromorts a day on average and ~0.06 for a healthy adult under 60; other time-critical emergencies roughly triple that to 0.2. A dead phone loses perhaps 15% (3-40%) of the benefit, because neighbours, landlines and cars remain: 0.2 x 0.15 = 0.03.

workLoss.basis: Without a working computer or phone a knowledge worker can only read on paper, think and write by hand: gross about 0.9 (0.7-1.0) of the day; x 0.7 for work made up = 0.63. Lower where an office, library or cafe with power is within reach (a local outage), higher in a regional one. No outage study isolates this. Cross-check: in a hypothetical three-day outage 21% of rural US households expect to lose income, mean $1,158 among them, about a third of three days' household income (LBNL ICE 2.0, https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2026-10/ice_2.0_nreca_final_report_28oct2026.pdf, read).

baselineDays.basis: Official safe time is 4 h for a closed fridge, 48 h for a full freezer and 24 h for a half-full one (CDC, https://www.cdc.gov/food-safety/foods/keep-food-safe-after-emergency.html). Real losses start later: 4.9M US households reported spoiled food in 2023 (AHS, https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2024/10/power-outages.html), about the 4.6M (3.5% of 131M) that NREL data imply had an outage over 24 h (https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy23osti/83092.pdf), though 23.6M had one of 6 h or more. So median practical coverage is about 10 h.

hardship.basis: Household loss: fridge $45 (15-130), freezer $110 (30-350), total about $155; divided by 2.5. Anchors: Con Edison pays up to $280 on an itemised list and $655 with proof (https://www.coned.com/en/services-and-outages/claim-form/residential-spoilage-claim-form); marketing surveys put the loss at $117-200 an outage (search snippets, unverified); only 31% discard fridge food and 37% thawed frozen food (RTI 2011, https://rti.org/news/most-americans-are-not-prepared-ensure-food-safety-during-power-outages), which is why the expected fridge loss is below the value of the contents. Day 3 onward: $5 per household-day for shopping daily and eating shelf food, guess.

mortality.basis: Foodborne illness kills about 3,000 Americans a year (recalled CDC estimate) = 0.025 micromorts per person-day, mostly the old and immunocompromised; perhaps 0.005 for a healthy adult. Diarrhoeal illness rose after the 2003 New York blackout and was tied to meat (OR 2.7) and seafood (OR 4.8) eaten afterwards (Marx et al. 2006, search snippet). I assume risk triples on the days spoiled food is still being eaten.

workLoss.basis: About an hour per household to clear spoiled food and an extra shopping trip, on the one or two days the need counts, spread over 2.5 people and often done outside working hours. Guess.

baselineDays.basis: Portable concentrator batteries last 2-4 h and up to 12 h with external packs at the lowest setting (Molinari et al. 2017, https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/41187); an E cylinder holds about 680 L, 5.7 h at 2 L/min (recalled). In the 2003 blackout 23 of 255 patients at one New York emergency department within 24 h came for device failure (Greenwald 2004, search snippet). CPAP has no backup, so its coverage is 0.

hardship.basis: CPAP-class user: a night of broken sleep, sleepiness and headache, worsening as sleep debt builds. Lower bound is what users already pay for the therapy, a few dollars a night. No WTP study found.

mortality.basis: CPAP-class user. Upper bound from observational data: untreated severe sleep apnoea had 0.7 more fatal cardiovascular events per 100 person-years than CPAP-treated (Marin 2005, recalled) = 19 micromorts a day; randomised trials found no mortality benefit. Drowsy driving adds under 1. Chosen so that base x 100 reproduces the life-supporting estimate, which is the number with evidence behind it.

workLoss.basis: Base case CPAP for sleep apnoea: two weeks' withdrawal raised sleepiness (Epworth +2.7) but did not worsen psychomotor or driving-simulator performance (Kohler et al. 2011, randomised, search snippet); one night's withdrawal did impair simulated driving (Filtness et al., search snippet). Add an hour or two to find somewhere to power the device. For a life-supporting device (oxygen) the day goes to reaching a hospital or a place with power: 0.6 or more, the hi.

baselineDays.basis: Nothing ordinary in a home replaces the network, so cover is zero once service is gone. Cell-site backup (Verizon: up to 8 h of battery at every macro site, 24-72 h where a generator is fitted; https://www.lightreading.com/security/what-atandt-verizon-and-t-mobile-are-doing-to-harden-their-networks/d/d-id/769216) belongs in the window length; 0.3 day is the allowance to use if a hazard file starts the comms window when grid power fails.

hardship.basis: Texas, Feb 2021: of those who lost cell service 43% called it very or extremely serious, against 68% for losing power (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf); 0.65 x the residential power-outage value of $21-33 per person-day (ICE 2.0 $53.68 per household-day; FEMA $33.04) gives $14-21 (both power values from step 2). The low end leans toward FEMA's residential value of $0.67 for communications loss, which is the price of service, not a willingness to pay (https://fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_standard-economic-values-methodology-report_2023.pdf); the fall after a week is a guess.

mortality.basis: Bottom-up: time-critical emergencies run at very roughly 5-10 per million healthy adults per day and being unable to phone for help costs perhaps 1-3 percentage points of survival (recalled figures, not fetched), giving 0.05-0.3. Upper bound from Puerto Rico after Maria: a third of excess deaths were from delayed care and 9% of households could not reach 911 over an average 41 days without cell service (https://www.wunderground.com/cat6/excess-deaths-and-toll-puerto-rico-hurricane-maria), which works out at about 0.6-0.9 per healthy adult-day.

workLoss.basis: About three quarters (0.55-0.9) of a knowledge worker's output needs the internet: of time in Microsoft 365 the average user spends 57% communicating (meetings, chat, email) and 43% creating (https://news.microsoft.com/2023/05/09/introducing-the-microsoft-365-copilot-early-access-program-and-the-2023-work-trend-index/, read), and much creation uses cloud files and search; in a UK survey 28% could not work at all without the internet and 7% could manage a full day (Yesss Electrical survey, February 2022, sample not stated, https://www.itwire.com/telecoms-and-nbn/almost-50-of-brits-couldn%E2%80%99t-complete-half-a-day%E2%80%99s-work-without-the-internet.html, read). Times 0.65 because messages and meetings are easily deferred: 0.49.

baselineDays.basis: Days until the first regular drug runs out, at a random moment. This is a spread over the refill cycle and across people, not parameter uncertainty: lo and hi are the 5th and 95th percentile of that spread, and the engine should integrate over it (about 10% have under 3 days, 18% under 7, 33% under 14, 62% under 30). Anchors: 89.7% of households had a 3-day supply (BRFSS, https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm6136a1.htm); 82% of medication users aged 50-80 had 7 days (NPHA 2019, snippet only); refills are picked up with 3-9 days still in hand and roughly half of maintenance days come from 90-day fills (see .md).

hardship.basis: No willingness-to-pay study found. Built from a utility loss per day (about 0.03, 0.06 and 0.09 across the three steps, reflecting that most users of blood-pressure, lipid or thyroid drugs feel nothing for days while antidepressant, pain, reflux, stimulant and contraceptive users are affected sooner) times roughly $450 per quality-adjusted life-day, plus $5-10 a day of worry. Non-fatal events are a small addition at this risk level. 40% of US adults say they could not go more than a week without their regular medication before serious effects (Healthcare Ready 2022, https://healthcareready.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/July-Analysis_HcR-2022-Domestic-Preparedness-Poll-Summary_Final-7-18.pdf), which supports a material worry component.

mortality.basis: For a user aged 15-59 of non-critical regular drugs. Reasoning: such a user's all-cause risk is of the order of 10 micromorts a day; if their drugs prevent about 10% of it at steady state, full loss of effect costs about 1 a day, reached only after washout (blood pressure returns over days to two weeks, lipids over weeks), with antidepressant discontinuation adding risk in weeks 1-4. No trial measures this directly. Checked against Puerto Rico after Maria: with the multipliers below, 14.4% of households unable to get medication and about 15 unmet days each, the curve gives roughly 200 deaths, against 300-450 if medication was about 30% of the roughly 1,000-1,500 deaths attributed to interrupted care (https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/a-third-of-hurricane-maria-deaths-stemmed-from-healthcare-disruption-nejm/524517/). Texas 2021 recorded no deaths attributed to lack of drugs, as the curve predicts for a 2-4 day window.

workLoss.basis: Averaged over common drugs: most (statins, blood-pressure drugs) cause no symptoms in the first days; antidepressant discontinuation, asthma and pain drugs do; insulin is serious. Plus an hour or two on the first days chasing a supply. Gross 0.12 x 0.7. Guess.

hardship.basis: drugs.json: the two over-the-counter kits together relieve about $1.10 of hardship per person per day without a pharmacy.

mortality.basis: None claimed.

workLoss.basis: A cold costs a worker 8.7 work hours, 2.8 absent and 5.9 at reduced output (Bramley, Lerner and Sarnes 2002, J Occup Environ Med 44:822, abstract via Europe PMC); adults average two to three colds a year (https://www.cdc.gov/common-cold/about/index.html, read): 22 hours. Doubling for headaches, pain, stomach upsets and allergies gives about 45 hours, 2.5% of an 1,800-hour year. If over-the-counter drugs would relieve a fifth of that (my guess, 5-50%): 0.005.

baselineDays.basis: One 6 L flush per cistern, stretched by not flushing every use. If the sewer works and any water can be hauled (6 L per flush), the toilet keeps working; that is improvisation inside the curve, not baseline stock.

hardship.basis: FEMA gives no residential value for wastewater loss and says $0 is unlikely (https://fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_standard-economic-values-methodology-report_2023.pdf). I take toilet and hand-washing as roughly a third of FEMA's $66.26 welfare loss for all indoor water use (about $76 now), reached only after deferral runs out: $25 from day 4. Day 1 is low because one day without a flush is an inconvenience. Cross-check: Christchurch households lived with chemical toilets for months without leaving, so the daily cost sits below the cost of relocating.

mortality.basis: Bounded by Christchurch 2011 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3729075): 18 excess notified gastroenteritis cases; at 10-100 community cases per notification over 3-6 million person-days without sewerage that is 0.003-0.06% illness per person-day, x 5-15 deaths per million cases = 0.0002-0.01. An unpublished survey claiming a 14-fold rise would give about 0.3. Later steps rise because Christchurch had an organised response (toilets delivered, chlorination) that a long collapse would lack.

workLoss.basis: Improvising a bucket toilet, carrying waste, walking to a public toilet and hand hygiene: about an hour (0.3-2.5) a day. Gross 0.1 x 0.7. Guess.

baselineDays.basis: Wallet cash only: 76% of US consumers carry cash, mean $69 (Fed Diary 2026, https://www.frbservices.org/binaries/content/assets/crsocms/news/research/2026-diary-consumer-payments-choice.pdf), so two wallets hold roughly $60-140 against a need of $50 a day for 2.5 people. Euro-area median is 59 euros per person (about 2 days; ECB SPACE 2024); the 45% of US and 35% of euro-area consumers who keep a reserve (US mean $364) are already prepared and are not the baseline.

hardship.basis: No willingness-to-pay study found. Each step is the chance that the household must buy something that day times the value lost, plus time spent searching: days 1-2, 0.3 x $15 + $4 (the pantry is intact; in Spain's 28 April 2025 blackout spending fell 34% on the day but only 15% net after two days, https://www.caixabankresearch.com/es/analisis-sectorial/consumo/impacto-economico-del-apagon-detalle); days 3-7, 0.6 x $30 + $6 (after Helene a family of four with $80 could not cover fuel and food, and neighbours paid for each other, https://carolinapublicpress.org/66855/cash-only-economy-surprised-nc-helene-survivors/); days 8-30, 0.9 x $40; later, some adaptation through shop credit, barter and substitute currencies as in Argentina in 2002.

mortality.basis: No death in the Texas 2021, Hurricane Irma or Greek 2015 bank-closure records in prior-art.md is attributed to being unable to pay. The remaining path is an unbought drug or fuel, which is mostly counted on the medication and warmth needs.

workLoss.basis: Time spent searching for a working ATM, borrowing, arranging credit with shops or queueing: about half an hour a day (0.05-1.5 h). Gross 0.05 x 0.7. Freelancers who cannot be paid lose income but not output, so that is excluded. Guess.

baselineDays.basis: By definition nothing kept at home covers a day out of it. What an unprepared household falls back on (a relative's spare room, a credit card) is already inside the hardship curve, which is built from where displaced people in fact stay.

hardship.basis: Days 2-7 = money about $50 + lost income about $10 + discomfort about $30. Money: surveys cited in Jiang et al. 2023 (https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10447248) give $88 per evacuating household per day (Lili, 2002) and $83 (Katrina and Rita, 2005), about $160 and $140 at 2026 prices, or $54-63 per person at 2.6 people; a bottom-up check (27% in hotels at $113-178 a room (fiscal 2027 federal per diem and the October 2026 national average rate, both from search snippets) shared by 2.5 plus $25 food, 62% hosted at about $10, fuel $10) gives $38-44. FEMA values a displaced day at one GSA room per family plus meals per diem less $9 food at home (https://fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_standard-economic-values-methodology-report_2023.pdf), which is the all-hotel upper case of roughly $105 per person. Day 1 adds the journey out and back (6-10 hours per adult). Later steps fall as hotels give way to rentals and routine returns, and are guesses; discomfort is a guess throughout.

mortality.basis: Day 1 carries the journey: about 250 extra miles out and back at roughly 0.005 micromorts per occupant-mile (1.19 deaths per 100 million vehicle-miles in 2024 per an NHTSA search snippet; about 63% of them vehicle occupants and 1.5 occupants per vehicle, both from memory) is 1.2, rounded up for fatigue, smoke and chaotic traffic. Later days are a guess for stress, unfamiliar housing and, after a month, depression (Household Pulse: odds of depression 1.8 times higher after one to four weeks displaced, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12374215). Cross-check: with the multipliers below, a four-day evacuation of a normal age mix costs about 6 micromorts per evacuee; the Hurricane Rita evacuation, the worst on record, cost about 19 among people outside care homes (about 56 deaths in roughly 3 million).

workLoss.basis: Profile by day of displacement (guess): 0.8 for days 1-3 (leaving, travelling, finding lodging), 0.4 for days 4-14 (temporary lodging, insurance and aid paperwork, a borrowed or no workspace), 0.15 after day 14 (settled in temporary housing, working remotely). Weighted over lognormal lengths with median 5-10 days and 90th percentile 45-60 days (hazards-ordinary.json windows), mean 20-25 days: 0.28; with median 3 and 90th percentile 14: 0.49. Household Pulse Survey 2021-24: 43% of displaced households back within a week, 23% within a month, 20% longer, 14% not returned (Paul et al. 2025, Risk Analysis, https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10205868/, read).

baselineDays.basis: Nothing ordinary in a home replaces files that are out of reach. What a phone or a synced folder still holds is counted in the share of each window that opens the need (notes), not as days of cover.

hardship.basis: 27% of US paid workdays are worked from home (WFH Research via FRED, October 2026: 27.06%; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/WFHCOVIDMATQUESTION). If a fifth of those rely on the household's own computer or files, and a day without them costs about $100 after the work made up later, that is about $5 per working adult-day; with records, bills, schoolwork and personal projects ($1-2) and averaged over members, about $4 at first. It rises as bills, claims and deadlines are missed. Lo: almost everything is on the phone or the employer's machine. Hi: a self-employed member whose livelihood is on the computer.

mortality.basis: None: being without one's files is not dangerous. Records matter for health only through medication and emergency care, which are other needs.

workLoss.basis: Gross about 0.8 (0.5-0.95): most knowledge work needs one's own documents, mail and logins (see workLoss.information for the internet share, about three quarters); meetings by phone, reading and planning remain. Times 0.7 for work made up. Losing the computer itself adds a day or two of buying and restoring, which is in the range; losing data with no backup costs work permanently, which is not. Guess.

hardship.basis: None claimed.

mortality.basis: medical.json, trauma channel: between the slow-care and no-care rates.

workLoss.basis: The need's harm is the risk of dying of an emergency without care; on the great majority of such days nothing happens and no time is lost. Caring for an untreated injured household member is small in expectation. Guess.

localOutage.label: Local power cut
localOutage.definition: The home is completely without grid power for 6 hours or more from a cause that is not a regional disaster: equipment failure, vehicle strike, planned work, an ordinary thunderstorm or wind event, or a storm outage that ends within 12 hours. Outages of 12 hours or more caused by a regional storm, winter storm, heat wave, hurricane or wildfire shut-off belong to those hazards.

westernEurope.basis: CEER Benchmarking Report 6.1, Tables 7 and 15 (unplanned, including exceptional events, 2016): SAIDI Switzerland 9, Germany 13, Denmark 15, Austria 24, Italy 37, Great Britain 38, France 49, Spain 54, Portugal 64, Ireland 80 minutes; SAIFI 0.2-1.5. Population-weighted about 35 minutes and 0.7 interruptions a year. With a log-normal spread of durations (sigma 1.1-1.3, my assumption) about 3% of interruptions last 4 h or more: 0.7 x 0.03 = 2%, cut to 1.5-2% because repeat outages cluster on the same homes. System-wide blackouts add 1.15%: Italy 2003 (56M people) and Iberia 2025 (59M) among about 390M people over 25 years. https://ceer.eu/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/C18-EQS-86-03_Benchmarking_Report_6.1.pdf

buenosAires.basis: ENRE, September 2024 to February 2025 semester: Edenor SAIFI 1.39 and SAIDI 3.58 h, Edesur 4.12 and 7.37 h (https://econojournal.com.ar/?p=120080), so about 2.8 and 7-8.5 interruptions a year averaging 2.6 h and 1.8 h. City comunas had 25% (Edenor) and 60% (Edesur) of the company-wide frequency in ENRE semester 46 (https://www.argentina.gob.ar/sites/default/files/informesemestral_desempeno_edenoredesur_semana46.pdf): about 0.7 and 4.2 a year. With a log-normal spread of durations (sigma 1.2, my assumption) 17% and 10% of interruptions last 4 h or more, so 11% and 35% of households a year; weighted 45/55 by customers (my estimate) = 24%, or 26% with an exponential spread. Plus 5% for force-majeure blackouts that the ENRE headline figures leave out, less 7.5% counted under heatWave: 22-24%, rounded to 25% because Edesur's other semester looks worse (annual SAIDI 16.4 h). Suburbs: about 50%.

us.basis: AHS 2023: 25.4% of households had a complete outage in 12 months and about 70% of those had one of 6 h or more, so 17.7% (https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2024/10/power-outages.html). Minus 6.9% a year for regional-event outages of 12 h or more (EIA and NREL arithmetic in the .md) leaves about 11%. Urban 22.8% and rural 35.4% for any outage, so scale by 0.9 and 1.4.

pOccur.basis: True by the definition of the event.

power.basis: No source gives the duration distribution of non-major outages of 6 h or more. EIA 2015-2025: CAIDI without major event days is 109-124 minutes (https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_11_01.html); NREL assumes such outages end within 12 h (PNNL-33340). I assume 90% end within 12 h and 99% within about two days.

pOccur.basis: Home internet stops with the router, but mobile service normally continues on tower batteries and generators; both fail only in a minority of longer local outages. No measurement found.

comms.basis: Shorter than the power window because towers hold several hours of battery (recalled, not checked).

coldShare.basis: For a cold-winter household, the share of local outages on days cold enough to chill an unheated home. December to February is 25% of the year, but non-storm outages peak in summer (47% of weather-related major outages fall in May-September, Climate Central) and the worst winter outages sit under winterStorm.

hotShare.basis: For a hot-summer household: about 40% of outages fall in June to August (guess from the Climate Central seasonal share) times about 30% of summer days with dangerous heat.

feasible.basis: Power is on a short drive away. AHS 2023: 8.4% of households with any outage stayed away overnight (2.9M of 33.9M), so few bother, but nearly all could.

earliestDay.basis: Within an hour or two; longer at night or without a car.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: About 20 miles of driving at $0.70 a mile plus an hour of packing at $20.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Hotel: US average daily rate $177.65 in the week of 11-17 October 2026 (CoStar, https://www.hospitalitynet.org/news/4135070/us-hotel-results-for-week-ending-17-october) x 1.12 tax / 2.5 people + $15 of meals out = $95. Staying with relatives or friends: about $10. Blend 40% hotel, 60% hosts (44% of Texans who left in 2021 went to a local relative, UH survey) = $44.

staple.basis: No warning, but shops outside the small affected area are open and stocked once the outage starts; fails at night or without transport.

specialty.basis: A local event causes no regional run on generators, heaters or power stations, but few households buy one for an outage expected to end in hours.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: CPSC counts about 70 generator CO deaths a year, 157 in 11 years tied to weather outages (prior-art.md). 14 a year over about 59 million person-events of 6 h+ outages (17.7% x 335M) is 0.24 micromorts, concentrated in generator owners and long cold outages; I take a sixth of that for a short outage in a home without a generator.
Texas 2021 had 10 fire deaths over about 14 million people with long outages (0.7 micromorts) in extreme cold; a half-day outage in ordinary weather is guessed at 3% of that.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: AHS 2023: 14% of households with an outage of any length lost food (4.9M of 33.9M) and 1.0% had basement water from sump-pump failure (343,000). For 6 h+ outages I take 20% x $90 of food plus 0.5% x $4,000 of water damage; the dollar amounts are guesses.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

power.basis: At least 4 h (0.17 day) by definition. Anchored on the Iberian blackout, where Spain had 35% of demand back after 7.5 h, 61% after 11.5 h, 87% after 15.5 h and 99% after 17.5 h (Red Electrica figures in press, search snippets, https://www.energias-renovables.com/panorama/el-100-de-las-subestaciones-de-la-20250429), and on rare urban cable or substation failures of one to four days (Berlin 2019, 2025 and January 2026, recalled). Same shape as the United States pattern for routine outages but with a shorter tail.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

water.basis: Municipal supply only; loss of a building pump is handled by the pumped-water setting. Waterworks have standby power, so pressure is lost only in a minority of towns in a system-wide blackout (reports from Iberia conflict: one source lists water as uninterrupted, another says mains failed widely).

shareTreatable.basis: Mostly no flow rather than unsafe water; guess.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

comms.basis: Counted from when service is actually lost, not from the power cut. A neighbourhood fault leaves mobile coverage up; in a wide-area blackout cell-site batteries last two to four hours (more than half of mobile users in much of Spain lost all signal at the peak in April 2025, Ookla data quoted by GSMA, search snippet).

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

payments.basis: Cards and cash machines fail where the power is out; in a neighbourhood fault a working shop is a few streets away, so only wide-area blackouts count. Iberia 2025: shops shut or took cash only for about 10-16 h (press, search snippet).

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

food.basis: Shops closed during a wide-area blackout; never more than about a day.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

emergencyCare.basis: Congested emergency lines, stuck lifts and dark junctions slow ambulances during a wide-area blackout; guess.

coldShare.basis: About 35% of outages fall in the three winter months and about a third of winter days are dangerously cold in a cold-winter part of Western Europe: 0.35 x 0.35 = 0.12. The Iberian (April) and Italian (September) blackouts were in mild weather.

hotShare.basis: Dangerous heat covers 5-15 days a year (1.5-4% of days) in a hot-summer part of Western Europe; outages inside declared heat waves are counted under heatWave.

feasible.basis: A local fault leaves the rest of the city working, so nearly anyone can go to family or a hotel; in a system-wide blackout (about a third of these events) there is nowhere to go and transport stops. Guess.

earliestDay.basis: Leaving makes sense once it is clear the cut will last; a few hours.

staple.basis: No warning; ignored by the engine below half a day.

specialty.basis: No warning.

severeStorm.label: Severe storm
severeStorm.definition: A regional storm that is neither tropical nor a winter storm (derecho, tornado outbreak, severe thunderstorm complex, windstorm, atmospheric-river wind) and that leaves the home without grid power for 12 hours or more. Storm outages shorter than 12 hours count under localOutage.

westernEurope.basis: Customers cut off in named storms, divided by all customers and years. France: 3.45M (Lothar and Martin 1999), about 1.7M (Klaus 2009), about 1M (Xynthia 2010), 1.2M (Ciaran 2023) and smaller storms, about 10M over 27 years on 37M customers = 1.1% a year. Great Britain about 1.2% (Arwen about 1M, Eunice, St Jude, Darragh). Ireland about 8% (Ophelia 385,000, Darragh 395,000, Eowyn 768,000 on 2.4M customers in eight years). Portugal about 1.5% (Kristin about 1M of 6.4M). Germany, Italy, Spain, Benelux, Austria and Switzerland 0.2-0.5%. Population-weighted 0.74%. Counts other than Arwen, Eowyn and Kristin are recalled or from search snippets.

buenosAires.basis: The storm of 17 December 2023 cut power to about 400,000 users in the city and suburbs at the peak (government figure, search snippet), 7% of about 5.8M; the storm of 4 April 2012 was of similar reach (recalled). Storms that leave 50,000-200,000 users out (1-3%) come once or twice a year. That gives 4-6% a year for the metropolitan area; a city flat on underground low-voltage cables sees perhaps half or less.

us.basis: EIA 2015-2025: major event days add a mean 258 minutes and 0.33 interruptions per customer-year (https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_11_01.html). With NREL's major-event duration table (50.3% over 12 h; mean 27 h from my bin midpoints) that is 0.138 large outages a year, so 6.9% of customers a year with 12 h or more from all causes. I assign 35% to severe convective and wind storms (58% of weather-related major outage events by count, Climate Central, but shorter than hurricane and ice outages): 2.4%.

pOccur.basis: True by the definition of the event.

power.basis: NREL/PNNL 2022 Table 13, mean of the Central, Eastern and Western regions (little hurricane influence), conditional on exceeding 12 h: 65% exceed 1 day, 30% 2 days, 12% 3 days, 5.5% 4 days, 3.2% 5 days, 1.1% 7 days (https://www.pnnl.gov/main/publications/external/technical_reports/PNNL-33340.pdf). Log-linear interpolation gives p50 1.35 and p90 3.2. NREL's own p99 is about 7 days; raised to 9 because the authors say the method undercounts long outages and urge caution beyond 5 days.

pOccur.basis: Mains homes only: a storm-caused boil notice or loss of pressure. Treatment plants and pumping stations mostly have backup power; EPA attributes only 2.2% of 2021 boil-water advisories to power outages and 1.4% to natural disasters. Homes on wells or booster pumps are excluded here because the engine's pumped-water setting ties their tap to the power window.

water.basis: Net of relief: bottled water is on sale a short drive away within a day or two, well before a boil notice is lifted. No measurement of that delay was found.

shareTreatable.basis: Mostly boil notices with water still flowing; the rest is loss of pressure.

pOccur.basis: Share of events in which local shops are shut or unreachable for more than half a day: unpowered stores and roads blocked by trees. No US measurement found for non-winter storms.

food.basis: Net of relief: stores on generators and shops a short drive away are open within a day or two in ordinary US storms, far sooner than the last customers are reconnected.

pOccur.basis: Both mobile and home internet down. Upper analogue: Texas February 2021, where 47% lost mobile service and 71% internet (UH survey); ordinary wind storms damage fewer towers.

comms.basis: Mobile service usually returns before household power as carriers bring generators to towers; no duration data found.

pOccur.basis: Mains homes only: loss of water pressure or sewer backup when lift stations lose power. Pumped-water homes are handled by the engine's pumped-water setting.

sanitation.basis: Pressure is restored before boil notices are lifted.

pOccur.basis: Local pharmacies shut while unpowered; same reasoning as the food window.

medication.basis: A pharmacy a short drive away is open within a day or two.

pOccur.basis: Blocked roads and overloaded 911 delay ambulances in the first hours to a day of a major wind event.

emergencyCare.basis: Main roads are usually cleared within a day.

pOccur.basis: Shops that open on generators or without network often take cash only; ATMs are down with the power.

payments.basis: Ends as power and network return to shops, which are restored before most homes.

pOccur.basis: Homes made uninhabitable by tornado, wind or tree damage, as a share of households with a 12 h+ storm outage. Census Pulse data put all-cause disaster displacement at 1.3% of adults a year (base-rates.md); the tornado and wind share was not found.

displacement.basis: Pulse durations for all disasters: nearly half under a week, a tenth over six months (base-rates.md).

coldShare.basis: Severe convective storms are a warm-season hazard; only autumn and winter windstorms (Pacific Northwest, Northeast) coincide with cold.

hotShare.basis: 47% of weather-related major outages fall in May-September (Climate Central), and derechos peak in June and July; the June 2012 derecho was followed by a heat wave.

feasible.basis: The damaged area is tens of miles wide, so unaffected towns are within an hour or two, but local roads are blocked and nearby hotels fill. 42% say they would relocate in a 3-day outage (ICE 2.0, prior-art.md).

earliestDay.basis: After roads are cleared of trees and lines.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: About 100 miles of driving at $0.70 a mile, plus packing time.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Same blend as localOutage: hotel $95 a person-day from the $177.65 average daily rate (https://www.hospitalitynet.org/news/4135070/us-hotel-results-for-week-ending-17-october), hosts about $10, 40/60.

staple.basis: Few people shop on a severe-thunderstorm watch, and after the storm local shops are shut for the first day.

specialty.basis: Generators, fuel cans, ice and chainsaws sell out regionally within a day of a large event.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: NWS 2016-2025 means: 51 tornado and 57 wind deaths a year (https://www.weather.gov/media/hazstat/81year_2025.pdf). If 60% fall among the 8.4 million people a year in such events (2.5% x 335M) that is 7.7 micromorts; x 0.8 for a healthy adult in a site-built home. The 60% and 0.8 are guesses.

About 14 weather-outage generator CO deaths a year (CPSC, prior-art.md) over roughly 23 million person-events of 12 h+ outages (6.9% x 335M) is 0.6 micromorts averaged over all homes; a quarter of that without a generator, in warm weather.
Texas 2021: 10 fire deaths over about 14 million people with long outages, 0.7 micromorts, driven by improvised heating; a warm-season outage is guessed at a seventh of that.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Texas 2021: 47% reported spoiled food even in freezing weather (UH survey). I take 55% x $130 of fridge food, 25% x $200 of freezer food and 2% x $4,000 of basement water. Dollar amounts are guesses. ICE 2.0: 20% of households would lose income in a 3-day outage, mean $1,157 among them (prior-art.md); not included.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

power.basis: Share still without power, pooled over four storms of about a million customers each. After 1 day: Arwen 18% (Ofgem), Eowyn about 55%, Kristin and Ciaran about 45-50% (interpolated). After 3-4 days: Arwen 4%, Eowyn 27% (204,000 of 768,000). After 7 days: Arwen 0.4%, Eowyn 13%. After 14 days: Kristin 3% (30,000 of about 1M, E-Redes), Eowyn under 1%. Ciaran: 90% back within 5 days (Enedis, search snippet). Pooled 40%, 14%, 5% and 1%. https://ofgem.gov.uk/publications/ofgem-publishes-full-report-following-six-month-review-networks-response-storm-arwen https://www.thejournal.ie/around-100000-people-still-without-water-storm-eowyn-6605973-Jan2025/ https://www.e-redes.pt/en/news/2026/02/11/two-weeks-after-kristin-depression-970000-customers-power-restored

Far less common in large cities. Days are net of tankers and shops.

winterStorm.label: Winter storm
winterStorm.definition: A snow, ice or extreme-cold event that leaves the home without grid power, piped gas or its normal heating for 12 hours or more while it is below freezing outside.

westernEurope.basis: Exposed means a place with regular frost and snow: Germany, Benelux, Britain, Ireland, Austria, Switzerland, northern and upland France, Italy and Spain; about 130M households. Household-events over 25 years: Munsterland 2005 (about 100,000 households), Girona 2010 (220,000 customers), Northern Ireland 2010 (40,000 without water), Italy 2012 (120,000), Abruzzo 2017 (300,000), Britain and Ireland 2018 (about 330,000 without water or power), south-east France 2019 (330,000) = about 1.5M, plus about 2.5M households snowed in around Madrid in January 2021. 4M / 130M / 25 = 0.12% a year. Counts recalled or from search snippets.

buenosAires.basis: Exposed means the whole metropolitan area. Guess. Cold-wave gas emergencies came in May 2024 and July 2025; in both, industry and vehicle-gas stations were cut to protect homes, and no residential supply was cut in the city, but several thousand homes in Mar del Plata lost gas for more than a day in July 2025 (press, search snippets). Winter power faults during demand peaks are already inside the localOutage figure; this entry adds only the gas route and the coincidence with cold.

us.basis: Exposed = a place where a multi-day spell below freezing occurs in most winters (about 70% of US households, guess). AHS 2021 by metro, share uncomfortably cold for 24 h+ times share blaming a utility interruption: Atlanta 0.9%, Washington 0.7%, Chicago 0.9%, Boston 1.1%, Philadelphia 0.9%, Detroit 1.7%, Seattle 2.0% (https://stacker.com/stories/real-estate/how-heating-problems-compare-among-15-largest-metros). Median 0.9% / 0.65 for the 12 h threshold = 1.4%, plus a Uri-class year (Houston 45%, Dallas 32%) once in 50-100 years = 2.0%. Cross-check: 20% of the 6.9% all-cause rate, over 70% of households, is also 2.0%.

pOccur.basis: Nearly all such events are power failures; a few percent are gas-supply or fuel-delivery failures with the grid up.

power.basis: NREL/PNNL 2022 non-southern regional mean conditional on 12 h (p50 1.35, p90 3.2 days; see severeStorm), with the tail lengthened for ice storms, which NREL's 2015-2021 sample barely contains. Texas February 2021: mean 42 h and median 36 h without power among the 69% who lost it; longest single block mean 31 h (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf).

pOccur.basis: Piped-gas loss in cold snaps is rare in the US (wellhead freeze-offs in Texas 2021; a New Mexico outage in 2011, recalled). No frequency data found.

gas.basis: Gas relights are house by house and take days once pressure is lost (recalled from the 2011 New Mexico event).

pOccur.basis: Mains homes only (pumped-water homes are handled by the engine's setting). Texas 2021: 49% of residents lost running water and over 17 million were under boil notices (UH survey; https://journals.plos.org/water/article?id=10.1371/journal.pwat.0000137). Texas was about 27% of US winter-storm person-events in 2015-2025 (14M of 52M); weighting it at 0.55, other southern events (10%) at 0.4 and northern events (63%) at 0.05 gives 0.22. The last two rates are guesses.

water.basis: Texas 2021: median 48 h without running water; people with running water could not drink it for a mean 40 h in the survey week; 63% had difficulty getting bottled water; boil notices lasted a mean 8.0 days (range 1-36). Net of relief I count until shops and distribution sites work, about 2 to 5 days there.

shareTreatable.basis: Tap water under a boil notice, or snow and ice to melt, on about half the days; the rest are days with nothing from the tap and nothing to melt. Boiling or melting needs a heat source.

pOccur.basis: Texas 2021: 75% of all residents had difficulty obtaining food or groceries (UH survey); 'difficulty' is weaker than 'no way to obtain', so I take about two thirds of that for affected households.

food.basis: Roads are impassable and shops shut for the cold spell itself, usually 1 to 3 days; a multi-day driving ban as in Buffalo in December 2022 (recalled) sets the tail.

pOccur.basis: Texas 2021: 47% of all residents lost mobile service and 71% internet (UH survey); households with long outages will be somewhat above the 47%, other storms below.

comms.basis: Assumed to track the power window with towers restored somewhat earlier; no duration data found.

pOccur.basis: Mains homes with no running water (the water window above), less those able to flush with stored or melted water.

sanitation.basis: Follows loss of running water (Texas 2021 median 48 h).

pOccur.basis: Pharmacies shut or unreachable on ice; set a little below the food window because chains reopen early.

medication.basis: Same road and store closures as food.

pOccur.basis: Ambulances delayed or unable to reach homes on ice and snow; hospitals in Texas 2021 lost water pressure. No frequency data found.

emergencyCare.basis: Lasts while roads are impassable.

pOccur.basis: The few shops open during a regional outage are often cash-only.

payments.basis: Ends when shops regain power and network.

pOccur.basis: Burst pipes making the home unlivable. AHS 2023: 673,000 units had frozen pipes in outages, 2% of the 33.9M outage households; Texas 2021: 31% reported water damage and 29% difficulty finding a plumber.

displacement.basis: Repairs after a regional freeze queue for weeks because plumbers and materials are short.

coldShare.basis: True by the definition of the event.

hotShare.basis: Cannot coincide with heat.

feasible.basis: Texas 2021: 18% of residents left home when they lost power and heat; 44% of those went to a local relative and 3% left the state (UH survey). Icy roads make driving dangerous (22 crash deaths in Texas) and the affected area can be hundreds of miles wide.

earliestDay.basis: When roads are passable again; immediately for those with a warm house nearby.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: A longer drive than in a wind storm, in bad conditions.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Same blend as localOutage: hotel $95 a person-day from the $177.65 average daily rate (https://www.hospitalitynet.org/news/4135070/us-hotel-results-for-week-ending-17-october), hosts about $10, 40/60.

staple.basis: Texas 2021: 61% bought extra food and 58% bottled water before the storm (UH survey), so most who tried succeeded; shelves of bread, milk and water empty in the last day.

specialty.basis: Heaters, propane, firewood and generators sell out in the days before a forecast storm; only 10% of Texans bought generator fuel.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: Texas 2021: 19 CO deaths (DSHS, prior-art.md) over about 14 million people with 12 h+ outages (29.5M x 0.915 x 0.69 x 0.75) = 1.4 micromorts; halved to exclude generator deaths, which belong to the generator's side risk. Of those who stayed, 26% heated with a gas oven and 8% used a grill indoors (UH survey).
Texas 2021: 10 fire deaths over about 14 million people = 0.7 micromorts all ages; x 0.7 for a healthy adult.
Texas 2021: 22 vehicle and 9 fall deaths (DSHS, prior-art.md) over about 14 million people = 2.2 micromorts all ages; x 0.7 for a healthy adult, since falls are concentrated in the old.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Texas 2021: 31% of residents had water damage, an upper case for homes not built for cold. I take 8% x $2,500 of deductible or uninsured repair plus $60 of food and $40 of other losses.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

heatWave.label: Heat wave
heatWave.definition: Three or more consecutive days on which the outdoor heat index reaches about 40 C (105 F), or the local National Weather Service extreme-heat warning level, so that a home without working cooling stays at or above about 31 C indoors. The grid usually stays up.

westernEurope.basis: Exposed means lowland Western Europe south of about 52 N plus the hot interiors further north. Years with such a spell since 2015: nearly every year in Madrid, Rome and Milan; about half in Paris and Frankfurt (2015, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2022, 2025, recalled); about one in eight in London. Check: with the heat window below, 0.6 x about 65 all-ages micromorts = 39 a year under the cooling curve for people without air conditioning, against roughly 90-100 observed across Western Europe in 2024 (Italy 19,038, Spain 6,743, Germany 6,282, France 2,451 from a search snippet, plus my allowance of 4,500 for the rest, in 390M people) and 37-323 by country.

buenosAires.basis: Exposed means the whole metropolitan area. The weather service's own definition (maximum and minimum both above the 90th percentile, 32.3 C and 22 C, for three days) was met 17 times in 2005-2015, 1.5 a year (Chesini et al. 2019, https://www.scielo.br/j/csp/a/LQhDy3myvTsfK7vdNxyJckM/?lang=es). Spells at my stricter threshold: December 2013, January 2022, March 2023, February 2024, January 2025, December 2025 to January 2026 (all but the first recalled or from search snippets): six in thirteen summers, five of them in the last five. Check: 0.5 x about 50 all-ages micromorts = 25 a year under the cooling curve, against about 29 a year observed in the city in 2005-2015.

us.basis: Exposed = a place where warning-level heat occurs in most summers (South, Southwest, lower Midwest, mid-Atlantic). No household-level frequency was found; the figure is definitional. Check: with cooling.md's all-ages curve and the heat durations in `heat`, 0.5 a year gives about 17 micromorts a year per person without cooling, or roughly 350 deaths over an assumed 20 million such people, against perhaps 500-900 certified indoor heat deaths a year (recalled CDC totals, not checked).

pOccur.basis: Climate Central: 48 heat-caused major outages in 2000-2023, two a year. At a guessed 300,000 customers each that is 0.4% of customers a year, mostly rotating cuts of an hour or two. AHS 2023: 1.0% of households (1.3M) with air conditioning were uncomfortably hot for 24 h+ because of a power cut of any cause, storms included. I take 0.5% a year for a heat-driven cut of 6 h or more, which is 1% of events at 0.5 a year.

power.basis: Local transformer and feeder failures are repaired within hours to a day; the tail is a network failure such as Queens in July 2006 (about a week, recalled). A city-wide multi-day blackout in a heat wave has not happened in the US and belongs to gridLong.

pOccur.basis: Ambulance and emergency-room overload at the peak of record heat (British Columbia and the Pacific Northwest, June 2021, recalled); not seen in ordinary US heat waves.

emergencyCare.basis: Lasts for the peak days of the event.

Length of the dangerous heat itself, during which a home without working cooling has unmet cooling days whatever the grid does. British Columbia 2021 lasted 7 days and France 2003 about 12 (cooling.md); the hottest US climates run longer.

hotShare.basis: True by the definition of the event.

feasible.basis: Cooled places (relatives, libraries, malls, cooling centres, motels) are within reach of most homes; the people who die are those who do not go. Visiting cool places has an odds ratio of 0.34 for death (cooling.md).

waterSystemFailure.label: Tap water failure
waterSystemFailure.definition: The public water system serving the home issues a boil-water, do-not-drink or do-not-use notice covering the home, or loses pressure, for 24 hours or more, when no hurricane, earthquake, flood or winter storm is under way. Private wells are excluded; their failures follow power outages.

westernEurope.basis: Ireland is the regional worst: boil notices covered about 189,000 people in 2025 and 254,000 in 2023, 3.5-4.8% of the population (EPA figures in press, search snippets). England and Wales: Franklaw 2015 (about 300,000 households), the March 2018 thaw (about 200,000), Hampshire 2024 (58,000), Brixham 2024 (17,000), Tunbridge Wells 2025 (24,000) and others, about 0.7M household-events in 11 years on 25M households = 0.25% a year (counts recalled or from search snippets). Germany, the Netherlands and northern France are similar or lower; southern Italy and parts of Spain higher (Messina 2015, Sicily 2024). Mid 0.6%.

buenosAires.basis: Guess. AySA reports low pressure or loss of supply over wide areas several times a year: after power failures at plants and pumping stations (June 2019, March 2025, 15 January 2026), burst mains, low river levels at the intakes and annual intake cleaning. Most last under a day and are absorbed by the roof tank; I put events of 24 hours or more for a given building at one in 25 years, more in the outer suburbs.

us.basis: No national count of people affected exists: EPA found 4,036 advisories for 2021 from 20 responding states and web searches, and states need not report (EPA 810-R-24-003). Kentucky alone logged 36,673 in 2004-2020, about 2,160 a year (search snippet, https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4441/16/3/443). My estimate: 30,000 advisories a year x 300 people = 9 million person-events, 2.7% of 335 million, plus 0.2-0.5% for city-wide failures (Jackson, Houston, Austin, Memphis, Richmond, recalled). Both multipliers are guesses.

pOccur.basis: Share of events large enough that local shops are stripped of bottled water, or in which the household cannot shop the same day. 80% of advisories are main breaks or pressure loss covering part of a system (EPA), where shops nearby stay stocked.

water.basis: Net of relief: the days before bottled water can be bought or collected. Jackson 2022: most residents lost running water on 30 August and the National Guard began distributing water on 31 August (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson,_Mississippi_water_crisis). The advisory itself runs far longer; see grossDays.

shareTreatable.basis: Tap water keeps flowing and boiling or disinfecting suffices on most advisory days. Subtract about 8% for days with no flow (Jackson 2022: 5 of 49 days) and about 4% for chemical contamination that treatment at home does not fix (Flint, Toledo 2014, Charleston 2014, recalled).

coldShare.basis: Seasonal coincidence only; main breaks cluster in freeze-thaw weather. Heating still works, so this should not create unmet warmth days.

supplyShock.label: Shortages in shops
supplyShock.definition: With no physical damage where the household lives, for 7 days or more local shops are out of several staple categories at once (at least a tenth of an ordinary grocery basket unobtainable on a given trip), or most local fuel stations are dry: panic buying, a pipeline, port or trucking stoppage, or a fuel crisis.

westernEurope.basis: Episodes by country since 2000: Britain three (fuel protests 2000, March 2020, fuel 2021) = 0.12 a year; France five (fuel depot strikes 2010, 2016, 2022, 2023 and March 2020) = 0.19; Spain two (March 2020, hauliers' strike March 2022) = 0.08; Germany, Italy and the Netherlands one or two = 0.04-0.08. Medicine shortages (antibiotics and children's paracetamol in winter 2022-23) add a little. Recalled apart from the British fuel crisis and March 2020.

buenosAires.basis: Episodes since 2001: December 2001 and 2002 (looting, shuttered shops), the 2008 farm lock-out (meat and dairy), March 2020, early 2022 (import-restricted goods), August 2019 and August 2023 (devaluations after primary elections: suppliers stopped deliveries, purchase limits, looting in August 2023), October 2023 (fuel), December 2023 (medicines): eight or nine in 25 years = 0.32-0.36. Some were mild in the city itself; mid 0.25. Mostly recalled; 2023 from search snippets.

us.basis: Count of episodes a US household met in 55 years, recalled rather than read: fuel crises of 1973-74 and 1979, the March 2020 panic, and the May 2021 Colonial Pipeline shutdown (about 15% of the population): about 3.2 in 55 years, 6% a year. The 2022 infant-formula shortage hit only households with infants; the October 2024 port strike lasted 3 days and stays below the threshold.

pOccur.basis: A true food window (no way to obtain any food) did not occur for ordinary households in March 2020: specific goods were missing, not calories. The small probability covers households that could not shop at all for some days (no fuel in a fuel shock, purchase limits and queues, no delivery slots).

food.basis: Partial shortage, not a window: see `partial`. About 12% (5-25%) of an ordinary basket was unobtainable for 2-4 weeks in March-April 2020 and single categories (toilet paper, sanitiser, flour, some canned goods) for 4-8 weeks.

coldShare.basis: Seasonal coincidence only; power and heating work, so it should not create unmet warmth days unless heating oil or propane deliveries are what is short.

hotShare.basis: Seasonal coincidence only; cooling works.

feasible.basis: A national shock leaves nowhere better to go; a regional fuel shock can be left only by a household with fuel in the tank.

earliestDay.basis: A day to decide and travel out of the affected region.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: A drive of a few hundred miles at $0.70 a mile.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Same blend as localOutage: hotel $95 a person-day from the $177.65 average daily rate (https://www.hospitalitynet.org/news/4135070/us-hotel-results-for-week-ending-17-october), hosts about $10, 40/60.

specialty.basis: The goods the shock is about (respirators and sanitiser in 2020, fuel cans in 2021, a particular formula in 2022) are gone first.

hardshipUsdPerPerson.basis: One to two extra hours a week of searching and queuing for 4-6 weeks at $20 an hour, shared among 2.5 people, is $30-100 a person; no survey of this cost was found.
