hurricane.label: Hurricane
hurricane.definition: A tropical storm or hurricane brings sustained tropical-storm-force wind (39 mph or more), storm surge or flooding rain to the home's area, so that the household loses power for six hours or more, is put under an evacuation order, or has its home damaged or cut off. Calibrated on the Gulf and Atlantic mainland; Puerto Rico and other islands have a far longer tail (Maria) and are not covered.

us.basis: Exposed = home in a Gulf or Atlantic coastal county. NOAA: a hurricane passes within 50 nautical miles every 5-7 years in south Florida, coastal North Carolina and southeast Louisiana and every 30-50 years in New England (https://www.noaa.gov/stories/what-are-chances-hurricane-will-hit-my-home). I take about 9%/yr for the Gulf and Southeast and 2.5%/yr for the mid-Atlantic and Northeast, half the exposed population each: 5.75%, rounded to 6%. Check: Pulse counts 0.84M-1.9M adults displaced by hurricanes a year, 1.5-3% of exposed adults, which needs an event rate of this size if a quarter to a third of events displace.

pOccur.basis: Share of households inside the tropical-storm-force wind field that lose power for six hours or more; Irma cut power to about two thirds of Florida customers (recalled, not checked).

power.basis: NREL/PNNL 2022 as read in step 2 base-rates (https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy23osti/83092.pdf): of hurricane major-event outages 52% exceed 1 day, 33% exceed 3 days and 2.5% exceed 7 days, a mean of about 2.2 days. My own tally of Florida storms in 2016-2025 (customer counts recalled from utility and press reports) gives about 2.8 days per affected customer. The engine's curve through 1.5 / 6 / 16 has a mean of 2.6 days; the 99th percentile sits above NREL's roughly 9 days because Ida, Laura, Michael and Helene left core areas dark for two to four weeks.

pOccur.basis: Tap water absent or under a boil notice. Large systems usually hold (Houston in Harvey) but smaller ones fail: Beaumont in Harvey, Lee County in Ian, Jefferson Parish in Ida, Asheville in Helene. No denominator found.

water.basis: Boil notices and pressure loss mostly clear in days; Beaumont about 10 days, Asheville about 53 days without potable water (both recalled, not checked). Pulse: 31% of displaced adults reported some or a lot of drinking-water shortage in the first month (https://andrewrumbach.substack.com/p/unpacking-the-us-census-data-on-natural-a97), which is before relief is netted out.

shareTreatable.basis: Most such days are boil-water notices with the tap still running; the rest are dry taps, though rainwater and floodwater can then be treated.

pOccur.basis: Shops shut and roads closed around landfall for most households in the wind field.

food.basis: Shops reopen on generators and relief points open within two to four days in typical storms. Pulse: 36% of displaced adults had some or a lot of food shortage in the first month (https://andrewrumbach.substack.com/p/unpacking-the-us-census-data-on-natural-a97); eight days after Andrew 27% of households relied on relief food (step 2 prior-art), so relief was reaching them.

pOccur.basis: Piped gas survives wind; it is shut off where surge or flood reaches the mains (New Jersey barrier islands after Sandy, recalled).

gas.basis: Flooded mains must be purged and each appliance relit; weeks, not days.

pOccur.basis: Pharmacies close with the shops and stay shut while power is out; emergency-refill rules help only before landfall.

medication.basis: Chain pharmacies reopen on generators within days; in destroyed cores (Mexico Beach, Fort Myers Beach) it takes weeks. No national series found.

pOccur.basis: Ambulance crews are held back once sustained winds pass about 45 mph, and flooded roads block access afterwards.

emergencyCare.basis: Half a day of suspended response is routine; 12% of Ian deaths were attributed to delayed or unreachable medical care (press reports of medical-examiner data, unverified). Days where surge or flood isolates an area.

pOccur.basis: Card terminals and ATMs fail with power and telecoms while some shops trade for cash.

payments.basis: Tracks the power window in the areas where shops reopen before the grid does.

pOccur.basis: Both mobile and home internet out. FCC outage reports showed well over half of cell sites down in the worst counties of Michael, Ian and Helene but under 10% in Houston during Harvey (recalled, not checked).

comms.basis: Most sites return within a week; mountain and barrier-island areas took two to three weeks.

pOccur.basis: Sewer lift stations fail without power or the home floods; Pulse: about 14% of displaced adults reported a lot of unsanitary conditions (https://andrewrumbach.substack.com/p/unpacking-the-us-census-data-on-natural-a97).

sanitation.basis: Follows the water and power windows; weeks where the sewer system itself is damaged.

pOccur.basis: Pulse: hurricanes displaced 1.9M adults in 2022 and over 0.84M in 2023 (https://andrewrumbach.substack.com/p/unpacking-the-us-census-data-on-natural ; https://weather.com/news/weather/news/2024-02-22-disasters-displaced-millions-in-2023). Against 47M-62M exposed adults that is 1.4%-4% a year, about 2% in a middling year; 2% / 6% = 0.33, shaded to 0.3 because some of those moves were voluntary and the engine handles them as leaving.

displacement.basis: Census Household Pulse, Dec 2022-Oct 2023 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12374215): of 2.43M displaced adults, 43% were away under a week, 25% a week to a month, 11% one to six months, 7% over six months and 14% never returned. Counting never-returned as resettled within six months gives roughly 9 / 140 / 600 days. I shorten that to 7 / 90 / 540 for hurricanes because most hurricane displacement is an ordered evacuation of two to six days that Pulse under-counts, and because Pulse's long tail (24% out over six months or never back in 2022) is several times the number of homes destroyed. Engine mean: 38 days.

coldShare.basis: Season is June to November; only late storms in the Northeast (Sandy, 29 October) are followed by cold.

hotShare.basis: Peak season is August to October on the Gulf and Southeast coasts, where outages mean no air conditioning in heat: 17 of 129 Irma deaths were heat-related (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/67/wr/mm6730a5.htm, via step 2).

feasible.basis: Days of warning and open roads before landfall; the remainder lack a car, money, mobility or somewhere to go. Phone data put Irma evacuation at 58% inside mandatory zones (search snippet, unverified), so most who stay choose to.

earliestDay.basis: Leaving is possible before the event starts; for those who wait, roads are blocked for one to three days afterwards.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Fuel for a 300-600 mile round trip plus lost time. Gellman et al. (https://jacobgellman.github.io/files/gellman_et_al_2024-cost_hurricane_evacuations.pdf) estimate a welfare cost of $343 per person evacuating under a mandatory order at Category 4-5 winds and $117 at Category 3, excluding lodging; fixed $250 plus my per-day figure gives about $560 for 2.5 people over 3.5 days, inside that range.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Whitehead et al. 2000, quoted in Gellman et al.: 16% of evacuees used a hotel, 6% a shelter, 70% friends or family. 0.25 x $85 (a $150 room shared by 2.5 people plus $25 of meals out) + 0.75 x $15 = $32.

staple.basis: Shops stay open and restock for two to three days but bottled water, bread, batteries and fuel run out in waves: GasBuddy reported 36-43% of Miami-area stations and 41-58% of Gainesville stations without fuel two to three days before Irma (search snippets of https://www.npr.org/2017/09/08/549536604/as-hurricane-irma-nears-gasoline-is-in-short-supply-for-floridians, page timed out).

specialty.basis: Generators, power stations, propane, fuel cans and plywood are gone within the first day of a watch in the forecast cone. No data found.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: Mainland storms 2000-2024 killed roughly 3,000 people, directly and indirectly (my sum of recalled NHC and CDC counts, about 1,400 of them Katrina; Gellman et al. list 369 for 2019-2023, https://jacobgellman.github.io/files/gellman_et_al_2024-cost_hurricane_evacuations.pdf): 120 a year over 60-80M exposed is 1.5-2 micromorts a year, or about 30 per event at 6%/yr. Half is direct, plus a fifth for clean-up and crashes: about 20; times 0.5-0.6 for ages 15-59, since nearly 60% of Katrina dead were over 65 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19187485/) though only 29% of Harvey dead were (https://nhess.copernicus.org/articles/18/1073/2018/): about 10.

hardshipUsdPerPerson.basis: About 1.5% of people hurt badly enough to need care, at $4,000 of treatment cost, lost time and pain each. No source; post-storm household surveys commonly report a few percent of households with an injury.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Bottom-up: 4.5% of apartments with serious contents damage x $8,000 x 75% uninsured (49% of renters hold a policy, FinHealth 2023 via search snippet, https://finhealthnetwork.org/research/climate-disaster-and-renters-insurance-whos-protected/, and no renters policy covers flood) = $270, plus a flooded car without comprehensive cover, about $80, plus small losses of $100-150: about $500. Top-down from uninsured residential flood loss in Harvey and Ian (recalled industry estimates) gives nearer $1,000 for renters as a whole. I take $600.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

earthquake.label: Earthquake
earthquake.definition: Ground shaking of Modified Mercalli intensity VII or more at the home (peak acceleration above roughly 0.2 g): strong enough to damage ordinary buildings, break pipes and cut power. Shaking that is only felt does not count.

westernEurope.basis: Exposed means a high-hazard zone: Italian seismic zones 1 and 2 (the Apennines, Calabria, eastern Sicily, Friuli; about 23M people), and smaller areas around Granada and Murcia, Lisbon and the Algarve, the Pyrenees and Basel. Italy 1976-2025: Friuli, Irpinia, Umbria-Marche, Molise, L'Aquila, Emilia and central Italy left about 600,000 people homeless (recalled; L'Aquila 55,000-65,000 and Amatrice 4,500 from search snippets): 12,000 a year / 23M = 0.05% a year made homeless; three to five times as many feel damaging shaking: 0.15-0.25%.

buenosAires.basis: Essentially absent. The city lies in the national code's lowest seismic zone (recalled); the only damaging shock on record is the Rio de la Plata earthquake of 5 June 1888, about magnitude 5.5, which cracked walls (recalled). One event of intensity VII in perhaps 30,000 years is a guess entered so that the model does not fall back on another location's figure.

us.basis: Exposed = the 28 million people in the USGS high-potential tier, who meet 0.1 g (intensity VI) about once in 72 years, 1.4%/yr, as a floor (Jaiswal et al. 2015: tier sizes read at https://www.usgs.gov/news/nearly-half-americans-exposed-potentially-damaging-earthquakes, the 0.1 g and 1-in-72 figures from a search snippet of https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70155520). Intensity VII needs about twice the acceleration, two to three times rarer at a given site, but the Los Angeles and Bay Area cores lie well above the floor. History: about 8M person-exposures to VII+ in 1971-2025 among about 20M high-hazard Californians is 0.7%/yr in a quiet half-century (my count). For the 57M in the moderate tier (Salt Lake City, Memphis, Charleston, Portland) use 0.1-0.3%.

pOccur.basis: Northridge blacked out all 1.4M LADWP customers and about 1M Edison customers, the whole intensity-VII zone (https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/local/timeline-the-northridge-earthquake/1977528/ for LADWP; the Edison count is recalled). Smaller quakes (Napa, Anchorage) cut power to a minority.

power.basis: Northridge: nearly half of LADWP customers restored by noon on day 1, Edison down to 150,000 that afternoon, all but 7,500 in Los Angeles by day 4 (https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/local/timeline-the-northridge-earthquake/1977528/). Christchurch still had about 150 homes dark after a month (https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/canterbury-earthquake/71075/restoring-last-of-services-after-quake-%27most-difficult%27). Tail for a Hayward or San Andreas rupture.

pOccur.basis: Dry taps plus boil-water notices. Northridge: about 36,000 LADWP customers dry on day 4 and 10,000 households on day 6 (https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/local/timeline-the-northridge-earthquake/1977528/), a few percent of the shaken area, with boil notices far wider. Christchurch lost water in most of the city.

water.basis: Northridge taps were back in one to two weeks. Christchurch reached 95% of residents after one month with the boil notice still in force (https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/canterbury-earthquake/71075/restoring-last-of-services-after-quake-%27most-difficult%27). The USGS HayWired scenario gives East Bay residents six weeks to six months (press reports of https://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/2021/3054/fs20213054.pdf, unverified).

shareTreatable.basis: Half the days are boil notices with water still flowing; the rest are broken mains, when only tankers, pools and water heaters are left.

pOccur.basis: Northridge: on day 6 service had been restored to 40,000 homes with at least as many still out (https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/local/timeline-the-northridge-earthquake/1977528/), so 80,000 or more of about a million households in the shaken area. Most were customers shutting their own valve.

gas.basis: Each appliance must be relit by the utility: one to two weeks after Northridge. Sendai's city gas took about five weeks in 2011 (recalled).

pOccur.basis: Shops close for clean-up, inspection and lack of power; damaged bridges and overpasses cut some districts off.

food.basis: Shops outside the damage zone are an hour away once roads are checked, and relief arrives within about three days in a rich country.

pOccur.basis: Pharmacies close with other shops; there was no chance to refill beforehand.

medication.basis: No data found; set a little longer than food because fewer outlets carry a given drug.

pOccur.basis: Emergency lines and hospitals are swamped at once; Northridge treated and released 2,300 people and admitted over 500 in the first day (https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/local/timeline-the-northridge-earthquake/1977528/) and several hospitals were evacuated.

emergencyCare.basis: The surge passes within a day or two unless hospitals are themselves out of action.

pOccur.basis: Follows power and telecoms where shops reopen first.

payments.basis: Follows the power window.

pOccur.basis: Networks congest immediately, and cell sites on four to eight hours of battery fail where power stays off.

comms.basis: Follows the power window; text messages usually get through sooner than calls.

pOccur.basis: Needs both water and intact sewers. Rare at intensity VII, common where the ground liquefies.

sanitation.basis: Christchurch: a month after the February 2011 quake about a quarter of households still had no working toilet (https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/canterbury-earthquake/71075/restoring-last-of-services-after-quake-%27most-difficult%27); the eastern suburbs used chemical toilets for many months (recalled).

pOccur.basis: Northridge left about 20,000 homeless (USGS, search snippet) of roughly 3M people at intensity VII+, under 1%, plus tenants of several thousand red- and yellow-tagged buildings. HayWired projects 77,000-152,000 displaced households in a region of about 2.6M (press reports, unverified). Christchurch lost roughly a tenth of its housing.

displacement.basis: Earthquake displacement is by damage, not by order, so the short evacuations that dominate the Pulse split (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12374215) are missing: only its longer classes apply. Repair or rebuilding takes months to years. Engine mean: 89 days.

coldShare.basis: Earthquakes ignore the season, so this is the share of the year with dangerous cold where winters are cold (Seattle, Anchorage, Reno, Salt Lake City).

hotShare.basis: Share of the year with dangerous heat in hot-summer places (inland southern California, the Central Valley).

feasible.basis: Bridges and overpasses close, fuel pumps lack power and a great earthquake damages everything within driving range; after an ordinary damaging quake the unaffected area is an hour away.

earliestDay.basis: Roads have to be inspected and cleared first.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Fuel and a lost day or two for a 100-300 mile round trip.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Same lodging mix as for hurricanes (https://jacobgellman.github.io/files/gellman_et_al_2024-cost_hurricane_evacuations.pdf) but with hotels nearby full.

staple.basis: Follows from zero warning: nothing can be bought before an event that is not foreseen.

specialty.basis: Follows from zero warning: nothing can be bought before an event that is not foreseen.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: Northridge: 33 injury deaths in Los Angeles County (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9698136/), 57 in all (https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/local/timeline-the-northridge-earthquake/1977528/), over roughly 3M people at intensity VII+: 11-19 micromorts. My recalled comparisons: Loma Prieta 63 deaths over about 1.5M (40, mostly one viaduct), Whittier Narrows 8, Napa 7, Anchorage 2018 0, Christchurch 185 over 370,000 (500). Scenarios: HayWired 800 deaths over 3-4M (200-270). Weighting ordinary events at about 10 and one in ten at 200 gives about 30 at all ages, a little less for adults under 60.

hardshipUsdPerPerson.basis: Northridge: 138 hospital admissions (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9698136/) and 7,000-9,000 treated injuries (USGS and press, search snippets) over about 3M is 0.3% needing care, at about $8,000 each, $25; plus minor injuries to several percent at $200 each.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Contents worth about $25,000 with damage of roughly 2-5% at intensity VII, 5-15% at VIII and more at IX (my reading of loss-model damage ratios, not checked): about 6% on average, $1,500. About 5% of insured California renters, themselves a third to a half of renters, held earthquake cover in 2016 (CEA blog, search snippet, https://portal.earthquakeauthority.com/blog/2018/helping-protect-bay-area-renters), so essentially all of it is uninsured.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

power.basis: Restored within days outside the collapsed centres; guess. Same pattern as a moderate United States earthquake.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

gas.basis: Networks are shut for safety and reopened street by street after inspection; one to three months in L'Aquila (recalled).

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

water.basis: Broken mains; days are net of tankers. Guess.

shareTreatable.basis: Guess.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

food.basis: Italian civil protection has field kitchens running within one to three days; guess.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

comms.basis: Congestion at once, then loss of sites; guess.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

payments.basis: Guess.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

medication.basis: Guess.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

emergencyCare.basis: Local hospitals damaged or overwhelmed (the L'Aquila hospital was evacuated, recalled).

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.
Same evidence as this window's basis.

displacement.basis: Homes are closed until inspected; in L'Aquila tens of thousands stayed out for years and parts of the centre for more than a decade (recalled).

coldShare.basis: Apennine towns are cold from November to April: L'Aquila was in April with frost at night, the January 2017 shocks came during heavy snow. Guess.

hotShare.basis: Amatrice was in August. Guess.

feasible.basis: The damaged area is tens of kilometres across; the state houses people in hotels on the coast.

earliestDay.basis: Once roads are checked.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Return travel for the household to relatives or a hotel, about EUR 60 (EUR 10-300) by train or car; my estimate, no price page read. Scaled by 1.5 here because the affected area is wide and nearby rooms are scarce. EUR 1 = USD 1.099 (ECB reference rate for 19 Nov 2026, https://api.frankfurter.dev/v1/latest?from=EUR&to=USD,GBP).

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Half of a EUR 110 double hotel room plus EUR 20 of extra meals = EUR 75 a person a day; EUR 10 when staying with family, EUR 145 at peak prices; my estimate, no price page read. Scaled by 1.5 here because the affected area is wide and nearby rooms are scarce. EUR 1 = USD 1.099 (ECB reference rate for 19 Nov 2026, https://api.frankfurter.dev/v1/latest?from=EUR&to=USD,GBP).

staple.basis: No warning.

specialty.basis: No warning.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: Italian earthquake deaths since 1990: 11 + 30 + 309 + 27 + 299 + 2 = 678 (recalled, the two large figures from search snippets) = 19 a year / 23M exposed = 0.85 micromorts a year; divided by 0.002 events a year = 420 per event. L'Aquila alone: 309 / about 100,000 strongly shaken = 3,000; Emilia 2012: 27 / about 500,000 = 54.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Guess. Earthquake insurance is rare in Italy; the state pays for most reconstruction, slowly.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

power.basis: Scaled-down copy of the Western Europe profile; no local evidence exists.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.
Same evidence as this window's basis.

water.basis: Scaled-down copy; guess.

shareTreatable.basis: Guess.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

emergencyCare.basis: Guess.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

coldShare.basis: Guess.

hotShare.basis: Guess.

feasible.basis: Guess.

earliestDay.basis: Guess.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Taxi or remis across the city, or fuel and tolls to relatives outside it, about ARS 40,000 (ARS 8,000-190,000); my estimate, no price page read. Scaled by 1.5 for this hazard. USD 1 = ARS 1,585 (official retail selling rate, 19 Nov 2026, https://dolarapi.com/v1/dolares/oficial).

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Half of a three-star double room listed at ARS 77,000-128,000 a night (Despegar listings seen in a search snippet, https://www.despegar.com.ar/hoteles/hl/982/s3/i1/hoteles-3-estrellas-en-buenos+aires) = USD 24-40, plus about ARS 15,000 (USD 9) of extra meals; USD 5 when staying with family, which is the usual choice. Scaled by 1.5 for this hazard. USD 1 = ARS 1,585 (official retail selling rate, 19 Nov 2026, https://dolarapi.com/v1/dolares/oficial).

staple.basis: No warning.

specialty.basis: No warning.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: Copied from Western Europe: the building stock has no seismic design, so it would behave like old European stock or worse. Guess.

wildfire.label: Wildfire or heavy smoke
wildfire.definition: A wildfire puts the home under an evacuation order or warning, or brings at least three days of heavy smoke there (daily wildfire PM2.5 above about 55 micrograms per cubic metre, an air-quality index of 151 or more). About nine events in ten are smoke alone; the evacuation cases are the worst tenth.

westernEurope.basis: Exposed means a home in or beside forest or scrub in Portugal, Spain, southern France, Italy or Greece; not a city-centre flat. Evacuations: more than 42,000 residents in Spain in 2025; 320,000-330,000 in France and Spain by late July 2026, of whom 110,000-220,000 in the Gironde (press, search snippets); about 36,000 in the Gironde in 2022 and 19,000 on Rhodes in 2023 (recalled). That is of the order of 100,000 a year over the last decade, against an exposed population I put at 10-40 million (no source).

buenosAires.basis: Exposed means the whole metropolitan area (smoke only). Smoke episodes in the city: April 2008 (delta fires from 5 April over about 207,000 ha; smoke closed roads and stopped landings at the city airport for days), 2020 and August 2022 (smell of smoke across the city and northern suburbs): three notable episodes in 18 years, one of them severe. Search snippets and recall.

us.basis: Exposed = home in the western wildland-urban interface. Smoke: over 8M people a year had at least one day above 100 micrograms of smoke PM2.5 in 2016-2020, up 27-fold in a decade (https://phys.org/news/2022-09-wildfire-unraveling-decades-air-quality.html); that is about 10% of the 78M people in the Census West region (recalled), and I take 12% for interface homes, which lie nearer the fires. Evacuation: 1.1M Californians were ordered out in 2017-2019 (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5w85z07g); my tally for 2017-2025 is about 250,000 a year in California and 50,000 elsewhere, over some 22M interface residents: 1.3%/yr (0.4-3%). Sum 13%.

pOccur.basis: Evacuation rate 1.3%/yr divided by event rate 13%/yr. Compliance is high: 3-13% of those ordered out stayed (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5w85z07g).

displacement.basis: Wong et al. surveys: most evacuees were away one to eight days and 3-32% came back two weeks or more after the fire began (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5w85z07g). The 11 fires destroyed over 30,000 structures for 1.1M ordered out, so roughly one evacuated household in twenty lost its home and was out for a year or more. That is shorter in the middle and longer in the tail than the Pulse split (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12374215), whose fire category is mostly house fires. Engine mean: 21 days.

pOccur.basis: Precautionary shut-offs in fire weather and burnt lines. California's October 2019 shut-offs reached over 2M people (recalled).

power.basis: Shut-offs last one to five days, until wind drops and lines are inspected.

pOccur.basis: Systems that lose pressure in a burn-over draw in combustion products: Santa Rosa, Paradise, Lahaina, Altadena and Pacific Palisades all had do-not-drink orders (recalled).

water.basis: Weeks for neighbourhoods at the edge of a burn, a year or more inside it.

shareTreatable.basis: The contaminants are benzene and other volatile organics, which boiling and ordinary filters do not remove.

pOccur.basis: Shops stay open through smoke; they close in shut-off areas and behind road blocks.

food.basis: Short and local.

pOccur.basis: As food, plus prescriptions left behind in a rushed evacuation, which the displacement need should carry.

medication.basis: Short and local.

pOccur.basis: Crews are committed to the fire and roads are closed in the threatened zone.

emergencyCare.basis: Lasts while the fire front is active nearby.

pOccur.basis: Cash-only trading during power shut-offs.

payments.basis: Follows the power window.

pOccur.basis: Burnt lines and towers, and cell sites running out of battery in shut-offs.

comms.basis: Follows the power window; weeks where towers burn.

coldShare.basis: Fire season is summer and autumn; winter wind-driven fires (Marshall, December 2021; Los Angeles, January 2025) are the exception.

hotShare.basis: Smoke and shut-offs coincide with heat waves, and smoke forces windows shut.

feasible.basis: Roads are open in a smoke episode, but clean air may be hundreds of miles away and work and school continue.

earliestDay.basis: A household can leave as soon as smoke arrives.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Fuel and time for a few hundred miles; a smoke plume is regional.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Wong et al.: 49-70% of evacuees stayed with family or friends, 13-23% in a hotel, 2-5% in a public shelter (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5w85z07g). Same arithmetic as for hurricanes.

staple.basis: Shops stay open in a smoke episode. In an evacuation there is no time, but little that could be bought then would help.

specialty.basis: Respirators and air purifiers sold out across the Bay Area within a day or two in November 2018 and across the West in September 2020 (recalled press reports); delivery takes days.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: 5 days x 75 = 375 microgram-days. Chen et al. 2021 give +1.9% all-cause deaths per 10 micrograms of wildfire PM2.5 over three days, and another pooled estimate gives 1.5% (search snippets, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2542-5196(21)00200-X): 56-71% of one day's mortality. For a healthy adult at 7.4 micromorts a day, halved because acute deaths fall on the old and sick and cut by 0.7 for flattening at high concentrations: 1.5-1.9. Raised to 3 because long-term response functions applied to the same dose give about 19.

hardshipUsdPerPerson.basis: Richardson et al. 2012: willingness to pay $84 per person to avoid a day of smoke symptoms, against $9.50 of medical cost per exposed person per day (search snippet, https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/70032380). 5 days x one person in three symptomatic x $84 = $140; cost of illness alone, $48.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: The 11 largest California evacuations of 2017-2019 killed 144 of 1.1M ordered out, 130 micromorts each (fatalities row and evacuee totals in https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5w85z07g); my tally for 2017-2025 nationally is about 330 deaths over 2.8M, 120 each. Adults under 60 run about 0.3 of the average (72 of 84 identified Camp Fire dead were 60 or older, AARP via search snippet): 40 per evacuation event, times the 0.1 share of events with an evacuation.

hardshipUsdPerPerson.basis: Burns, crashes and falls in the one event in ten with an evacuation; no data read.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Given an evacuation order about 3% of apartments burn (4.7% of all evacuated homes: over 30,000 structures, perhaps 20,000 of them homes, for 1.1M people or 420,000 households, https://escholarship.org/uc/item/5w85z07g; apartments less often than houses). 3% x $25,000 of contents x 51% uninsured (FinHealth via search snippet, https://finhealthnetwork.org/research/climate-disaster-and-renters-insurance-whos-protected/) = $380, plus about $70 of deductibles and smoke cleaning: $450; times 0.1.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

pOccur.basis: Same evidence as this window's basis.

flood.label: Flood
flood.definition: Floodwater from rain, a river, a failed drain or dam, or the tide, other than in a named tropical cyclone (those are under hurricane), enters the home's building or cuts off its street, so that the household is flooded, ordered out or marooned.

westernEurope.basis: Exposed means living in a mapped flood-prone area: about 12% of Europeans, 52M people (EEA, 2021, search snippet, https://climate-adapt.eea.europa.eu/en/observatory/publications-data/analysis-data/exposure-to-potential-flood-prone-areas). People flooded each year in the EU and UK: 172,000 by rivers and 100,000 by the sea (JRC figures on the EEA page, read, https://climate-adapt.eea.europa.eu/en/observatory/topics/health-impacts/flooding). 272,000 / 52M = 0.52% a year. The range allows for ground floors against upper floors and for places with weak defences.

buenosAires.basis: Exposed means the low parts of the Maldonado, Vega, Medrano, Cildanez and Riachuelo basins in the city, and the Reconquista, Matanza and Lujan flood plains in the suburbs. The city had damaging floods in 2001, 2010, 2012 and 2013 (recalled apart from 2013): four in thirteen years. None of that scale has been reported in the city since the Maldonado (2012) and Vega (2019) relief tunnels, while suburbs flooded in 2014, 2015, 2024 and 2025. So about one year in 25-60 for an exposed city block now, more often in the suburban flood plains. Guess.

us.basis: Exposed = home in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area or one of First Street's 14.6M substantial-risk properties (https://www.preventionweb.net/publications/view/72504, search snippet): by definition at least 1%/yr of water reaching the building, more for lots well inside the line. NFIP paid 101,494 claims in 2024 on about 4.7M policies, 2.2%, and 13,000-112,000 a year in 2014-2017 (FEMA brochure and ValuePenguin, search snippets): about 1.2% a year. Events that close the street or bring an order without wetting the building roughly double it. Check: Pulse has 665,000-670,000 adults displaced by floods in each of 2022 and 2023 (https://andrewrumbach.substack.com/p/unpacking-the-us-census-data-on-natural); if half live in mapped-risk homes that is 1.2-1.4% of their 24M adults, or half the events.

pOccur.basis: Home flooded (about 1.2%/yr) or ordered out, over the 2.5%/yr event rate; Pulse flood displacement gives the same 1.2-1.4%/yr.

displacement.basis: Census Household Pulse, Dec 2022-Oct 2023 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12374215): of 2.43M displaced adults, 43% were away under a week, 25% a week to a month, 11% one to six months, 7% over six months and 14% never returned. Floods are the case the split fits best, since a wetted house needs drying, stripping and rebuilding: I use it nearly as it stands, counting never-returned as resettled within six months (9 / 140 / 600) and trimming slightly for short precautionary evacuations. Engine mean: 45 days.

pOccur.basis: Utilities cut supply to flooded streets and the storm that brings the flood brings outages.

power.basis: A wetted panel or meter must be inspected or replaced before reconnection, by which time the household is usually displaced.

pOccur.basis: Flooded treatment works and private wells: Des Moines 1993, Jackson 2022, eastern Kentucky 2022 (recalled). Wells in a floodplain are contaminated in most floods.

water.basis: Boil notices average about five days (step 2); Des Moines went 12 days without tap water in 1993 and Jackson seven weeks under a boil notice in 2022 (recalled).

shareTreatable.basis: Mostly boil notices and contaminated wells; floodwater itself carries sewage and fuel and is a poor source.

pandemicModerate.label: Pandemic on the scale of COVID-19
pandemicModerate.definition: A newly emerged pathogen spreads worldwide, reaches the household's country and kills at least as many people as COVID-19 did (6.5 million reported deaths by the end of 2022, 0.08% of the world; excess-death estimates are two to four times higher) but fewer than about 1% of the world's population, with infection fatality well under 1% in adults under 60. Shops, utilities and pharmacies keep working; hospitals are strained in waves. Excludes pandemics on the scale of 1957, 1968 or 2009 (under about 4 million deaths at today's population) and everything in pandemicSevere.

forecast.basis: P(COVID-scale or worse) minus P(severe, about 0.2%). Sources for the first term: 2-3%/yr (Madhav et al. 2023, Metabiota catalogue, https://www.cgdev.org/sites/default/files/estimated-future-mortality-pathogens-epidemic-and-pandemic-potential.pdf); 2.5-3.3% (Metabiota 2021 via CGD); 19% for more than 20 million deaths in 2023-2032, about 2.1%/yr, from a base rate of 2 such events in 123 years (Cambeiro 2023); 0.2-0.8%/yr (Marani et al. as corrected in 2023: recurrence 523 or 129 years depending on the intensity used); 5% for more than 25 million deaths in 2022-2031, about 0.5%/yr (Metaculus, search snippet). Median of these about 1.8%; low end is Metaculus and corrected Marani, high end Metabiota.

pessimistic.basis: Upper published views: 4.2%/yr for a respiratory pandemic killing 10 million or more (Madhav et al. 2023, Table 6), less about 0.8% that would be severe; 3.3% (Metabiota 2021 upper bound); a tripling of the emergence rate 'in coming decades' (Marani et al. 2021), which applied to Madhav's 2-3% gives 6%; plus human-caused epidemics, which biosecurity experts put at 1.5%/yr for more than 100,000 deaths once language models match expert virologists, a threshold SecureBio reports was passed in April 2025 (Forecasting Research Institute 2025, https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/forecasting-biosecurity-risks-from).

pOccur.basis: Shops stayed open throughout 2020 in the US, Western Europe and Argentina, so the window opens only for a household that is isolating with a sick or quarantined member and can get neither a delivery slot nor a friend to shop. Census Household Pulse, April-July 2020: of adults in food-insufficient households (about a tenth of adults, recalled), 15.9% said they could not get out to buy food and 8.2% could not get delivery (UCLA analysis, search snippet), which is 1-2.5% of all households.

food.basis: Length of an isolation period (10-14 days under 2020 guidance); delivery slots were unobtainable for two weeks or more in several US cities from mid-March to mid-April 2020 (press reports, search snippets). The 99th percentile allows for a Shanghai-type confinement (27 March to 1 June 2022, with real food shortages), which no democracy imposed. Partial shortages are not this window: US stores were out of 13% of items at the late-March peak against 5-7% normally.

pOccur.basis: Pharmacies stayed open and prescribers moved to telephone. The window is a specific drug being out of stock locally, or an isolating household with nobody to collect. In April 2020 nearly 90% of US community pharmacists reported some drug shortage since 1 March, but over 83% of shortage drugs had alternatives and shortage counts were back to normal by May (search snippets, https://ncpa.org/newsroom/news-releases/2020/04/16/90-percent-community-pharmacists-report-drug-shortages-covid-19).

medication.basis: No series found for how long individual patients went without. Median set by an isolation period, tail by the two to three months for which salbutamol inhalers and hydroxychloroquine were short in spring 2020 (recalled).

pOccur.basis: Chance that the household's local hospitals and ambulances are strained in at least one wave. National adult intensive-care occupancy was above 75% for at least 12 consecutive weeks as of 25 October 2021 (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/wr/mm7046a5.htm); 54% of COVID inpatients in 558 US hospitals in March-August 2020 were in hospitals in the top decile of surge (Kadri 2021, search snippet). Some regions escaped each wave.

emergencyCare.basis: Days of strained, not absent, care: use the trauma channel's 'careStrained' rate (about 0.2 micromorts a day at 15-59). Two to three local waves of 3-10 strained weeks each over two years. Check: 60-75 days x 0.2 = 12-15 micromorts at 15-59; top-down, 28% of 522,368 US excess deaths from March 2020 to January 2021 were not attributed to COVID (Woolf 2021, https://news.vcu.edu/article/US_deaths_normally_change_less_than_2_each_year_In_2020_they), 440 micromorts at all ages, of which perhaps a quarter was delayed care and about 0.3 of the all-age rate applies at 15-59: about 30. Same order.

feasible.basis: A pandemic leaves no unaffected region to go to within weeks; borders of the few places that kept it out (New Zealand, Taiwan) closed to non-residents. Moving to a rural second home lowers contact but is not an exit: about 5% of New York City residents (420,000) left between 1 March and 1 May 2020, mostly from the richest districts (New York Times phone-data analysis, search snippet).

earliestDay.basis: Possible at once for those with somewhere to go, until internal travel limits or border closures.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Travel plus setting up remote work and schooling elsewhere; no source.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Second rent or a long-stay rental over many months, shared across the household; no source.

staple.basis: Food as a whole stayed on sale: at the late-March 2020 peak US stores were out of 13% of items against 5-7% normally (search snippet). Particular staples vanished: toilet paper was out for part of the day at 70% of stores on 23 March, 73% on 12 April and 48% on 19 April, 'deeply deficient for over 50 days' (NCSolutions via Reuters, https://www.fox6now.com/news/shortages-easing-on-coronavirus-hit-toilet-paper-supplies-not-yet-where-we-want-them-to-be); flour for about a month and yeast into late July in places.

specialty.basis: 2020 record, by item, in lateBuyDetail. N95s: 'most consumers still aren't able to buy N95 masks' on 27 January 2021, a year in (NPR, https://www.wgbh.org/news/national/2021-01-27/why-n95-masks-are-still-in-short-supply-in-the-u-s). Thermometers: shipping dates of May or June on 31 March. Freezers: most models out or back-ordered to late May through August by 20 April. Only households that bought in January or early February 2020, before the public did, got respirators; the mid is my guess at the share who would act that early across all specialty items.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: US COVID deaths at 15-59 (CDC, https://data.cdc.gov/resource/9bhg-hcku.json; I take 39% of the 55-64 band as 55-59) over 197 million people: 46,200 in 2020 = 234 micromorts; 96,700 in 2021 = 491; 32,600 in 2022 = 165; 179,200 to September 2023 = 910. Two-year event = 725. Western Europe was about half that at these ages (recalled). The range covers a pathogen that spares the working-age (low) or one with a 1957- or 2009-like age pattern at COVID's total (high).

hardshipUsdPerPerson.basis: Attack rate 0.35 x about $1,320 per infection = $460. Per infection: 65% symptomatic (recalled) x 10 days x $70 = $455; 2% hospitalised (guess) x $10,000 = $200; long illness: 0.65 x 7% of symptomatic adults with symptoms at three months (6.2% overall, 10.6% of women and 5.4% of men aged 20+; mean 4 months if not hospitalised, 15% still ill at 12 months: Wulf Hanson 2022, https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2022.18931) x 0.08 quality-adjusted years (disability weight about 0.2 for about 0.4 years) x $182,500 a year ($500 a day, as food.json uses) = $665.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Cost of illness only, two adults: 0.35 x 2 x about $550 per adult infection. Per infection: 7 isolation days x $200 x 25% of workers with no paid sick leave (BLS March 2020: 75% of private-industry workers had it, search snippet) = $350; 2% hospitalised x $1,300-4,000 out of pocket (KFF and JAMA Network Open, search snippets) = $50; 4% with long illness x a quarter losing about three months' pay = $150. Income lost to the wider downturn is the separate financialLoss exposure.

In August 2020, 25% of US adults said someone in their household had lost a job and 32% that someone had taken a pay cut; 42% one or both (Pew, https://www.pewresearch.org/social-trends/2020/09/24/economic-fallout-from-covid-19-continues-to-hit-lower-income-americans-the-hardest/, search snippet). Size: US wages and salaries ran roughly 3.5% below trend in 2020 (recalled, not checked), about $330 billion or $2,500 per household, some $6,000 per affected household. Transfers more than replaced this on average in the US; they did not in Argentina.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

days.basis: Own illness: attack rate 0.35 (tail-pandemic.json) x 4.3 days per infection = 1.5. Per infection: 0.65 symptomatic x 4 days (absence and reduced output; 3.6 in a vaccine-maker's model, Beck et al. 2025, read; median return to work 10 calendar days among 30,396 Dutch employees who reported sick, https://www.sjweh.fi/article/4077, read) = 2.6, + 1.5% hospitalised x 35 days (42 in Beck) = 0.5, + long COVID 0.65 x 6.2% ill at three months (Wulf Hanson 2022, in tail-pandemic.json) x 85 working days x a third of output lost (Brookings 2022: about a quarter out of work and 45% on reduced hours, read) = 1.1. Caring: 1.5 other members x 0.35 x 0.65 x 1 day x 0.6 borne by this adult = 0.2. Check: the illness lost-worktime rate of US full-time workers was 0.9% in 2019 and 1.3% in 2020 and 2021 (BLS CPS table 47, read): 0.8% x 250 = 2.0 days over the two years.

pandemicSevere.label: Pandemic far worse than COVID-19
pandemicSevere.definition: A pandemic that kills more than about 1% of the world's population within five years, or would without extreme countermeasures, because infection fatality is several percent or more in adults under 60 as well as in the old. Natural (a 1918-type influenza, an H5N1-type virus that keeps high lethality while becoming transmissible) or engineered. Hospitals cannot cope, and enough workers may stay home to interrupt supply. Excludes agents so lethal and contagious that nothing a household does would matter.

forecast.basis: Pathogen killing more than 1% of humanity within five years, tournament medians annualised for 2023-2030: superforecasters 0.04% engineered + 0.07% natural = 0.11%/yr; biosecurity experts 0.18% + 0.14% = 0.32% (Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, Table 23, as excerpted and annualised in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.14289). 1918-intensity event: 0.11%/yr (879-year recurrence, Marani et al. as corrected 2023). Respiratory pandemic killing more than 80 million: 0.8%/yr; more than 100 million: 0.6% (Madhav et al. 2023, Tables 5-6). Low end is superforecasters shaded for rich countries, high end Metabiota.

pessimistic.basis: Upper end of published views. Tournament biosecurity experts for 2030-2050: 0.35% engineered + 0.21% natural = 0.56%/yr (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.14289). Metabiota: 0.8% natural alone. Forecasting Research Institute 2025: 46 experts put a human-caused epidemic of more than 100,000 deaths at 0.3%/yr, rising to 1.5% if language models match top virologists at troubleshooting, which OpenAI's o3 did in April 2025; only part of that would be this severe. Metaculus: 5% (1-10%) that an engineered pandemic infects a billion people within five years of AGI, about 1%/yr (search snippet). Ord 2020: 1 in 30 for existential catastrophe from engineered pandemics by 2100. Amodei 2026: 'a serious risk of a major attack' with casualties 'in the millions or more' within a few years; no number. The high end is a reader with short AGI timelines who takes the 1.5% as mostly severe.

pOccur.basis: No pandemic has tested this in a modern economy. For: a system-dynamics model finds 'greater than a 25% reduction in labor availability' produces 'significant and widespread food shortages' (Huff et al. 2015, https://doi.org/10.1007/s13412-015-0275-3); US planning assumed up to 40% absent in the two peak weeks of a severe influenza (HHS 2005, search snippet); fewer than half of 1,100 New York emergency and hospital workers were both willing and able to work in a 'serious pandemic' (Columbia 2010); in 2020 infection of 3.5% of meat-plant workers cut US meat output by 40%; shops and warehouses hold about five days (IFP). Against: 5% of all US workers absent in January 2022 broke nothing; in 1918, with case fatality above 2.5%, cities kept food on sale; grain stocks cover the US for over a year.

food.basis: Days with no food obtainable at all, net of rationing and army or municipal distribution, which I assume starts within one to four weeks. The 99th percentile stands for the 'Wildfire' case of Gopal et al. 2023, in which essential services break down. The engine's food-mortality curve is steep after day 30, so results are sensitive to this tail; it is a guess.

pOccur.basis: Drug supply runs through long international chains (active ingredients from India and China) and through pharmacies staffed by people in contact with the sick; both failed briefly in 2020 at far lower stakes. No quantitative source.

medication.basis: Longer than the food window because production cannot be improvised or substituted locally and stocks in the chain are a few weeks to a few months. No source.

pOccur.basis: COVID-19, with infection fatality under 1%, filled intensive care in most US regions for months; an agent several times deadlier overwhelms hospitals wherever it spreads, and a third of hospital workers said they would not report in a severe pandemic (Johns Hopkins 2010, search snippet).

emergencyCare.basis: Two or three waves of 6-10 weeks, as in 1918 (all waves within 8-9 months in one country, https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/12/1/05-0979_article), plus recovery; longer if suppression stretches the epidemic out. Use the trauma channel's 'careAbsent' rate for about a third of these days (wave peaks) and 'careStrained' for the rest: about 0.5 micromorts a day at 15-59.

pOccur.basis: Qualitative basis only. The US grid regulator called COVID-19 a 'people event' whose main risk was loss of control-room and maintenance staff, and utilities sequestered operators (NERC 2020, search snippet); no outage resulted. Gopal et al. 2023 and ALLFED 2026 argue that at high lethality essential workers stop working and services fail in cascade, without giving a threshold. Mid = an ordinary outage of six hours or more during three peak months (17.7% of households a year, step 2 base-rates, so about 4%) repaired late, plus a few percent for wider failure.

power.basis: Ordinary faults repaired two to five times more slowly by depleted crews; tail for fuel-supply or staffing failure at plants. No source.

pOccur.basis: Same reasoning as power; treatment plants need few operators but depend on power and on chemical deliveries. No outage of this kind occurred in COVID-19. No quantitative source.

water.basis: Set equal to the power window with a shorter tail. No source.

shareTreatable.basis: Most failures would be loss of treatment or pressure (boil notices) before dry taps.

feasible.basis: Nowhere stays unaffected for long, and borders and internal travel close faster the deadlier the agent; a remote second home is isolation, not exit, and is covered by the stay-home effect.

earliestDay.basis: Only before movement restrictions.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Travel at crisis prices plus setting up elsewhere; no source.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Long-stay accommodation for many months; no source.

staple.basis: In 2020 a household could still buy weeks of food once the threat was plain (0.92). With several times the fear and less warning, a larger share of shoppers stock up at once and shops ration; no data.

specialty.basis: Respirators sold out within weeks in 2020 and stayed scarce for a year for a far milder disease; governments would also requisition stocks for essential workers, whose needs 'far exceed stockpiles' (ALLFED 2026, search snippet).

micromortsPerPerson.basis: 0.30 x 0.03 = 0.9%. Low: 0.12 x 0.012; high: 0.5 x 0.16. Anchor: 1918 killed about 0.65% of the US population and about 2.7% of the world (675,000 and about 50 million; US figure recalled), with case fatality 'above 2.5%', a third of the world infected and nearly half of deaths at ages 20-40 (https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/eid/article/12/1/05-0979_article). Fatality and attack rate are probably negatively related, since people hide from deadlier agents, which narrows the product.

hardshipUsdPerPerson.basis: 0.30 x about $10,000 per infection: two to three weeks of severe illness, mostly without hospital care, at $300-500 a day, plus lasting damage in some survivors. No source.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Cost of illness, two adults: 0.30 x 2 x about $3,000 (a month off work, care costs). No source.

A year in which output falls 5-20%: the 'ultra' influenza scenario of McKibbin and Sidorenko (2006) loses 12.6% of world output in the first year, 5.5% in the US and 11.1% in the UK (search snippet); applied to US median household income of about $80,000 and concentrated on those who cannot work from home.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

days.basis: Own illness: 0.3 x 0.9 symptomatic x 12 working days (two to three weeks of severe illness and convalescence, tail-pandemic.json) = 3.2, plus lasting debility 0.3 x 10% x 40 days x 0.4 = 0.5 (guess). Caring with hospitals overwhelmed: 1.5 other members x 0.3 x 0.9 x 5 days x 0.6 = 1.2. Total 4.9. Checks: CBO's severe scenario (30% infected) has survivors miss three weeks for illness, fear or caring (via https://www.milliman.com/en/insight/sick-days-a-human-capital-perspective-on-pandemic-influenza, read): 0.3 x 15 = 4.5; B.F. Goodrich, Akron, lost 102 + 165 days per 100 male and 142 + 505 per 100 female employees to influenza in the years to October 1918 and 1919 (Public Health Reports 1922, https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/68112/cdc_68112_DS1.pdf, read): 2.7-6.5 days per worker.

nuclearNear.label: Nuclear war reaching your region
nuclearNear.definition: Nuclear weapons detonate on the household's own country in a large-scale attack (roughly 100 warheads or more), or in a smaller attack that puts the home inside a damaged area or under a fallout plume, and everyone in the household is alive one hour after the first detonation. In a large-scale attack every surviving household in the country counts, whether or not fallout reaches it, because power, supply and medical care fail nationally; the fallout exposure is therefore a mean over households, most of which receive little dose.

forecast.basis: Large-scale attack on the US 0.07%/yr x alive after the first hour 0.88 = 0.062%, plus under 0.001% for limited strikes. The 0.07% sits between the tournament superforecasters' 0.06%/yr for a nuclear catastrophe (https://forum-bots.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YyBoSSaWpNacLnCji), Samotsvety's London-hit rate blended over calm and crisis years (0.07%) and Rodriguez's 0.38%/yr US-Russia exchange x 0.2-0.3 for escalation to the homeland.

pessimistic.basis: Large-scale attack 0.25%/yr x 0.88. The 0.25% is Rodriguez's 0.38%/yr for any US-Russia exchange (https://rethinkpriorities.org/research-area/how-likely-is-a-nuclear-exchange-between-the-us-and-russia/) x about 0.5 for escalation, plus China and North Korea; Barrett et al.'s 0.9%/yr for inadvertent US-Russia war (90% interval 0.02-7%) sets the upper bound.

forecast.basis: Large-scale attack on Western Europe 0.07%/yr x 0.85 of the population in attacked or immediately downwind countries x 0.82 alive after the first hour = 0.049%. Samotsvety (https://forum-bots.effectivealtruism.org/posts/2nDTrDPZJBEerZGrk): London hit 0.36% in the year from October 2022; about 0.03%/yr without a crisis (0.132% x 23%).

pessimistic.basis: 0.25%/yr x 0.85 x 0.82, the same pessimistic war rate as for the United States; Samotsvety's March 2022 crisis-level figure for London alone was 0.8%/yr x 18% = 0.14%/yr.

forecast.basis: No nuclear-armed state has a reason to strike Argentina and fallout from Northern Hemisphere wars reaches the south only as trace global fallout. One in a million a year stands for accidents and scenarios nobody has listed.

pessimistic.basis: Three times the forecast figure; still negligible beside nuclearFar.

pOccur.basis: Hundreds of detonations, high-altitude pulse and loss of fuel and staff take the grid down nearly everywhere; hydro-fed islands may hold.

power.basis: No modern study gives restoration times after a nuclear attack. US EMP Commission 2008: restoration of some damage 'certainly months and in some instances years'; irreparably damaged large transformers take one to two years plus backlog (http://www.empcommission.org/docs/A2473-EMP_Commission-7MB.pdf).

pOccur.basis: Pipeline compression, control and production depend on power and staff.
Treatment and pumping stop with power; OTA 1979 notes water pressure gone in damaged areas.

water.basis: Net of relief: tankers and organised wells reach most survivors within weeks, taps take as long as the grid. No data; wide range intended.

shareTreatable.basis: Rivers, rain, wells and standing water in pipes and tanks remain obtainable and can be filtered and disinfected; the exception is the first days inside a fallout zone, when fetching it costs dose.

pOccur.basis: Shops hold one to three days of food and regional warehouses about a month for their area (EMP Commission 2008); distribution needs fuel, power and payment systems.

food.basis: Net of relief: with nine in ten people and most grain stocks surviving, I assume some rationed distribution within two to six weeks for most households; in the worst tenth nothing organised for three months or more. A guess with no data behind it.

pOccur.basis: Pharmacies shut and the supply chain is long and import-dependent.

medication.basis: Longer than food because drugs cannot be improvised or sourced locally.

pOccur.basis: Surviving hospitals are swamped: OTA 1979 expects injuries about equal to fatalities.

emergencyCare.basis: Until hospitals have power, supplies and staff again.

pOccur.basis: Card networks and banks need power and communications; OTA 1979 expects 'large credit, monetary, contractual, and legal problems'.

payments.basis: Follows power and communications. Whether notes keep their value is a separate, open question.

pOccur.basis: Telecom sites carry 4 to 72 hours of backup power (EMP Commission 2008); broadcast radio is the service most likely to survive.

comms.basis: Counted from loss of service. Mobile and internet return with regional power; no data.

pOccur.basis: No water to flush for most; sewage pumping stops. About 70% of these days are lack of flush water, which hauled water cures.
Homes damaged by blast or fire at the edge of struck areas, and homes where the fallout dose rate stays too high to live in after the shelter period.

coldShare.basis: A 60-day median window overlaps a 120-day cold season with probability (120 + 60) / 365 = 0.49; longer windows and any soot-driven cooling raise it.

hotShare.basis: (90 + 60) / 365 = 0.41 for a 90-day hot season; cooling from soot would lower it, longer windows raise it.

feasible.basis: After a large-scale attack there is almost nowhere unaffected within reach: no fuel sales, no flights, borders shut. Feasible mainly in limited attacks and for households with a full tank near an untouched border.

earliestDay.basis: Dose rate falls as t^-1.2: about 1% of the one-hour rate at two days and 0.1% at two weeks, so travel becomes tolerable after one to three days outside the heaviest plumes and one to two weeks inside them.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: A journey of 1,000 km or more with scarce fuel bought at crisis prices, and abandoned possessions.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Lodging and food as a displaced person in a place itself short of supplies.

staple.basis: About 0.6 that there is usable warning x 0.6 that shops still hold food and water during the scare.

specialty.basis: Potassium iodide, respirators, radios and meters sold out within days in March 2011 and February-March 2022 (recalled).

micromortsPerPerson.basis: United States. Philippe et al. (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/who-would-take-the-brunt-of-an-attack-on-u-s-nuclear-missile-silos/): an 800 kt ground burst on each of 450 silos kills 1.4M by acute radiation on average (0.34-4.6M by day of year) if people shelter four days, twice that without shelter. x 1.3 for typical behaviour = 1.8M, plus about 0.8M from other ground bursts (guess) = 2.6M of 295M survivors = 0.9% acute, or 8,800 micromorts; later cancer adds about 2,400 unweighted (1,000 if weighted 0.4). Taken as 10,000.

us.basis: As above. High end: Cold War counterforce studies gave 1-20M deaths of 225M, 14M under 'reasonable' shelter assumptions (OTA 1979, https://atomicarchive.com/resources/documents/effects/ota/chapter-4-4-2.html), and about 10M for an unsheltered population (Harvey et al. 1992). Low end: Harvey's under 1M with shelter, fewer ground bursts, favourable wind.

westernEurope.basis: No silo fields, so fewer ground bursts, and masonry housing lets through about half the dose of US light-frame houses (radiation researcher: 0.10-0.13 against 0.22-0.28); but hardened headquarters sit beside London, Paris and Brussels. No published estimate found.

buenosAires.basis: Not applicable: the hazard has near-zero probability there.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: OTA 1979: injuries about equal fatalities. 3-20% of first-hour survivors are in light-to-moderate damage zones, about 30% of them seriously hurt, 20-40% of those die without care: 0.2-2.4%, taken as 0.6%.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

nuclearFar.label: Nuclear war elsewhere
nuclearFar.definition: Nuclear weapons kill more than 1,000 people in a war that leaves the household's own country without large-scale attack and its home outside any damaged or fallout area. Event mix for these two locations: about 62% limited use abroad (ten detonations or fewer), 33% regional war with tens to hundreds of detonations (India-Pakistan, Korea, a NATO-Russia exchange confined to another theatre), 5% a larger war that spares the household's country.

forecast.basis: Any use killing over 1,000 people 0.7%/yr minus 0.07% for large-scale attack on the US and 0.03% for limited strikes on it. Sources for the 0.7%: tournament 0.49-0.55%, Good Judgment 0.40%, Rodriguez 1.1%, Metaculus 1.8% (https://forum-bots.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YyBoSSaWpNacLnCji).

pessimistic.basis: 1.8%/yr (Metaculus 34% by 2050) minus 0.25% and 0.05%. The UK National Risk Register 2025 scores a limited nuclear conflict between two other states at 5-25% over its assessment period.

forecast.basis: Same arithmetic as for the United States: 0.7% minus 0.07% and 0.03%.

pessimistic.basis: Same arithmetic as for the United States: 1.8% minus 0.25% and 0.05%.

forecast.basis: Any nuclear use killing over 1,000 people: tournament 0.49-0.55%/yr, Good Judgment 0.40%, Rodriguez 1.1%, Metaculus 1.8%; geometric mean 0.79%, taken as 0.7% (https://forum-bots.effectivealtruism.org/posts/YyBoSSaWpNacLnCji). About 0.1% of it is great-power war.

pessimistic.basis: Metaculus 34% by 2050 = 1.8%/yr; about 0.3% of it great-power war (Rodriguez 0.38%/yr for a US-Russia exchange).

pOccur.basis: Panic buying empties shops for some days in the worst events; in March 2020 toilet paper was out at 70% of US grocers yet food stayed obtainable (base-rates.md).

food.basis: Net of relief. Both regions grow more grain than they eat, so the harm from a soot-driven harvest loss is price, carried on financialLoss, not absence.

pOccur.basis: Chance that a given regular drug cannot be had from any pharmacy because its ingredients come from a struck or blockaded country (India and China make most generic ingredients; recalled).

medication.basis: Until substitute suppliers or products are found; drug shortages in peacetime commonly run for months.

pOccur.basis: Market closures and bank runs in the first days of the worst events; cards normally keep working.

payments.basis: Counted only while a household with a card and an account cannot pay at all.

pOccur.basis: Satellite losses, cable cuts or cyber spillover in the worst events; no data.

comms.basis: Counted from loss of service.

feasible.basis: The effects are prices, jobs and supply chains, which are global; there is no unaffected place to go.

earliestDay.basis: Not a meaningful option here.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: International relocation; placeholder.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Placeholder.

staple.basis: Shops stay open and restock; a few goods run short for days.

specialty.basis: Potassium iodide, respirators and radiation meters sold out within days across Europe and North America in March 2011 and early 2022 (recalled).

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: 0.62 x $700 + 0.33 x $6,000 + 0.05 x $30,000 = $3,900, shaded to $3,000. The $6,000: food bill of $10,000 up 25% for two years ($5,000 over two years, partly offset) plus a 10% chance of losing $20,000 of earnings. No market has priced a nuclear war since 1945.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

pOccur.basis: Argentina grows more than ten times its own calorie needs, and about four times even after a 150 Tg winter if feed and biofuel crops go to people (ORCG and ALLFED 2023). Shops empty only briefly, in panics or when prices are frozen.

food.basis: The long tail is the severe-winter case with policy failure, where the same report says net output barely covers needs and prices would soar. For most households that is a price problem, carried on financialLoss.

pOccur.basis: Chance that a given regular drug cannot be had: 0.15 great-power war x 0.7 + 0.30 regional war x 0.3 = 0.2. About 80% of active ingredients are imported, 46% from China and 18% from India (German trade agency, search snippet).

medication.basis: Local laboratories formulate most medicines but run out of ingredients; supply returns as trade re-forms. No data.

pOccur.basis: 0.15 x 0.7 + 0.30 x 0.1 + 0.55 x 0.01 = 0.14: a bank holiday or payment-system stop is likely after a great-power war and possible after a regional one.

payments.basis: Counted only while a household with a card and an account cannot pay at all; Argentina's 2001-02 bank holidays ran days at a time (recalled). The larger harm is on financialLoss.

pOccur.basis: Loss of northern data centres, cables and satellites in a great-power war; no data.

comms.basis: Counted from loss of service.

feasible.basis: The effects are global; Buenos Aires is already among the places people would flee to.

earliestDay.basis: Not a meaningful option here.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Placeholder.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Same as the locations researcher's Buenos Aires figure.

staple.basis: Shops stay open; imported goods run short over months, not days.

specialty.basis: Imported specialty goods are thinly stocked and would not be replenished.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: 0.55 x $400 + 0.30 x $2,500 + 0.15 x $13,000 = $2,900, shaded to $2,500. Argentine residents hold roughly $220-255 billion in dollar notes and unregistered foreign deposits (INDEC, end-2025, search snippet), about $5,000 a head, very unevenly; what a dollar note is worth after a war that wrecks the United States is unknown.

gridLong.label: Grid failure for weeks or months
gridLong.definition: Collapse of the transmission grid over a whole country or a region of 10 million people or more, caused by a geomagnetic storm, a cyber or physical attack, an electromagnetic pulse or a cascading technical failure, that leaves the household without grid power for at least 72 hours. Outages confined to the footprint of a storm, hurricane, earthquake or cold wave belong to other hazards; a pulse that is part of a nuclear attack on the country belongs to nuclearNear. About 30% of these events last a week or more and 20% two weeks or more.

forecast.basis: Sum of four routes. Storm: 0.4%/yr for a Carrington-class storm x 5% of households out 72 h or more = 0.02%. Attack: 0.2% x 0.25 in the footprint x 0.4 = 0.02%. Cascade needing a black start: 0.3% x 0.07 = 0.02%. Stand-alone pulse 0.005%. The storm factor weights NERC's view (hours to days) above Lloyd's (https://assets.lloyds.com/assets/pdf-solar-storm-risk-to-the-north-american-electric-grid/1/pdf-Solar-Storm-Risk-to-the-North-American-Electric-Grid.pdf).

pessimistic.basis: Lloyd's view. Storm: 1%/yr (Riley's 12% a decade) x 12% (Lloyd's 20-40M Americans at risk of 16 days to 2 years) = 0.12%. Attack: 0.5%/yr (Lloyd's 2015 puts a 93M-person cyber blackout inside the 1-in-200 benchmark) x 0.28 x 0.5 = 0.07%. Cascade 0.05%, pulse 0.02%. Sum 0.26%.

forecast.basis: Great Britain: the National Risk Register 2025 puts total grid failure at 1-5% in five years (0.45%/yr) with full restoration taking up to 7 days; x 0.4 of households out 72 h or more = 0.18%. Continent: national blackouts hit 1.15% of people a year (Italy 2003, Iberia 2025) but ended within a day; 0.05% for the 72-hour tail plus attack. Weighted 17:83 = 0.07%, rounded up. https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6787ea8e1124a2c3ceb646bf/National_Risk_Register_2025.pdf

pessimistic.basis: Top of the UK band (1%/yr x 0.5) applied to a fifth of the population, the UK register's 5-25% two-year likelihood class for cyber attacks on infrastructure, and a Lloyd's-type storm outcome at high latitudes; about four times the forecast.

forecast.basis: Two system-wide collapses in about 25 years (16 June 2019, 48M people, 6-14 h; 1 March 2023, recalled) = 8%/yr, x 0.7-2.3% chance that restoration takes over 72 h (log-normal, median 8 h, sigma 0.9-1.1) = 0.06-0.18%. Storm risk is low at Buenos Aires's magnetic latitude.

pessimistic.basis: A grid run down as Venezuela's was: in March 2019 most of that country lost power for five to seven days and again later in the month (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Venezuelan_blackouts). Three times the forecast.

pOccur.basis: True by definition of the event.

power.basis: Mixture. 70% of events have no major equipment damage and end in 3-7 days (UK register: full restoration up to 7 days; Lloyd's 2015: mean 3.8 days, two weeks to 90% restored). 30% need transformers or generators replaced: median 20 days, tenth 120 days or more (Lloyd's 2013: 16 days to 1-2 years; new transformers take 5-16 months; EMP Commission: one to two years). Mixture gives about 6 / 30-44 / 230-290.

pOccur.basis: The UK register lists gas among services lost in a national blackout; many compressors are gas-driven and keep running. Texas 2021 showed gas supply failing when its own facilities lost power.

gas.basis: Assumed to return shortly after power.

pOccur.basis: TAB 2011: storage and backup power in German water systems are designed 'to bridge supply interruptions lasting just a few hours', generator fuel lasts about five days; Venezuela 2019: about two thirds of people without water wholly or partly. Larger US and UK works have more backup, hence below 1.

water.basis: Starts on day 1-3 and is net of relief: tankers, standpipes and emergency wells (Germany keeps 5,200) cover a growing share after the first week or two, as in Puerto Rico where households averaged 68 days without water against 84 without power.

shareTreatable.basis: Low-pressure or unsafe tap water, rivers, rain, water heaters and tanks stay obtainable on most days and can be boiled or disinfected.

pOccur.basis: TAB 2011: shelves empty within 2 to 5 days, warehouses stop within 2 days, and shop and household stocks are 'likely to be used up by the end of the first week'. EMP Commission 2008: supermarkets hold 1 to 3 days. So the window opens around day 3-5, in about half of events.

food.basis: Net of relief: cash sales in the first days, then official distribution from warehouses, which hold about a month's food for their area (EMP Commission). No measurement exists for a rich country.

pOccur.basis: TAB 2011: after 24 hours most surgeries and pharmacies are shut; drugs grow scarce during the first week; even hospital pharmacies with 14 days of stock cannot meet demand.

medication.basis: Starts on day 1 and ends when pharmacies reopen or relief dispensing is organised.

pOccur.basis: TAB 2011: marked decline in health care after 24 hours, emergency calls cannot get through, and collapse of medical care is likely by the end of the first week. Emergency generators generally carry under 72 hours of fuel (EMP Commission 2008).

emergencyCare.basis: Starts on day 1-3. Hospitals get first call on fuel and mobile generators, so this ends before household power returns.

pOccur.basis: TAB 2011: card payment and cash machines stop at once and most bank counters close within days. Venezuela 2019: cards unusable in the first days.

payments.basis: Nearly as long as the power window; what is on sale is sold for cash.

pOccur.basis: Cell sites carry 2-8 hours of battery and telecom sites 4 to 72 hours of backup (TAB 2011; EMP Commission 2008); Venezuela lost 96% of telecom capacity on day 3.

comms.basis: Counted from loss of service, about 0.3 to 1 day after the power fails; battery radio keeps working.

pOccur.basis: TAB 2011: without water toilets cannot be flushed and become blocked. About 70% of these days are lack of flush water, which hauled water cures; 30% are sewer pumping failures.

coldShare.basis: A 6-day event overlaps a 110-day cold season with probability 0.32; raised because collapses are likelier at winter peak load (the UK scenario assumes winter; Texas 2021).

hotShare.basis: (90 + 6) / 365 = 0.26, raised a little for summer-peak collapses (US Northeast, August 2003; Buenos Aires heat waves).

feasible.basis: United States. An unaffected region usually exists within 300-1,500 km (three separate interconnections; a storm hits high latitudes and coasts hardest) but few fuel stations have backup power (EMP Commission 2008), so reach is what is in the tank. In Texas 2021, 18% of affected people left home.

earliestDay.basis: It takes a day or two to learn that restoration will be slow and where the power is on; roads jam on the first day.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: A round trip of 600-1,500 km by car at about $0.45 a km, or bus or air fares for the household.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: The ordinary-hazards researcher's blend: hotel $95 a person a day, relatives or friends $10, mixed 40:60.

staple.basis: No useful warning, but for the first day or two some shops sell for cash before shelves empty (TAB 2011: 2 to 5 days).

specialty.basis: Generators, stoves, fuel and batteries go in the first hours.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: The Berkeley Lab survey in prior-art.md: in a 3-day outage 20% of households lose income, $1,157 each, about $77 per household-day. Mean event length about 17 days x $60 a day (more hourly workers idle, partly offset by employers and aid) = $1,000, plus about $200 of refrigerated food, rounded down.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

bankingCrisis.label: Bank freeze or currency crisis
bankingCrisis.definition: Within 12 months the household either cannot freely use its bank deposits for three days or more (bank holiday, deposit freeze, withdrawal limits, forced conversion), or holds a currency that loses 30% or more of its value against other major currencies or 25% or more of its domestic purchasing power. Bank failures resolved without loss of access, slower inflation, and exchange controls that leave local-currency deposits usable do not count by themselves.

forecast.basis: No US freeze or one-year currency loss of this size since the bank holiday of March 1933: 0 in 93 years, so the rule of succession gives 1% as an upper end. Advanced economies had 2 deposit freezes in about 1,700 country-years 1970-2017 (0.12% a year), both inside the euro (https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/wp/2018/wp18206.pdf); I take 0.05% for a freeze plus 0.15% for a dollar collapse.

pessimistic.basis: Dalio expects a debt 'heart attack' within about five years (https://fortune.com/2026/05/08/ray-dalio-america-national-debt-reshape-economy-heart-attack/) and Rogoff 'some kind of debt crisis, financial repression, inflation, maybe something more dramatic' within 5 to 10 years: about 10% a year for a debt crisis. Both describe 1970s-style inflation, so I take 15% of such crises to reach this threshold.

forecast.basis: Cyprus 2013 and Greece 2015 are 2 freezes in about 460 euro-area country-years since 1999 (0.43%), or 0.1% a year weighted by the population of western Europe (12 of 430 million people over 27 years). Iceland 2008 is the only currency collapse of this size in the region since 1999. I take 0.3%, between the two (https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/wp/2018/wp18206.pdf).

pessimistic.basis: A return of 2010-15 conditions, when 2 of about 17 euro members froze deposits within six years (2% per country-year). Rogoff names the UK, France and Belgium as candidates for a debt crisis (https://247wallst.com/personal-finance/2026/08/29/a-harvard-economist-says-the-debt-reckoning-is-coming-and-names-who-pays-for-it/).

forecast.basis: The peso lost 30% or more against the dollar in 5 of the 35 years since 1992 (2002, 2018, 2019, 2022, 2023; official December averages), 14%, and in 5 of 25 since 2002, 20% (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_exchange_rates_of_Argentine_currency); the IMF database dates 9 crisis onsets in 6 distinct episodes in 1970-2017, 12-19% a year. I take 15%: a fiscal surplus and a unified rate against the 2027 election and country risk of 840-950 points.

pessimistic.basis: Since controls began in 2011 the official peso lost 30% or more in 4 of 15 years and 25% or more in 10 of 15, and every presidential election year (2011, 2015, 2019, 2023) brought a devaluation or new controls. Álvarez Agis says the 2027 financial programme 'no cierra' and asks for controls back (https://eleconomista.com.ar/economia/advertencia-alvarez-agis-2027-en-vez-una-corrida-cambiaria-vamos-tener-una-maraton-n99269/amp).

pOccur.basis: About one third of events would be freezes and not currency falls, times a 0.6 chance that a household with a card still meets days of cash-only sellers and empty ATMs. In Greece 2015 and Cyprus 2013 cards kept working in shops.

payments.basis: Days on which the household cannot pay, not the length of the controls. Five of six bank holidays in the IMF database lasted 4-8 days and Greece's 21 (https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/wp/2018/wp18206.pdf); the US holiday ran from 6 March 1933 and banks holding 90% of resources were open by 15 March (https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/bank-holiday-of-1933).

pOccur.basis: No day without access to food is recorded in Cyprus 2013, Greece 2015 or Iceland 2008, where foreign currency was rationed to food, medicine and oil. The figure allows for shops shutting during a panic.

food.basis: No rich-country case to measure; lengths taken from the one-to-three-day shop closures seen in Argentina.

feasible.basis: Leaving does not restore access to money held in home banks, and controls block transfers abroad. It helps only a household that already holds funds outside the country.

earliestDay.basis: Time to arrange travel abroad without normal access to funds.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Travel abroad for a household of two or three; not priced.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Lodging and food abroad beyond normal living costs; not priced.

staple.basis: An alert household could still draw a week or two of cash and buy food in every case but Cyprus. Only a fifth to a quarter of deposits left before the freezes in Argentina (85 to 67 billion) and Greece (about 50 billion euros), mostly large balances, so most households did not act.

specialty.basis: Foreign currency, gold and transfers abroad are rationed first: Iceland restricted currency purchases from 10 October 2008 and Greece barred transfers abroad on the first day.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Reference deposit $20,500 times loss share 8% (1.5-27%). The mid is the mean loss per event.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

pOccur.basis: Most western European events would be freezes, but in Greece card purchases in shops were exempt and ATMs paid EUR 60 a day, and in Cyprus ATMs paid a daily limit. The window is the days of empty ATMs and cash-only sellers.

payments.basis: Greek banks were shut for almost 20 days from 29 June 2015 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_controls_in_Greece); Cypriot banks shut on 18 March 2013 for 8 days by the IMF's count. Limits then ran to September 2019 in Greece and April 2015 in Cyprus without stopping daily spending.

pOccur.basis: None recorded in Cyprus, Greece or Iceland; Greece capped import approvals at EUR 20 million a day with priority for medicines and food.

food.basis: No case to measure.

feasible.basis: Leaving does not unfreeze deposits; it helps only a household with funds already abroad.

earliestDay.basis: Time to arrange travel without normal access to funds.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Travel to a neighbouring country; not priced.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Lodging and food beyond normal living costs; not priced.

staple.basis: Cash could be drawn until the last weekend in Greece and not at all in Cyprus; food stayed on sale in both.
