specialty.basis: Transfers abroad and foreign currency were blocked from the first day in both Cyprus and Greece.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Reference deposit $10,000 times loss share 9% (1-35%). The mid is the mean loss per event.

pOccur.basis: Freezes are about one in six Argentine episodes (1989-90 and 2001-02 out of some eleven onsets since 1975), and in 2001-02 debit cards kept working while much of retail took only cash: 0.15 x 0.6.

payments.basis: Bank holidays of 4 days from 1 January 1990 and 5 days from 31 December 2001 (https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/wp/2018/wp18206.pdf), and 19-25 April 2002 (from the money-docs file). The limit of 250 pesos a week then ran for a year but covered ordinary spending.

pOccur.basis: Shops shut for one to three days during re-pricing and looting in mid-1989 and December 2001; those days are also counted under civilUnrest, so this is the remainder. Price controls remove single products, not access to food.

food.basis: Length of the looting waves: seven days in December 2001, 35 hours in Córdoba in 2013.

pOccur.basis: One clear case in some eleven episodes: in January 2002 wholesalers delivered about 30% of pharmacy orders and diabetics could not find insulin (https://www.pagina12.com.ar/diario/sociedad/3-463-2002-01-04.html). It concerns imported drugs, not all pharmacy access.

medication.basis: The 2002 shortage was reported from the first days of January and the government guaranteed insulin from 10 January after a Brazilian donation (search snippet).

feasible.basis: Leaving does not unfreeze deposits; it helps only a household with funds already abroad, such as an account in Uruguay.

earliestDay.basis: Time to arrange travel without normal access to funds.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Ferry or flight to Uruguay for a household; not priced.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Lodging and food in Uruguay beyond normal living costs; not priced.

staple.basis: Cash and food stayed obtainable up to the announcement in 1989 and 2001, and Argentine households are practised: individuals now buy about 3 billion dollars a month (Álvarez Agis, October 2026).

specialty.basis: Since April 2025 individuals can buy dollars without limit, so an alert household can still convert while the rate is inside the band. Under the 2019-25 controls it could buy USD 200 a month at the official rate (search snippet); beyond that it paid a parallel premium that passed 100% in May 2013 and reached 200% in October 2023.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Reference deposit $4,500 times loss share 35% (15-70%). The mid is the mean loss per event.

civilUnrest.label: Serious unrest
civilUnrest.definition: Within 12 months the household's city or district has serious rioting or looting, a riot curfew or state of siege, or disorder sustained over days, or there is armed conflict on home territory. Peaceful mass protest and single clashes confined to a government quarter do not count.

forecast.basis: Share of residents living in a city under riot curfew or with serious rioting: about 0.6% a year over 1965-2026 and 1.5% over 2015-2026, nearly all from 2020, when at least 200 cities imposed curfews (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Floyd_protests) covering some 60 million people (search snippet). The 1960s and 1992 populations are my estimates.

pessimistic.basis: A wave on the scale of 2020 every five to seven years. Verisk Maplecroft ranks the US first among Western democracies and fifth in the world for unrest risk (https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/international/2026/02/17/858246.htm); Dalio put a civil war 'of some sort' at 35-40% (Financial Times, May 2024, search snippet).

forecast.basis: By commune: France about 4% a year (274 towns in 2005, city centres in 2018-19, at least 672 communes in 2023, autumn 2026; my estimate is that these hold 15-35% of the population each time), England about 1% (2011, 2024), other countries about 0.3%; weighted by population, 1% (https://www.publicsenat.fr/actualites/parlementaire/emeutes-de-2023-un-cout-colossal-estime-a-un-milliard-deuros-selon-le-rapport-du-senat).

pessimistic.basis: Verisk Maplecroft's gauge of large-scale unrest in Europe is at its highest since 2021 and insurers are capping riot cover (https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/international/2026/11/12/892199.htm). France already runs at about 4% on this measure; I add 0.1% a year for war reaching western Europe.

forecast.basis: Greater Buenos Aires had looting waves or a state of siege in 1989, 2001, 2013 and 2023: four in the 43 years since 1983, 9% a year for the region. The city proper was hit in 2001 (7 of 39 deaths, a state of siege of about 36 hours) and in 1989, 2-5% a year (https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_de_diciembre_de_2001_en_Argentina).

pessimistic.basis: The regional frequency of 9% applied to the household, on the view that a currency break around the 2027 election would bring a December like 2001. No published forecast found.

pOccur.basis: Curfews are overnight and shops elsewhere stay open. In 2020 Target cut hours at about 200 of 1,900 stores and Walmart shut hundreds for a day (search snippets); in Los Angeles in 1992 mail delivery stopped and stores burned across the riot area.

food.basis: Riots last 5-8 days (Los Angeles 29 April to 3 May 1992) with shops shut for part of that; the 99th percentile stands for armed conflict.

pOccur.basis: Homes burned are rare: at least 100 families among roughly 3 million households in the affected English boroughs in 2011 (my population estimate), 1,100 buildings in Los Angeles. Most of the figure is the conflict share of 3%, in which a third of households move.

displacement.basis: Weeks to rehouse after a fire; months to years in armed conflict.

pOccur.basis: No general shutdown has been ordered during riots in the US or western Europe; France's president threatened one in 2023 and none was applied (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahel_Merzouk_riots). The figure covers local damage and armed conflict.

comms.basis: No case to measure.

pOccur.basis: Cards keep working in shops that are open; the window needs ATMs and branches out of use and cash-only sellers.

payments.basis: Same length as the food window.

pOccur.basis: Pharmacies are looting targets: CVS shut stores in 20 states in 2020 and 16 were damaged in Minneapolis-St Paul (search snippet). Another pharmacy is usually within reach by day.

medication.basis: Length of the riot.

pOccur.basis: Ambulances and fire crews are delayed or kept out while rioting is active; about 3,600 fires were set in Los Angeles in 1992.

emergencyCare.basis: Nights of active rioting.

feasible.basis: Riots are local and curfews apply at night, so a household can reach relatives or a hotel outside the district by day. Lower in armed conflict.

earliestDay.basis: The morning after the first night.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Fuel or tickets to a place outside the city; not priced.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Hotel shared by the household, or little when staying with relatives; not priced.

staple.basis: Shops outside the affected district, and by day inside it, stay open and stocked; an alert household can buy a week of food and fill prescriptions before nightfall.

specialty.basis: Items people rush for locally sell out; no data.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: Riots, 0.5: 19 deaths among some 60 million under curfew in 2020 (0.3 per million) and 55-63 among the 3.5 million residents of Los Angeles in 1992 (16-18; population recalled), most of them on the street. Armed conflict, 300 (50-3,000) in 3% (0.5-10%) of events, from Northern Ireland in 1972 and Ukraine in 2022 (both recalled). 0.5 + 0.03 x 300.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Riots, about $20: insured losses of $1-2 billion in 2020 are $45-90 per household under curfew, nearly all commercial. Armed conflict, $15,000 of lost income, damage and moving in 3% of events.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

pOccur.basis: More than 1,000 shops were damaged in France in 2023, 2,584 in England in 2011 and at least 3,000 in France in 2026, a small share of all shops; rioting is at night and shops elsewhere stay open.

food.basis: Waves lasted 8 days in 2023, 6 in 2011 and 21 in 2005; the 99th percentile stands for armed conflict.

pOccur.basis: At least 100 families were made homeless in England in 2011. Most of the figure is the conflict share of 2%, in which a third of households move.

displacement.basis: Weeks to rehouse after a fire; months to years in armed conflict.

pOccur.basis: No shutdown was applied in France in 2023 or England in 2011, though both governments discussed one.

comms.basis: No case to measure.

pOccur.basis: 366 bank branches were among the shops damaged in France in 2023, so local ATMs fail; cards keep working in open shops.

payments.basis: Same length as the food window.

pOccur.basis: Pharmacies are among looted shops but another is usually within reach by day.

medication.basis: Length of the riot.

pOccur.basis: Fire and ambulance crews are delayed during active rioting; London's fire brigade fought over 100 serious fires in 2011.

emergencyCare.basis: Nights of active rioting.

feasible.basis: Rioting is confined to some districts and to the night; trains and roads out run by day, though France stopped buses and trams at 9 pm in 2023.

earliestDay.basis: The morning after the first night.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Train tickets or fuel; not priced.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Hotel shared by the household, or little when staying with relatives; not priced.

staple.basis: Shops are open by day and outside the affected districts.

specialty.basis: No data.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: Riots, 0.2: 2 deaths in France in 2023, 3 in 2005, and 5 in England in 2011 among roughly 8 million people in the affected boroughs (my estimate), 0.6 per million. Armed conflict, 300 (50-3,000) in 2% (0.3-8%) of events (recalled anchors). 0.2 + 0.02 x 300.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Riots, about $10: 12,031 vehicles burned in France in 2023 among roughly 11 million households in the 672 communes (my estimate) is 0.1% losing a car, half uninsured for fire. Armed conflict, $12,000 in 2% of events.

pOccur.basis: Looting in Argentina targets food shops and shopkeepers shut in advance: in December 2013 thousands of shops in Greater Buenos Aires closed early, and in August 2023 many in Once and Flores shut on rumours alone (https://chequeado.com/el-explicador/saqueos-en-el-conurbano-que-videos-circularon-y-que-paso-en-cada-municipio/).

food.basis: Seven days of looting in December 2001, two to three days in the conurbano in August 2023, 35 hours in Córdoba in 2013 (https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saqueos_en_Argentina_de_2013).

pOccur.basis: Homes are not the target of looting waves; the figure is mostly the conflict share of 1%.
No shutdown found in any Argentine episode.

comms.basis: No case to measure.

pOccur.basis: Small shops prefer cash, and banks and ATMs shut where there is rioting; in 2001 the unrest coincided with the withdrawal limit, which is counted under bankingCrisis.

payments.basis: Same length as the food window.

pOccur.basis: Pharmacies shut with other shops for the same days.

medication.basis: Length of the looting wave.

pOccur.basis: Ambulances delayed where streets are blocked or police are absent, as in the 2013 police strikes.

emergencyCare.basis: Days of active disorder.

feasible.basis: Looting is confined to some districts; the 2001 state of siege lasted about 36 hours and did not close roads out of the city.

earliestDay.basis: The next morning.

fixedUsdPerHousehold.basis: Bus tickets or fuel at local prices; not priced.

usdPerPersonDay.basis: Lodging at local prices, or little when staying with relatives; not priced.

staple.basis: Waves start in other provinces days earlier and shops stay open until rumours reach the neighbourhood.

specialty.basis: No data.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: Riots, 0.5: 7 deaths in a city of about 3 million in December 2001 (2.4 per million) and 11 in the province, most of them demonstrators or looters; none in the metropolitan area in 2013 or 2023. Armed conflict, 300 in 1% of events (recalled anchors). 0.5 + 0.01 x 300.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Riots, about $5 in lost days of informal work and damage; armed conflict, $5,000 in 1% of events. Shop owners lose far more: 400 million pesos among about 1,000 shops in Córdoba in 2013.

cyberOutage.label: Blackout from an attack or software failure
cyberOutage.definition: Grid power out for a day or more across a metropolitan region or larger because of a cyberattack, sabotage of grid-connected assets, or a failure of software or AI-run operations (including data-centre load events), not weather. An attack that destroys long-lead equipment (dozens of large transformers or generators) and keeps power off for weeks is gridLong.

us.basis: Kept at 0.1% on revision (20 Nov 2026). Pilot medians at face value: 1% x 12% = 0.12%, plus ~0.05% from $1-10bn events, shaded to 0.1%. Cross-check with Sentinel's 'Consider cyberarmageddon' (19 Nov 2026; 33%, 10-60%, for a week-long non-natural outage of power, telecoms, payments or water for 1M+ people in an OECD country by end-2028): ordinary events give about 0.06% a year per resident for week-plus outages, of which I give power a tenth (its forecasters: power is 'not the most likely trigger'), divided by the 10% of attack blackouts that last a week under the new windows = 0.06%; plus a 1% yearly chance of a disruption year at the scale of its 4.9% tail x 3% of households losing power for a day = 0.03%; total 0.09%. Lo: sceptic in the line of Maschmeyer. Hi: pilot upper quartile with uplift (7-10%) x 12%. https://blog.sentinel-team.org/p/consider-cyberarmageddon

westernEurope.basis: Kept at 0.08% on revision (20 Nov 2026): twice baseline, as for the US. Sentinel's 33% by end-2028 for a week-long non-natural OECD outage treats all members alike and, converted as in the US entry, supports the same order (about 0.09%). The nearest misses are European: Poland, 29 December 2025 (over 30 wind and solar sites and a heat plant, no loss of supply), a UK generator shut for four days in July 2026, and arson on Berlin's cables (January 2026: 45,000 households and 2,200 businesses for about four and a half days in frost), which shows how long a physical hit lasts. Lo: none of these was a cyberattack that cut supply. Hi: intent to destroy, in winter. https://blog.sentinel-team.org/p/consider-cyberarmageddon

buenosAires.basis: Revised 20 Nov 2026 from 0.03%. Twice baseline (incidents reported to CERT.ar rose from 200-400 a year to more than 700 in 2026, and AI-run intrusion campaigns pick targets by weakness), plus a share of the disruption-year tail in Sentinel's 'Consider cyberarmageddon' (4.9% for more than 100M human-years of disruption in 2028), which a self-spreading attack would carry beyond the OECD: 1% a year x 1% of Buenos Aires households losing power for a day = 0.01%. Sentinel's 33% headline covers OECD countries only. Lo: reporting, not attacks, rose. Hi: weak defences on a grid that already fails often. https://blog.sentinel-team.org/p/consider-cyberarmageddon

power.basis: Given a day or more. Physical hits are repaired with spares in days: Moore County, North Carolina (gunfire, 3 December 2022, up to 40,000-45,000 customers; 'virtually all power had been restored' about four days later, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moore_County_substation_attack); Berlin (arson, September 2025, about 50,000 households and businesses for about 60 hours; January 2026, up to 45,000 households and over 2,000 businesses, all reconnected on 7 January, about four and a half days in frost; https://www.cbsnews.com/news/berlin-power-outage-vulkangruppe-left-wing-arson-attack-called-terrorism/). Cyberattacks so far were undone in hours by manual operation (Ukraine 2015, about 225,000 customers, 1-6 hours; Kyiv 2016, about 75 minutes). Accidental cascades end within a day or two (Iberia 2025: 'about ten hours in most of the Peninsula', 99% of demand back after about 18.5 hours). Tail: damage at many substations at once, or attacks repeated on restoration, short of destroying transformers. In Venezuela's national blackout of 7 March 2019, blamed by the government on sabotage, Reuters reported reliable service restored only four to six days later in most major cities (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Venezuelan_blackouts). Was 2, 6, 14.

water.basis: Pressure loss and boil-water notices when pumps lose power; treatment plants and towers hold a day or more. p99 lengthened from 8 to 10 days with the power tail. Guess.

comms.basis: Cell sites run hours on batteries and 24-72 hours where a generator is fitted (comms.json); in a long blackout mobile service follows power, less the sites operators reach with portable generators. p99 lengthened from 12 to 14 days. Guess.

payments.basis: Card terminals and ATMs need power and network; shops with generators sell for cash. Follows the power window, slightly shorter. Was 2, 6, 14.

food.basis: Shops close without power and chilled stock is lost; most reopen on generators or restock within days. p99 lengthened from 7 to 10 days. Guess.

medication.basis: New: pharmacies close without power or their claims and dispensing systems; in a week-long outage the household must travel to one outside the area. Guess.

sanitation.basis: Toilets fail with water pressure in high-rise buildings and where sewage lift stations lack generators. p99 lengthened from 10 to 14 days. Guess.

power.basis: Slower restoration: Edesur and Edenor already take days after heat-wave failures, and spares are imported.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: As for a severe storm (hazards-ordinary.json): improvised power and cooking.
As for a severe storm (hazards-ordinary.json): candles and improvised cooking.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

paymentsOutage.label: Payment systems down
paymentsOutage.definition: For a day or more the household cannot pay by card, use ATMs or reach its main bank, because of an attack on, or a software failure in, the bank, its core-banking or card processors, the card networks or interbank systems, while shops stay open and no bank is insolvent (that is bankingCrisis).

us.basis: Revised 20 Nov 2026 from 0.15% on Sentinel's 'Consider cyberarmageddon'. Its 33% (10-60%) by end-2028 for a week-long non-natural outage of power, telecoms, payments or water for 1M+ people in an OECD country is about 0.06% a year per resident from ordinary events (0.16 events a year x ~5M people out a week / 1.40bn). I give payments half (pure software; the closest OECD precedent is a Korean bank's 3-7 day lockout in 2011), x1.3 for lockouts below 1M (credit unions, 2023), divided by the 22% of payments outages that last a week (days 3, 10, 35) = 0.18%. Its 4.9% tail for more than 100M human-years of disruption in 2028, taken as 1% a year at today's capabilities x 30% of households losing cards and bank access for a day, adds 0.3%: total 0.48%. Lo: the post's own Laplace rule (9% over two years), no tail. Hi: its 60%, and a 5% disruption year in which half of households lose payments. https://blog.sentinel-team.org/p/consider-cyberarmageddon

westernEurope.basis: Revised 20 Nov 2026 from 0.15%: as for the US, since Sentinel's 33% for a week-long non-natural outage covers every OECD country alike (https://blog.sentinel-team.org/p/consider-cyberarmageddon); the Bank of England's July 2026 warning applies directly.

buenosAires.basis: Revised 20 Nov 2026 from 0.25%. Ordinary events at 1.5 times the US ordinary part (0.18% x 1.5 = 0.27%), for a few shared processors with weaker defences: a Red Link failure on 16-17 November 2026 hit the home banking of about 30 banks at once. Plus the disruption-year tail of Sentinel's 'Consider cyberarmageddon' (4.9% for more than 100M human-years of disruption in 2028), which would reach Argentina as readily as the OECD: 1% a year x 30% = 0.3%; total 0.57%. Sentinel's 33% headline covers OECD countries only. Lo: hours, not days, and not an attack. Hi: a wiper at one processor plus the US high case. https://blog.sentinel-team.org/p/consider-cyberarmageddon

payments.basis: Given a day or more. Bank systems wiped or encrypted come back in days for cards and cash machines and in weeks for everything. NongHyup, South Korea (12 April 2011): some 30 million account holders; ATMs and online banking back after two to three days, cards after three to four, data recovery expected by 22 April (https://spectrum.ieee.org/riskfactor/computing/it/south-korean-banks-weeklong-system-failure-affecting-30-million-an-inside-job); Sentinel's forecaster puts it at 3 to 7 days. Iran, June 2025: Pasargad limited services after about two days, Sepah basic cards after three, full recovery after ten, while online banking and ATMs were 'largely nonfunctional' twelve days on (https://www.iranintl.com/en/202507192001). Iran, June 2026: problems at four state banks from 13-14 June, failing again on 23 June, 'lasting more than two weeks'. About 60 US credit unions on one processor (from 26 November 2023): at NY Bravest FCU debit cards worked again after 12 days and online banking after 14. Coveware's last published average downtime after ransomware was 24 days (Q2 2022). Hours-long failures (Chase and Red Link, November 2026; CrowdStrike, 2024) fall below the threshold. Was 2, 7, 30.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

commsOutage.label: Mobile and internet down
commsOutage.definition: Mobile and home internet both unusable for the household for a day or more, across a national operator or a metropolitan region, because of an attack on, or a software or configuration failure in, the operators or the networks and cloud services they depend on. Natural disasters and power cuts are other hazards.

all.basis: Revised 20 Nov 2026 from 0.08% on Sentinel's 'Consider cyberarmageddon'. Its 33% by end-2028 for a week-long non-natural OECD outage converts to about 0.06% a year per resident from ordinary events; I give telecoms three tenths (KDDI's 61-hour outage of 31 million users in 2022 is its 'close hit'), halve it because the household is cut off only when mobile and home internet fail together, and divide by the 10% of outages that last a week (days 2, 7, 25) = 0.09%. Its 4.9% tail for more than 100M human-years of disruption in 2028, as 1% a year at today's capabilities x 10% of households = 0.1%; total 0.19%. Lo: the post's own Laplace rule (9% over two years). Hi: its 60%, and a 5% disruption year cutting off a quarter of households. https://blog.sentinel-team.org/p/consider-cyberarmageddon

comms.basis: Given a day or more. KDDI, Japan (2 July 2022, a router replaced in maintenance): up to 39.15 million lines; the outage proper lasted 61 hours 25 minutes and full recovery was declared after about 86 (https://watch.impress.co.jp/docs/news/1428430.html). Kyivstar, Ukraine (12 December 2023, Russian attack): 24.3 million mobile subscribers and 1.1 million home-internet customers; 'without mobile signal and internet for two days', voice nationwide by 14 December, all services including 4G by 16 December, 100% by 20 December (https://therecord.media/ukraine-kyivstar-hack-high-impact). Tail: an attack that bricks equipment, as with Viasat's KA-SAT modems (24 February 2022; nearly 30,000 replacement modems shipped by 30 March; https://www.viasat.com/perspectives/corporate/2022/ka-sat-network-cyber-attack-overview/). Rogers (2022), Optus (2023) and AT&T (2024) were restored within a day and fall below the threshold. Was 1.5, 5, 14.

payments.basis: Card terminals and ATMs that ride on the failed network; shops switch to other networks or cash. p99 lengthened from 7 to 10 days with the comms tail.

emergencyCare.basis: No way to call an ambulance from the failed operator; in Europe 112 roams onto other networks, in the KDDI outage emergency calls failed. Lengthened from 1, 2, 5 with the comms tail.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

cyberSupplyShock.label: Shops or pharmacies down from an attack or software failure
cyberSupplyShock.definition: For a day or more, the shops the household normally uses cannot sell it most of its usual food, or its pharmacy cannot fill its prescriptions, because of an attack on, or a software failure in, a retailer, distributor, logistics provider, till or payment system, or pharmacy-claims or e-prescribing system. Motor fuel is left out: the model has no fuel window.

all.basis: Revised 20 Nov 2026 from 1% (old definition). Twice baseline (GAO: up to 227 food-and-agriculture ransomware incidents in 2026, 'on pace to be one of the highest'; Anthropic: most criminal operations it disrupted were AI-run) = 0.8%, plus the disruption-year tail of Sentinel's 'Consider cyberarmageddon' (4.9% for more than 100M human-years of disruption in 2028), as 1% a year at today's capabilities x 30% of households whose usual shops or pharmacy stop = 0.3%; total 1.1%. Lo: volume is not consumer impact. Hi: the October 2026 attack that spoiled stock at hundreds of European supermarkets becomes typical, and a 5% disruption year. https://blog.sentinel-team.org/p/consider-cyberarmageddon

food.basis: The window opens only when no shop the household can reach sells food: a town or island served by the stricken chain, or a distributor that supplies most local shops. Coop Sweden (2 July 2021, ransomware through Kaseya): tills down, about 700 of 800 stores closed, all reopened 'within six days' (https://www.truesec.com/hub/blog/back-in-business-after-the-largest-ransomware-attack-of-all-time). UK Co-op (May 2025): about two weeks of shortages, Shetland shelves 'nearly bare', normal ordering from 14 May. UNFI (from 5 June 2025): main ordering platform back within 10 days, core ordering systems on 26 June, full core operations on 16 July, with Whole Foods stores missing items for weeks (https://www.grocerydive.com/news/unfi-cyberattack-contained-/751866/). Stop & Shop (November 2024): product shortages for about two weeks. M&S stopped online orders for 46 days (25 April to 10 June 2025), and Jaguar Land Rover's plants stopped from 1 September to 8 October 2025, with normal output only in mid-November: a firm's own recovery can take a month or more, though households switch shops or brands long before.

medication.basis: Pharmacy events are about half of the household-events counted in ai-cyber.json. Change Healthcare (21 February 2024): over 7,000 pharmacies and hospitals could not process prescriptions; more than 90% of pharmacies had workarounds within six days, and electronic prescribing with claims was 'fully functional' after 15 days (https://www.securityweek.com/change-healthcare-restores-pharmacy-services-disrupted-by-ransomware/). Hannaford's pharmacies had trouble filling prescriptions for about a day (November 2024). The tail is an attack on a pharmacy chain's own dispensing systems or on a drug wholesaler, which has not yet happened.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

aiFraud.label: Scam or account takeover
aiFraud.definition: Someone in the household loses money to an impersonation scam, or loses control of a financial, email or phone account, whether or not AI was used.

us.basis: Gallup: 10% of adults live in a household scammed in 2025; imposter scams are 'nearly one in three' FTC reports but lose money less often, so 2–3% of households; plus account takeover, Javelin's 6 million victims over about 132 million households (my assumption) = 4.5%, cut to 3% for overlap and vendor optimism. lo: BJS's 1.25% of adults plus takeover. hi: all scams.

westernEurope.basis: England and Wales: 7.8% of people were fraud victims in the year to March 2026, mostly card and bank fraud; about 71% of incidents involve a loss and 70% of those are fully reimbursed. I take roughly half of loss-bearing incidents as impersonation or takeover. Authorised push payment cases alone are 248,070, about 0.9% of UK households. No EU-wide annual prevalence exists.

buenosAires.basis: No survey gives Argentine fraud prevalence. Reports to the federal unit rose 21% in 2024 to 34,468, a small fraction of incidents. I assume the US rate, since impersonation by telephone and takeover of messaging accounts are common.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: ai-economy.json: mean unreimbursed loss per event in the United States.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

days.basis: Hours spent: identity-fraud victims averaged 10.4 hours in 2025, account takeover 17 (Javelin 2026, https://javelinstrategy.com/node/35385, read); BJS 2021: mean 3.9 hours for resolved and 9.1 for unresolved identity theft (https://bjs.ojp.gov/document/vit21.pdf, read). I take 10 hours per event, half of them in working hours (guess): 5 hours = 0.63 of an 8-hour day for the victim, 0.31 per adult.

greatPowerWar.label: War between great powers, short of nuclear
greatPowerWar.definition: A conventional war between the United States and China, or a Russia–NATO war of similar scale, that does not go nuclear. Its financial effects are not counted here: nothing on the list addresses them.

us.basis: Same chain with today's forecasts unadjusted: (1.3% + 1.0% x 0.5) x 0.88 = 1.6%. Lo: Polymarket prices a Chinese invasion of Taiwan by end-2026 at 1% and ODNI's March 2026 assessment sees no plan for 2027; hi: FutureSearch's 3% for a direct US-China war by end-2027 (2.4%/yr) plus Europe.

westernEurope.basis: (1.3% x 0.9 + 1.0%) x 0.88 = 1.9%. Lo: forecasters who read Q7452's 0.36%/yr as the right scale for Russia; hi: Metaculus Q8636 taken at face value plus FutureSearch's US-China figure.

buenosAires.basis: (1.3% x 0.8 + 1.0% x 0.35) x 0.88 = 1.2%. Ends as for the US entry, scaled by the same factors.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

houseFire.label: House fire (everyday)
houseFire.definition: The yearly risk of death and loss from fire at home, for a home with no working smoke alarm.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: Adult 15-59 in a home with no working smoke alarm. NFPA 2019-2023 home fire death rates by age give 5.2 per million for ages 15-59 (7.8 all ages; 8.6 in 2023 and 2024), so 5.4; divided by (1 - 0.84 x 0.55) because 84% of homes have a working alarm (CPSC 2024) that removes about 55%. https://content.nfpa.org/-/media/Project/Storefront/Catalog/Files/Research/NFPA-Research/US-Fire-Problem/oshomevictims.pdf

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: Home with no working alarm. Reported direct property damage $8.9bn a year in 2019-2023 and $11.4bn in 2024 over about 131M households is $68-87, about $85 in 2026 dollars; plus about $6 for 9,000-10,800 injuries at a guessed $70,000 each; scaled by 1.27 for the no-alarm state. Gross of insurance. https://content.nfpa.org/-/media/Project/Storefront/Catalog/Files/Research/NFPA-Research/US-Fire-Problem/osFireLoss.pdf

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

days.basis: Chance: 328,590 reported home fires a year over about 131M households = 0.25% (NFPA 2019-2023, fire-co.json); homes without alarms have 3.5-5 times as many reported fires (NIST TN 2020, fire-co.json) and are 16% of homes, so 0.25% / (0.84 + 0.16 x 4) x 4 = 0.68%; I use 0.6% (0.35-0.8%). Days per reported fire, guess: half are confined fires costing about half a day; of the rest about a third displace the household for about three weeks (Red Cross House, Philadelphia, 18 nights per family, snippet), costing 7.9 days on the workLoss.displacement profile plus 2.3 of paperwork and repairs (10.2), and two thirds cost 1.5 days: 0.5 x 0.5 + 0.5 x (0.35 x 10.2 + 0.65 x 1.5) = 2.5; 3 for unalarmed homes, whose fires grow larger. 0.006 x 3 = 0.018, plus 7.4M unreported fires a year (5.6% of homes) x 0.05 days = 0.003.

coIncident.label: Carbon monoxide at home (everyday)
coIncident.definition: The yearly risk of carbon monoxide poisoning at home from appliances, heaters, engines and vehicles, for a home with fuel-burning equipment and no alarm.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: CPSC 2020-2022: 238 consumer-product CO deaths a year, 126 in ordinary homes; minus about 18 from weather-outage generator use, plus a guessed 100 vehicle-exhaust deaths in home garages, is about 210 a year or 0.63 per million people; divided by 0.78 (homes with a CO source, a guess) and by (1 - 0.49 x 0.6) for the 49% with a working alarm. Adults 15-59 are at the population average. https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/Non-Fire-Carbon-Monoxide-Deaths-Associated-with-the-Use-of-Consumer-Products-2022-Annual-Estimates.pdf

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: CDC: more than 100,000 emergency visits and 14,000 hospital stays a year. At a guessed $3,000 per treated-and-released visit and $40,000 per admission that is about $0.8bn a year, $6 per household on average; about two thirds is home-related, scaled up for the no-alarm, fuel-burning home. https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

homeMedicalEmergency.label: Medical emergency at home (everyday)
homeMedicalEmergency.definition: The yearly risk of death from an emergency at home that is decided before the ambulance arrives: mostly cardiac arrest.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: Adult 15-59. CARES 2024 national estimate 263,711 EMS-treated arrests x ~36% aged 15-59 (CARES 2023 age figure) / 196M people = 48 per 100,000; x 73% at home x 90% fatal = 315; minus ~15% overdose arrests = ~270-280. https://mycares.net/sitepages/uploads/2025/2024_flipbook/inc/html/32.html

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

seasonalIllness.label: Seasonal respiratory infection (everyday)
seasonalIllness.definition: The yearly deaths from influenza, COVID-19 and similar infections that routine vaccination averts.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: medical.json, routine-vaccinations: yearly micromorts averted for an adult aged 15 to 59 of average risk against skipping all routine vaccines; 130 at ages 60 to 74 and 680 at 75 or over.

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

days.basis: Influenza: 6.1% of unvaccinated adults a year in moderate seasons (Tokars et al. 2018, https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/53814/cdc_53814_DS1.pdf, read) x 40% effectiveness x 2.8 days missed per episode (Keech 1998, abstract read) = 0.07, x 1.5 for reduced output at work = 0.10. COVID-19: about 12% of adults ill a year (43.6M and 33.0M illnesses in 2022-23 and 2023-24, CDC via search snippet, over 335M) x 23.5% of symptomatic infections averted x 3.6 days (Beck et al. 2025, a Moderna-authored model, read) = 0.10. Total 0.2. Lo is the Cochrane pooled result for influenza vaccine, 0.04 working days (-0.14 to 0.06) (https://www.cochrane.org/CD001269/ARI_vaccines-prevent-influenza-healthy-adults, read), with little from COVID; hi uses Nichol 1995 (52 fewer sick-leave days per 100 vaccinees, snippet).

violentCrime.label: Burglary and assault at home (everyday)
violentCrime.definition: The yearly risk of death and loss from burglary and assault at home.

micromortsPerPerson.basis: plans-skills-security.json, corrected: about 0.3 from burglary (FBI expanded homicide data, 80 to 110 a year) plus 0.8 from robbery at home.

financialUsdPerHousehold.basis: 8.2 burglaries per 1,000 households in 2024 (12.0 with trespassing; BJS) x [about $2,000 property loss (FBI mean for police-recorded burglaries was $2,661 in 2019, search snippet; survey burglaries include attempts and unreported cases, so lower) + about $2,000 for repairs, time and distress (guess, 500-6,000)] = $33; plus 7% of burglaries involving violence against a member (BJS 2003-2007) x $15,000 (guess, 5,000-40,000) = $9. https://bjs.ojp.gov/document/cv24.pdf

durationScale.basis: Uncertainty about how long disruptions of this kind last, applied to every window of the hazard.

days.basis: Burglary: 8.2 per 1,000 households in 2024 (BJS, plans-skills-security.json); in 9.7% a victim lost time from work, for <1 day (29.3%), 1-5 (49.0%), 6-10 (11.1%) or 11+ (10.7%) (NCVS 2008 Statistical Tables 87 and 89, https://bjs.ojp.gov/redirect-legacy/content/pub/pdf/cvus0804.pdf, read): mean 4.4 days, so 0.43 per burglary, 0.23 per adult at 1.9 adults per household; x 0.0082 = 0.002. Violence at home by outsiders, guessed at 5 per 1,000 adults a year (about a third of a violent-victimisation rate of about 22 per 1,000, recalled, less offenders from the household); 7.2% lose time, mean 4.9 days: 0.35 per victimisation, x 0.005 = 0.002. Total 0.004.

items.name: Bottled water in rotation
items.spec: Factory-sealed bottled water (40 x 0.5 L case = 20 L, or 1 gal jugs) bought ahead and drunk oldest-first. Ladder in litres per person at 3 L per person per day.
items.units: litre of bottled water per person

price.basis: Wholesale average $1.44 per gallon in 2023 = $0.38 per litre (https://bottledwater.org/how-much-does-bottled-water-cost/); Walmart 40 x 16.9 fl oz at $5.47 = $0.27 per litre (search snippet; page refused). Midpoint of the two; high end is branded or small packs.

lifeYears.basis: Printed best-by dates are typically about two years; sealed water stays safe longer but can pick up taste.

setupHours.basis: One larger shopping trip and a place to keep it.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Rotation happens through ordinary drinking.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Replacement cost is already in the price and life.

everydayShare.basis: Near 1 for households that drink bottled water anyway, near 0 for those that never do; the middle value is a population blend.

reliability.basis: Sealed and portable; the main failure is drinking the stock down and not replacing it.

items.name: Stored tap water
items.spec: Tap water in food-grade rigid containers (7 gal / 26 L jugs; a 55 gal barrel for the top steps), sanitised with bleach, kept cool and dark, refilled yearly. Ladder in litres per person at 3 L per person per day.
items.units: litre of stored water per person

price.basis: Container cost per litre: Reliance Aqua-Tainer 26 L at $19.88 (Walmart) to $24.95 (REI) = $0.76-0.96 per litre, both from search snippets because the pages refused the fetch. Low end: reused 2 L drink bottles or a 55 gal barrel at about $0.5 per litre. The water itself is under a cent.

lifeYears.basis: HDPE water containers last a decade or more indoors; spigots and seals fail first.

setupHours.basis: Choose, buy, sanitise, fill and label four to six containers.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: water-sanitation.json gives 0.5 hours a year for a 14-day store and says it scales with litres.

everydayShare.basis: No everyday use beyond an occasional supply interruption.

reliability.basis: Failures: leaks, a dirty container, water never refilled after a first use. Clean chlorinated tap water sealed in the dark stays safe well past the rotation date.

items.name: Know how to draw from the water heater
items.spec: One-off action for a home with its own storage water heater: find the cold-inlet valve and the drain valve, keep a short hose and a bucket beside the tank, and write on the tank: shut inlet, switch off power or gas, open a hot tap, drain. Gives access to the 115-190 L already in the tank.

price.basis: A short hose and a label; many homes already have both.

lifeYears.basis: Lasts until the household moves or the heater is replaced.

setupHours.basis: Find the valves, try the drain valve once, write the steps.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: A yearly sediment flush, which manufacturers recommend anyway.

everydayShare.basis: Knowing the shut-offs and flushing sediment have ordinary maintenance value.

reliability.basis: Fails when unsafe water entered the tank before the inlet was shut (boil-water events), when sediment blocks the drain valve, when the tank is damaged (earthquake, flood), or when nobody remembers.

items.name: Bathtub water bladder
items.spec: WaterBOB 100 gal (380 L) single-use bathtub liner with siphon pump, filled from the tap when a warning arrives.
items.note: Only useful when there is warning and the tap still runs; the 75 litres already allow for that.

price.basis: $39.99 at https://www.citymill.com/188370-water-bob; other retailers $25-40 in search snippets; the maker's site showed no price and was out of stock.

lifeYears.basis: Shelf life of the unused liner; one use consumes it.

setupHours.basis: Buy, read the instructions, store by the tub.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: None.

everydayShare.basis: No everyday use.

reliability.basis: Punctures, a tap fitting that does not match, not finding it in time. Dependence on warning is in the supply amount, not here.

items.name: Hollow-fibre water filter
items.spec: Sawyer Mini 0.1 micron hollow-fibre filter with squeeze pouch and backflush syringe; used once on tap water to learn it.

price.basis: Listed at $28.99 on https://www.sawyer.com/products/mini-water-filtration-system; high end is the larger Sawyer Squeeze.

lifeYears.basis: No expiry dry; ruined if frozen after first use. Field units under daily use with turbid water fouled within months to two years, which a household emergency would not reach.

setupHours.basis: Buy, read the instructions, filter and backflush once.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Check it is dry, complete and has not frozen.

everydayShare.basis: Real everyday value only for hikers and travellers.

reliability.basis: Invisible fibre damage from freezing, clogging in silty water, lost syringe, dirty-side to clean-side contamination by the user.

items.name: Chlorine dioxide tablets
items.spec: Chlorine dioxide purification tablets, pack of 30, one tablet per litre (Katadyn Micropur MP1 or Potable Aqua chlorine dioxide).

price.basis: Katadyn Micropur MP1 30-pack at $15.95 (Sportsman's) and $17.95 (Bass Pro, REI), $13.46 on sale; all from search snippets because the pages refused the fetch.

lifeYears.basis: Foil-sealed tablets carry roughly a five-year date (longlist; not checked on a label).

setupHours.basis: Buy and read the wait times.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Glance at the expiry date.

everydayShare.basis: Almost none outside travel and hiking.

reliability.basis: Expired packs, users who do not wait the four hours Cryptosporidium needs, weaker action in cold or cloudy water, taste rejection.

items.name: Plain bleach, dropper and dosing card
items.spec: One 81 fl oz bottle of plain unscented household bleach (5-9% sodium hypochlorite, not splashless or scented), replaced yearly, with a medicine dropper and a printed card: 2 drops per litre (8 per gallon), double if cloudy, wait 30 minutes.

price.basis: Clorox Disinfecting Bleach 81 fl oz, 7.5% sodium hypochlorite, $6.39 at Target (https://www.target.com/p/clorox-disinfecting-bleach-regular-81oz/-/A-77787198), plus about $2 for a dropper.

lifeYears.basis: Maker gives a one-year shelf life; strength falls roughly 20% a year after the first six months (one manufacturer statement, search snippet).

setupHours.basis: Check the label is plain bleach, print the card, tape the dropper to the bottle.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Swap the bottle yearly.

everydayShare.basis: Used for laundry and cleaning in households that buy bleach at all; zero in those that do not.

reliability.basis: Wrong product on the shelf (scented, splashless), old bottle, dosing by guess without the dropper, not waiting, cloudy water.

items.name: Water carriers
items.spec: Two closed 5 gal (19 L) carriers, collapsible or rigid, to bring water from a distribution point, neighbour, standpipe, rain or surface source; also for flush water.

price.basis: Two Reliance Fold-A-Carrier 5 gal at $11.49-12.99 each (search snippets; pages refused); rigid Hedpak $23.95 each per the longlist.

lifeYears.basis: Collapsible carriers crack at the folds sooner than rigid ones.

setupHours.basis: Buy and rinse.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Check for cracks.

everydayShare.basis: Camping and garden use for some households.

reliability.basis: Simple objects; failure is a split seam or not finding them.

adherence.basis: Needs a reachable source and someone able to carry 19 kg; stairs in tall buildings cut this.

fraction.basis: Hauled water flushes a toilet at 6 L a flush when the sewer still works; an improvised bucket does the same less well, so the increment is small.

items.name: Emergency toilet kit
items.spec: 5 gal bucket with snap-on seat and lid (Reliance Luggable Loo), one 6-pack of gel-lined double bags, a roll of 30 heavy 13 gal liners, 10 lb of cat litter or other absorbent, disposable gloves.

price.basis: Luggable Loo $21.99 (https://www.academy.com/p/reliance-luggable-loo-5-gallon-portable-toilet?sku=grey, read on the page) + one 6-pack of Double Doodie gel bags $17.97 (search snippet) + about $15 for liners, litter and gloves (my estimate) = $55. Only the bucket price was read on a retailer page, so the kit price is marked unverified.

lifeYears.basis: Bucket and seat last decades; gel bags several years.

setupHours.basis: Buy, assemble, agree where waste will be kept.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Check the bags.

everydayShare.basis: Camping or a bathroom renovation.

reliability.basis: Little to go wrong; the limit is bags and where to put full ones.

adherence.basis: Most households would use it once the toilet stops; some keep bucket-flushing instead.

fraction.basis: Against improvisation (bin bag in the dry bowl, any bucket, outdoors): contains waste and odour and keeps the user indoors. Does not restore flushing, hand-washing or waste collection. No measurement exists.

items.name: Hygiene bundle
items.spec: Two 8 oz bottles of alcohol hand sanitiser (60% or more), soap, 200 wet wipes, 20 heavy bin bags, kept in rotation. Bleach for surfaces is the separate bleach entry.

price.basis: Sanitiser about $8, wet wipes $8-20 per 200 (Wet Ones $19.70 per the longlist), soap $3, bin bags $10; search snippets and longlist figures, none read on a retailer page.

lifeYears.basis: Wipes dry out in about two years and sanitiser carries a three-year date (longlist).

setupHours.basis: Add to an ordinary shop and set aside.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Use and replace.

everydayShare.basis: All of it is used in ordinary life if rotated.

reliability.basis: Dried-out wipes, stock used up and not replaced.

adherence.basis: Hand hygiene is used at well under every opportunity even when supplies are at hand.

fraction.basis: Handwashing promotion prevents about 30% of diarrhoea episodes where water exists (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD004265_does-promoting-handwashing-reduce-diarrhoea); sanitiser and wipes are a weaker stand-in when there is none, and sanitiser does not work well against norovirus (https://www.cdc.gov/norovirus/prevention/index.html). Also restores some sense of being clean.

items.name: Sleeping bag or heavy blankets
items.spec: One synthetic rectangular sleeping bag rated 20 F (-7 C) per person, or two heavy wool or fleece blankets per person. Used on the existing bed; no separate mat.

price.basis: Kittery Trading Post product page read 19 Nov 2026: Slumberjack Middle Fork 20-30 F $59.95; the same page listed a 30 F bag at $32.99 and a 10-20 F bag at $99.99.

lifeYears.basis: Longlist gives 10+ years; synthetic fill loses loft slowly if stored loose.

setupHours.basis: Choose and order; no learning needed.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Air once a year.

everydayShare.basis: Camping and guests for some households; none for others.

reliability.basis: Nothing to fail; the risk is not finding it.

adherence.basis: Most owners would use it once the house is cold; frail or confused people may not.

fraction.basis: Mortality. Heat balance: asleep at 40 W/m2 with about 32 W/m2 of dry heat loss, comfort needs (33 - T)/(0.155 x 32) clo: 4.6 clo at 10 C, 5.6 at 5 C, 6.7 at 0 C. Ordinary bedding measures 0.90-4.89 clo (Lin and Deng 2008, https://research.polyu.edu.hk/en/publications/a-study-on-the-thermal-comfort-in-sleeping-environments-in-the-su-2/), so it stops sufficing near 9 C; a 20 F bag supplies roughly 6-7 clo. Physically the bag closes most of the gap, but a cold-climate household can already pile up duvets and coats, and many deaths follow falls, acute illness or not noticing the cold. Hence 0.3, not 0.8.

adherence.basis: Most owners would use it once the house is cold; frail or confused people may not.

fraction.basis: Warm nights and a warm wrap by day, but the house stays cold and the person is confined to the bag.

items.name: Warm layers
items.spec: Per person: thermal base-layer top and bottom, warm hat, gloves, two pairs of thick socks, for anyone who does not already own them.
items.units: set of layers for one person

price.basis: Longlist estimate $50-100; budget synthetic base layers sell for about $10 a piece. No retailer page could be opened.

lifeYears.basis: Clothing in regular winter use.

setupHours.basis: Check what each person owns; buy the gaps.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: None beyond normal laundry.

everydayShare.basis: Worn every winter in a cold climate; the longlist rates everyday use as high.

reliability.basis: Nothing to fail.

adherence.basis: People put on clothes when cold.

fraction.basis: Mortality. Seated at 58 W/m2 a person needs (33 - T)/(0.155 x 45) clo: 3.3 clo at 10 C, 4.0 at 5 C. Indoor winter clothing is 1.0-1.3 clo (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clothing_insulation); a base layer, hat and gloves add about 0.5-1 clo and cover the head and hands. Most cold-climate households own these already, so the marginal effect is small.

adherence.basis: People put on clothes when cold.

fraction.basis: Lets people move about the house and do tasks in comfort, which a sleeping bag does not.

items.name: One-warm-room plan
items.spec: Decide in advance which small room the household retreats to; keep window-film or spare blankets, tape and a door draught-stop to seal it; everyone sleeps there; know the nearest warming centre; agree a place to stay with relatives or friends; arrange a daily check on any older person living alone.

price.basis: Search snippets: 3M indoor window insulator kit for five windows $13.59 at Target and $15.99 at Fleet Farm; plus tape and a draught-stop. No retailer page opened.

lifeYears.basis: Film and tape adhesive age; the plan itself needs revisiting as the household changes.

setupHours.basis: Choose the room, measure windows, buy materials, talk it through, make two phone calls.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Review before each winter.

everydayShare.basis: Window film cuts heating bills if fitted every winter; most will keep it in the box.

reliability.basis: Plans are forgotten and materials go missing.

adherence.basis: A plan made once is followed by perhaps two households in three.

fraction.basis: Mortality. Three people give off about 300 W; in a sealed small room losing 50-100 W per kelvin that holds the room 3-6 C above the rest of the house. Many households would crowd into one room anyway, so the credit is only for doing it sooner and sealing it better, plus the check on an older person living alone.

adherence.basis: A plan made once is followed by perhaps two households in three.

fraction.basis: A few degrees warmer, at the price of crowding.

items.name: Indoor-rated propane heater with fuel
items.spec: A catalytic or radiant heater rated for indoor use, with oxygen-depletion and tip-over cut-offs, and 1-lb propane cylinders.

price.basis: Search snippets of Walmart listings: Coleman 16 oz 2-pack $9.87-10.47, 6-pack $41.99-48.97. The Walmart page itself returned a bot check.

fixedPrice.basis: Kittery Trading Post product page read 19 Nov 2026: $119.99. Search snippets show $75.99 to $145.43 at other retailers.

lifeYears.basis: Simple appliance used a few days a decade; pilot and thermocouple assemblies foul with age.

setupHours.basis: Buy, read the manual, test-fire once, decide which room and where the CO alarm goes.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Test-fire before each winter.

everydayShare.basis: Shared with a camp stove or grill in some households.

reliability.basis: Pilot or oxygen-sensor faults, unfamiliarity under stress, and the sensor shutting the unit off above about 7,000 ft.

micromortsPerDay.basis: CPSC: about 25 deaths a year from portable propane heaters, many in tents, campers and vehicles. If about 3M households run one about 15 days a year (guess), 45M household-days, 0.55 per household-day and about 0.2 per person. https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/Non-Fire-Carbon-Monoxide-Deaths-Associated-with-the-Use-of-Consumer-Products-2022-Annual-Estimates.pdf

Space heaters and heating stoves account for about 380-420 home fire deaths a year (NFPA, search snippet); over a guessed 40M using households x 90 days that is 0.11 per household-day, 0.045 per person; doubled for improvised outage use near bedding.

items.name: Room air conditioner for a home without one
items.spec: One 5,000-6,000 BTU window unit (or an 8,000-10,000 BTU portable unit where the windows will not take one) to keep one bedroom-sized room below 26 °C; fitted before summer and test-run each June.

price.basis: GE AHEC05AC 5,000 BTU listed at $169.00, on sale at $161.20, read on geappliances.com 19 Nov 2026. Low end is discount-store units seen in search snippets; high end is a portable unit (guess).

lifeYears.basis: Typical service life of a room unit, recalled; the GE and Midea pages give only a 1-year warranty.

setupHours.basis: Choose, buy, fit in the window, seal the gaps.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Net of everyday use: a June test run and filter rinse. Gross seasonal fitting and removal is about 1 hour.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Electricity on dangerous days only: about 450 W (Midea figure from a search snippet) x 12 h x 10 days = 54 kWh at about $0.15/kWh. Everyday running costs are covered by the everyday share.

everydayShare.basis: 88% of US households choose to have air conditioning for comfort alone (https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=52558), so in a hot-summer climate most of the cost is justified without any emergency.

reliability.basis: A recent unit test-run each June. Broken units are the main failure in old systems: in Maricopa County 2024, 88% of indoor heat deaths had an AC unit and 70% of those units did not work.

adherence.basis: NYC 2022 survey: 14% of adults with AC use it half the time or less when hot because of cost. BC 2021: of the 7% of decedents who had AC, only 15% had it running.

fraction.basis: Working home air conditioning OR 0.23 (0.1-0.6) in Bouchama 2007; 0.3 in Chicago 1995; 0.2 (0.1-0.7) in Chicago 1999. That is 77% removed; cut to 70% for confounding by wealth and health and because one room unit cools one room.

items.name: Battery fan and spray bottle
items.spec: One 10-inch fan that runs on D cells or a USB battery, 12 D cells (two sets) or a 20,000 mAh power bank, a trigger spray bottle, and a note of the rule: wet skin and clothing and sit in the airflow; above about 35 °C indoors (for the old) or 38 °C (for younger adults) use the water without the fan.
items.units: kit serving one or two people in one room

price.basis: Treva (O2COOL) 10-inch battery fan with AC adapter $34.99 read on target.com 19 Nov 2026; plus 12 D cells at about $15 and a spray bottle at about $3 (both estimates).

lifeYears.basis: Limited by the shelf life of alkaline cells (about 10 years, per the longlist) and by cheap fan motors.

setupHours.basis: Buy, test, store with the batteries outside the fan.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Yearly test.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: $15 of D cells replaced about every 7 years.

everydayShare.basis: Some use for camping, and on mains power in summer.

reliability.basis: Losses: leaked or borrowed batteries, kit not found.

adherence.basis: Same as the outage effect.

fraction.basis: Same reasoning as the outage effect.

adherence.basis: Same as the outage effect.

fraction.basis: cooling.json, battery-fan-kit note: fans relieve discomfort more than they prevent death.

items.name: Heat plan with indoor thermometer
items.spec: One page, written before summer: two cooled places within reach (one outside the local grid area or with backup power), their hours and how to get there; the trigger (act at 26 °C indoors for the old or ill, leave or cool actively at 31 °C); the routine (cool shower or wet cloths, covers shut by day, windows open at night, drink water); signs of heat stroke. Plus one indoor thermometer with a high-temperature alert.

price.basis: Govee H5075 Bluetooth thermometer with out-of-range phone alerts: $27.99 for three ($9.33 each), $9.99 each in a two-pack, read on us.govee.com 19 Nov 2026; single-unit price not captured, assumed about $12.

lifeYears.basis: Places close and people move, so the plan needs rewriting every few years.

setupHours.basis: Find and check the places, write the page, set the alert.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Spring check of hours, addresses and thermometer batteries.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Two AAA cells lasting about 6 months, per the Govee page; cell price estimated.

everydayShare.basis: The thermometer has some everyday use.

reliability.basis: Chance the plan is current and remembered when the heat arrives.

adherence.basis: The extra share of dangerous days on which a household spends several hours somewhere cooled because it has a plan and a trigger, beyond what it would improvise. No data found; a CDC-commissioned review found no direct evidence that cooling centres reduce deaths.

fraction.basis: Visiting cool environments OR 0.34 (0.2-0.5) in Bouchama 2007, cut from 66% to 50% for confounding (people who can go out are fitter) and because a 2-hour cooling break loses its physiological effect within about 2 hours of returning to the heat (Kenny 2024).

items.name: Daily check-in for someone living alone
items.spec: For a person aged 60 or over who lives alone: a named relative, friend or neighbour phones or visits twice a day whenever a heat warning is in force or the power is out in hot weather, holds a key, and has agreed in advance to move the person somewhere cooled or call an ambulance if they are confused, unwell or do not answer.

price.basis: A spare key for the checker; nothing else is bought.

lifeYears.basis: Arrangements lapse as people move or fall out of touch.

setupHours.basis: One conversation, a key, and agreeing what the checker will do.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: About 10 warning days a year x 2 contacts x 5 minutes x 2 people = 3.3 hours, counting the checker's time.

everydayShare.basis: The same arrangement covers falls, strokes and cold spells, and is ordinary good practice for anyone old who lives alone.

reliability.basis: Chance the checker is reachable, unaffected and in fact calls.

adherence.basis: Share of dangerous days on which the check happens and leads to action when needed.

fraction.basis: Increased social contact OR 0.40 (0.2-0.8); living alone OR 2.3 (Chicago 1995) and 8.1 (Chicago 1999). Halved from the implied 60% because contact alone often fails: in Chicago 1999 over half of decedents had been seen or spoken to on the day of death or the day before, and a Rome monitoring programme showed 25 against 29 deaths per 1,000 over-75s in summer 2015.

items.name: Sun-blocking window covers
items.spec: Blackout roller blinds or reflective insulating shades on the three or so windows that take direct sun, kept shut by day in hot weather. Where the building allows, exterior shade cloth, awnings or shutters instead, which work about three times as well.

price.basis: 3 x $39.99 for the IKEA FRIDANS blackout roller blind, 34 x 76.75 in, read on ikea.com 19 Nov 2026. Low end is reflective film or foil-faced board (estimate); high end is exterior shades (estimate).

lifeYears.basis: Ordinary life of a roller blind.

setupHours.basis: Measure, buy, fit three blinds.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: None beyond drawing them, counted once a year as a check.

everydayShare.basis: Dark bedrooms, privacy, and lower cooling bills: PNNL reports 15-25% summer cooling savings from high-efficiency shades.

reliability.basis: Fitted in place; little to go wrong.

adherence.basis: They work only if shut during the day; people at home often open them for light or air.

fraction.basis: Simulated home without AC in the 2021 Portland heat wave (Rempel 2022, via PNNL): hours in the danger heat-index bands fall 18% with interior roller shades, 23% with insulating shades and 55% with exterior shades. I take 18-23% and cut it by about a third because an unprepared household already has some curtains and can hang sheets or foil. https://basc.pnnl.gov/resource-guides/window-attachments-solar-control-and-energy-efficiency

items.name: A second flashlight or headlamp
items.spec: One compact LED flashlight on AA or AAA cells, 100+ lumens with a low mode, cells installed; kept in a fixed place.
items.note: Nearly every household already has a light; that is in the baseline. This entry is a second one.

price.basis: Coast G24 LED flashlight $14.99 read on https://www.webstaurantstore.com/search/led-flashlight.html. Step 2 found $14.99 for a GearLight two-pack and $29.95 for a ThruNite Archer 2A.

lifeYears.basis: LEDs outlast the body; the usual end is cell leakage or loss.

setupHours.basis: Buy, load cells, pick a place.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Yearly check.

everydayShare.basis: Used around the home and car.

reliability.basis: Dead or leaked cells and misplacement are common; no data found.

items.name: Spare alkaline batteries
items.spec: Sealed 24-pack of AA alkaline cells (or the size the household's lights and radio take), stored cool.

price.basis: Rayovac Ultra Pro 24 AA $10.49 and Energizer MAX 24 AA $19.99 read on https://www.webstaurantstore.com/search/aa-alkaline-batteries.html; step 2 found $8.49 for 12.

lifeYears.basis: Makers claim 10-year shelf life (recalled).

setupHours.basis: Add to a shopping trip.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Rotate into household use.

everydayShare.basis: Rotated stock is used in remotes and toys.

reliability.basis: Sealed cells rarely fail; the risk is that the household has raided the pack.

items.name: USB power bank
items.spec: Lithium-ion USB power bank kept charged, with cables for every phone in the home. Ladder in rated watt-hours: 10,000 mAh is 37 Wh.

price.basis: IKEA VARMFRONT 10,400 mAh / 37.44 Wh at $39.99 = $1.07/Wh (https://www.ikea.com/us/en/p/varmfront-portable-charger-dark-blue-00559615/); Anker Laptop Power Bank 25K at $91.19 = about $1.00/Wh (https://www.anker.com/collections/power-banks); Anker Zolo 20K at $54.79 = $0.76/Wh (NBC Select via step 2). Generic brands are near $0.50/Wh (recalled).

lifeYears.basis: Lithium-ion calendar ageing.

setupHours.basis: Buy, charge, add cables.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Top up every 3-6 months.

everydayShare.basis: Travel and long days out.

reliability.basis: Everyday use leaves it part-empty; a forgotten one self-discharges. No data found.

items.name: Folding solar charger
items.spec: Folding USB solar panel, 40 W nominal, used outdoors or on a sunny balcony with a power bank as buffer.

price.basis: FlexSolar 40 W $64, OutdoorGearLab list price via step 2; flexsolar.com returned an empty page.

lifeYears.basis: Fabric and connectors wear before the cells.

setupHours.basis: Buy and try it once in the sun.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: None beyond a yearly test.

everydayShare.basis: Camping only.

reliability.basis: Weather, winter sun, and flats with no outdoor spot; output through glass is far lower.

items.name: Portable power station
items.spec: Lithium iron phosphate power station with AC outlets, kept charged. Ladder in rated watt-hours. Units of 256 Wh give 300 W and cannot start most fridges; 1 kWh units give 1,500 W or more.

price.basis: EcoFlow River 2, 256 Wh, $239 = $0.93/Wh read on https://www.campingworld.com/ecoflow-river-2-portable-power-station-140737.html; Anker Solix C1000 Gen 2, 1,024 Wh, $799 list = $0.78/Wh (OutdoorGearLab via step 2). 1 kWh units are often discounted to $430-500 (recalled), hence the lower median.

lifeYears.basis: Seller states 80% capacity after 3,000 cycles (https://www.campingworld.com/ecoflow-river-2-portable-power-station-140737.html); calendar ageing will bind first.

setupHours.basis: Choose a size, charge, test the fridge or device on it.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Recharge every 3-6 months.

everydayShare.basis: Camping and tools for some owners.

reliability.basis: Low self-discharge; main risk is that it was left empty.

items.name: Medical-device backup battery
items.spec: A 1 kWh lithium iron phosphate power station dedicated to the device, left plugged in beside it in pass-through mode, with the device's DC lead where one exists, and a timed test of real run-time.

price.basis: Same hardware as power-station at $0.42-0.95 per Wh: Anker Solix C1000 Gen 2, 1,024 Wh, $799 list (OutdoorGearLab via step 2); EcoFlow River 2 at $0.93/Wh read on https://www.campingworld.com/ecoflow-river-2-portable-power-station-140737.html. Proprietary concentrator batteries cost several times more per Wh (recalled).

lifeYears.basis: As power-station.

setupHours.basis: Size it to the device, set up pass-through, time a real run.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Twice-yearly run-time test.

everydayShare.basis: Dedicated.

reliability.basis: Always on charge and next to the device.

items.name: Medical power plan with spare oxygen
items.spec: For a person on home oxygen, a ventilator or home dialysis: ask the equipment supplier for backup cylinders and a conserver, enrol in the utility's medical-baseline scheme and the local special-needs registry, and write down where to go and when to leave.

price.basis: Suppliers usually lend backup cylinders under the existing rental (recalled; no fee schedule found); registration is free.

lifeYears.basis: Until the prescription, supplier or address changes.

setupHours.basis: Calls, forms, writing the plan.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Check cylinder contents; renew enrolment.

everydayShare.basis: None.

reliability.basis: Cylinders may be part-empty; registries do not guarantee priority restoration.

adherence.basis: People delay leaving; 18% of Texans left home in 2021 (https://www.uh.edu/hobby/winter2021/storm.pdf).

fraction.basis: Leaving early for a powered place, before the backup runs out, removes the unmet days that follow; the share is my judgement.

items.name: Frozen water bottles and fridge thermometers
items.spec: Two appliance thermometers (fridge and freezer) and 4-6 one-litre bottles of water kept frozen in spare freezer space; in an outage move some to the fridge and keep doors shut.

price.basis: Taylor 5924 dial fridge/freezer thermometer $3.69 each, read on https://www.webstaurantstore.com/search/refrigerator-freezer-thermometer.html; two = $7.38. Bottles are reused.

lifeYears.basis: Dial thermometers last.

setupHours.basis: Fill and freeze bottles; place thermometers.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: None.

everydayShare.basis: Thermometers catch a warm fridge in normal times.

reliability.basis: Bottles get evicted when the freezer fills.

items.name: Home first-aid kit
items.spec: One consumer kit of about 300 pieces: adhesive bandages, gauze pads and rolls, tape, antiseptic wipes, a few gloves, cold pack, scissors, tweezers.

price.basis: $18.57 is the step 2 longlist figure (NBC Select, 17 Nov 2026), which I did not reopen; search snippets show $16-37 across sellers and $45 for the Red Cross-branded version.

lifeYears.basis: Adhesives, wipes and cold packs are dated 3-5 years; dry dressings last longer.

setupHours.basis: Buy, open, read the leaflet, choose a place.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Yearly check and restock, as the government lists advise.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Replacing plasters and wipes used in ordinary life.

everydayShare.basis: Almost all use is ordinary cuts, burns and blisters.

reliability.basis: Kits get raided and not restocked; contents are simple to use.

adherence.basis: Share of owners who find and use it in the moment.

fraction.basis: Nothing in the kit treats cardiac arrest, choking or overdose, which are over 99% of the baseline; a pressure dressing helps with severe bleeding only a little more than a clean cloth.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Cleaning and covering wounds when care is days away lowers wound infection; no study measures it. Most deaths in the window are heart attacks, sepsis and strokes that a kit cannot touch.

items.name: Bleeding-control kit
items.spec: One windlass tourniquet (C-A-T), one 6-inch pressure bandage, two compressed gauze rolls, gloves and shears, kept where it can be reached in under a minute.

price.basis: LA Police Gear lists the NAR public-access kit at $79.99-138.50 across basic to advanced versions; a C-A-T alone is $34.99 at narescue.com, so a self-assembled kit is about $45-55.

lifeYears.basis: NAR says an unused, sealed C-A-T has no shelf life; dressings are dated about 5 years. https://www.narescue.com/combat-application-tourniquet-c-a-t.html

setupHours.basis: Watching a how-to and practising once on a limb; without that the kit is close to useless (see adherence).

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Glance at the seal and dates.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Dressings replaced once in the kit's life.

everydayShare.basis: No ordinary use.

reliability.basis: Genuine tourniquets rarely fail; the risk is not finding the kit. Counterfeits break.

adherence.basis: PATTS trial: 16% of untrained laypeople applied a tourniquet correctly, 20% with flashcards, 88% just after hands-on training, 54.5% at 3-9 months. A typical owner sits between. Use 0.55 with firstAidSkill. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29801156/

fraction.basis: 235-480 US deaths a year from limb bleeding that a prompt tourniquet might have saved = 0.7-1.4 micromorts per person; a quarter at home with someone present (guess) = 0.26; half of those saved beyond what improvised pressure achieves (guess) = 0.13, over a baseline of 280.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: In events that injure people while ambulances cannot come, limb bleeding is a larger share of deaths; share assumed at a few percent of the hazard's trauma harm.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: In events that injure people while ambulances cannot come, limb bleeding is a larger share of deaths; share assumed at a few percent of the hazard's trauma harm.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Injury is about a sixth of the deaths that late care causes at ages 15-59 in my bottom-up sum, and limb bleeding a small part of that.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Injury is about a sixth of the deaths that late care causes at ages 15-59 in my bottom-up sum, and limb bleeding a small part of that.

items.name: Thermometer, pulse oximeter and blood-pressure cuff
items.spec: Digital thermometer, fingertip pulse oximeter and automatic upper-arm blood-pressure monitor.

price.basis: Search snippets: Zacurate 500DL oximeter $20-23 at Walmart; thermometer about $10 and cuff $35-60 from memory. Manufacturer pages refused to load.

lifeYears.basis: Consumer electronics with replaceable batteries.

setupHours.basis: Buying, and learning what readings should prompt a call.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Battery check.

everydayShare.basis: Most homes already own a thermometer; a cuff has real everyday value only where someone has high blood pressure.

reliability.basis: Cheap oximeters lack validation and read less accurately on dark skin and cold fingers; flat batteries.

adherence.basis: Share who check when ill and act on a low reading.

fraction.basis: A randomised trial of home oximeters in 1,217 COVID patients found no gain: days alive and out of hospital 29.4 against 29.5, deaths 5 against 3. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35385625/

items.name: First-aid and CPR course
items.spec: One adult takes a first-aid and CPR course, and refreshes it every two years.
items.units: one adult completing the course once

price.basis: Red Cross blended Adult and Pediatric First Aid/CPR/AED listings show $123-129 in search snippets (redcross.org returns HTTP 403); community and employer courses are cheaper or free.

lifeYears.basis: Certificate valid 2 years (Red Cross listing, snippet). Skills fade faster: 54.5% applied a tourniquet correctly 3-9 months after training. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29801156/

setupHours.basis: 2.5 h online (Red Cross listing, snippet) + about 2 h skills session (memory) + 1 h booking and travel (guess). Per adult trained.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Refreshing is modelled as retaking the course at end of life.

everydayShare.basis: About 29% of arrests happen outside the home (CARES 2024), where a trained person helps people the model does not count; job and childcare requirements add to this.

reliability.basis: Average retention of usable skill across the two years between courses.

adherence.basis: 0.85 that the trained member is the one present, x 0.6: a recently trained person starts CPR in about 75% of cases against 35% untrained with dispatcher coaching, which closes 60% of the gap. Swor 2006: trained bystanders OR 6.6 for giving CPR, yet a minority did, 37.5% of them citing panic.

fraction.basis: If a trained member were present and acted at every home emergency: 35% of home arrests witnessed x 70% where an untrained person would not have given effective CPR x 5 points of survival (2-9) / 0.89 fatal = 1.4%, plus 0.2% for choking. Hasselqvist-Ax 2015: 10.5% vs 4.0% 30-day survival, adjusted OR 2.15. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26061835/

adherence.basis: Trained member present and acting; more time to think than in a cardiac arrest.

fraction.basis: Lay first aid bears on injury (about a sixth of late-care deaths at 15-59) and on recognising a time-critical illness early enough to drive to care. A lay-responder and paramedic system in rural Iraq and Cambodia cut trauma deaths from 40% to 14.9% with 5.7 h to hospital. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12813342/

adherence.basis: Trained member present and acting; more time to think than in a cardiac arrest.

fraction.basis: Lay first aid bears on injury (about a sixth of late-care deaths at 15-59) and on recognising a time-critical illness early enough to drive to care. A lay-responder and paramedic system in rural Iraq and Cambodia cut trauma deaths from 40% to 14.9% with 5.7 h to hospital. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12813342/

items.name: Hands-only CPR self-training
items.spec: One adult watches a hands-only CPR video and practises for half an hour a year.

price.basis: Videos are free; the upper end is an optional inflatable practice manikin kit, price from memory.

lifeYears.basis: Brief training fades within months; retention after video training was not reported in the abstract I read.

setupHours.basis: Ten minutes of video, some practice, finding it.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Repeat is modelled as a new unit each year.

everydayShare.basis: Same reasoning as the course.

reliability.basis: Retention over the year.

adherence.basis: Assumed to close 35% of the gap to always acting (the course closes 60%), x 0.85 presence. In a simulation 0.7% of video-trained adults failed to attempt CPR against 23.5% of untrained; real arrests are unmeasured. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21386066/

fraction.basis: Same ceiling as the course: the gain if a prepared member were present and acted at every home emergency.

items.name: Home defibrillator (AED)
items.spec: One automated external defibrillator sold for home use, kept on the main floor, battery and pads in date.

price.basis: Philips lists the HeartStart Home with slim case at $1,664; other brands run lower and higher (search snippets).

lifeYears.basis: Eight-year warranty on this family of devices (search snippet); devices usually outlast it.

setupHours.basis: Choosing, registering, watching the training video with the household.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Monthly glance at the status light.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Battery $249 (Philips page) every 4 years + adult pads $68 every 2 years (search snippets for price and intervals) = 62 + 34.

everydayShare.basis: No ordinary use.

reliability.basis: Expired pads or battery, or the device is upstairs.

adherence.basis: HAT trial: the device was used in 32 of 58 witnessed home arrests (55%), in trained households; x 0.85 that a capable member is present. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18381485/

fraction.basis: If used at every witnessed home arrest: 35% witnessed x ~25% shockable at home (18% of all arrests, more when witnessed; guess) x 15 points of survival over waiting for the crew's defibrillator (guess, 0-25) / 0.89 = 1.5%.

items.name: Routine vaccinations up to date
items.spec: Per person per year: influenza every autumn; COVID-19 as recommended; tetanus booster every 10 years; from 50 pneumococcal once and shingles; RSV once at 75 or at 60 with risk conditions. Keep the record.
items.units: one person kept up to date for one year
items.note: Worth nothing extra to people who already keep up to date. Shown as a benchmark.

lifeYears.basis: The unit is defined as one year.

setupHours.basis: Checking what is due.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: One or two pharmacy visits; setupHours already covers the first year's checking.

everydayShare.basis: Set to zero so the benefit below is counted once, as modelled everyday harm averted, and not also netted out of cost.

reliability.basis: Vaccine effectiveness is already inside the micromort figures; this covers only missed timing.

items.name: Prescription buffer
items.spec: Extra supply of every regular prescription drug, and of what is needed to take it (needles, test strips), beyond the normal refill cycle; kept together in one pouch and used oldest first. Obtained by asking the prescriber for 90-day fills with refills, then refilling on the first day the plan allows each cycle (commonly once 75-80% of the supply is used, which banks about a week per 30-day fill or three weeks per 90-day fill), or by paying cash with a discount card for one extra fill of cheap generics, or by a vacation override. Controlled substances (opioids, stimulants, benzodiazepines, clinic-dispensed methadone) usually cannot be banked.
items.units: person-day of the full regimen, for one person on regular medication
items.note: For someone on a drug that is dangerous to miss, most of the value comes from the longest shortages: nuclear war and war between great powers.

price.basis: Cash prices with a free discount card, read on singlecare.com on 19 Nov 2026: lisinopril 10 mg, 90 tablets $3.78-6.78 ($0.04-0.08 a day); atorvastatin 40 mg, 30 tablets $5.93 ($0.20 a day); insulin glargine (Lantus) 10 mL vial $64.84 (about $2.60 a day at 40 units); Eliquis 5 mg, 28 tablets $156.92 ($11.20 a day). Mid is two or three generics. Banked through insurance by early refills, the outlay is only the usual copay paid sooner.

lifeYears.basis: Pharmacy labels usually give a one-year beyond-use date and manufacturer expiry is two to three years; rotation makes expiry irrelevant, so the effective life is the time until the regimen changes.

setupHours.basis: One request to the prescriber, one or two conversations with the pharmacy or insurer, and a calendar reminder for the first eligible refill day.
