upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Using the oldest first and rebuilding the buffer after a change of drug or dose.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: None beyond the drugs themselves; waste from regimen changes is in everydayShare.

everydayShare.basis: The buffer is consumed in normal use, and it also covers late refills, pharmacy stock-outs and travel. The remainder is stock wasted when a drug or dose is changed.

reliability.basis: Covers letting the buffer run down and not rebuilding it, expiry and loss. Automatic-refill and 90-day users already pick up refills with 3-9 days in hand, so discipline is plausible but not universal.

items.name: Core over-the-counter kit
items.spec: Store-brand acetaminophen 500 mg (100), ibuprofen 200 mg (100), aspirin 325 mg (100, to chew at the onset of a suspected heart attack), loperamide 2 mg (24), ten 1-litre packets of WHO-formula oral rehydration salts, and an antihistamine (cetirizine 10 mg, 30). Liquid children's acetaminophen or ibuprofen if there are children.

price.basis: Only the rehydration salts were read on a seller's page: TRIORAL 15 one-litre packets $16.99 (https://triselfcare.com/). The five store-brand bottles are taken at $4-6 each from memory.

lifeYears.basis: Labelled expiry is two to three years. In the federal Shelf Life Extension Program 88% of 3,005 lots were extended at least a year, by 66 months on average (Lyon 2006, PMID 16721796).

setupHours.basis: One shopping trip and reading the dosing labels.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: A yearly look at dates and replacing what was used.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Replacement is the capital cost recurring at end of life.

everydayShare.basis: The analgesics and antihistamine are used in ordinary life and most households already hold some; the rehydration salts and loperamide are used rarely.

reliability.basis: Simple, stable products; the main failure is finding the bottle empty.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: drugs.json aspirin effect, recomputed at present-day case fatality for adults under 60 (Gupta et al. 2014: 1.8 to 2.3% in hospital at ages 30 to 54).

adherence.basis: Chance the symptoms are recognised and aspirin is chewed, net of the roughly half of households that hold aspirin anyway.

fraction.basis: Aspirin when no emergency care can be reached, scaled to the medical researcher's base of 1.2 micromorts a day for an adult aged 15-59. Heart attacks at that age run at about 1.2 per 1,000 a year (recalled), or 3.4 per million a day. ISIS-2: 9.4% v 11.8% vascular death at five weeks, 23% lower odds; with no other care the baseline is higher, so I take 4 points (2.4-8). 3.4 x 0.04 = 0.14 micromorts a day, 11% of 1.2.

items.name: Wider over-the-counter kit
items.spec: Antacid and famotidine, a laxative (polyethylene glycol), a decongestant, a cough suppressant, hydrocortisone 1% cream, petroleum jelly or antibiotic ointment, an antifungal cream, and bite and sunburn gel.

price.basis: Eight to nine store-brand items at $4-8 each, from memory; no page read.

lifeYears.basis: Labelled expiry two to three years; creams and liquids keep less well than tablets.

setupHours.basis: One shopping trip.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Yearly check of dates.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: None beyond replacement at end of life.

everydayShare.basis: All are used in ordinary life; some will expire unused.

reliability.basis: As for the core kit.

items.name: Emergency antibiotic pack
items.spec: Prescription pack sold after an online consultation, with a written guide: one adult course each of amoxicillin-clavulanate, azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, doxycycline and metronidazole (the Jase Case now adds five other drugs). One per household.

price.basis: Jase Case $289.95 on a reseller's listing read 19 Nov 2026 (https://tacda.org/?p=43596); jasemedical.com refused the fetch. The low end allows for cheaper competitors, not checked.

lifeYears.basis: Labelled expiry one to three years from dispensing. Shelf Life Extension Program: 88% of 3,005 lots of 122 products were extended at least a year, 66 months on average, with wide variation between lots (Lyon 2006, PMID 16721796).

setupHours.basis: Online consultation and reading the guide before it is needed.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: A yearly look at dates.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: None; replacement is at end of life.

everydayShare.basis: Not meant for use while a clinician can be reached; some value on remote travel.

reliability.basis: In date enough to work and findable. Choosing the right drug is in adherence, not here.

adherence.basis: Chance a lay person with the booklet treats the right illness with the right drug for long enough.

fraction.basis: Set to give 0.36 micromorts a day at full adherence on the medical researcher's no-care base of 1.2 a day for an adult aged 15-59. My own sum is higher, about 0.8: with no antibiotics and no hospital, bacterial pneumonia, kidney, skin and wound infection and appendicitis would kill such adults at roughly 50 per 100,000 a year (pneumonia needing hospital runs at about 12 per 10,000 a year at this age and killed a fifth or more before antibiotics; recalled figures), and correctly chosen oral drugs avert about 60%. That is two thirds of the 1.2 base, which suggests the base leaves out slow infections; I use the cautious figure. US infectious mortality fell 8.2% a year from 1938 to 1952 as antibiotics arrived (Armstrong 1999). Net of harm from the drugs, roughly 10-20 micromorts per course from allergy and gut infection.

items.name: Battery or crank radio
items.spec: One portable AM/FM receiver with the NOAA weather band (FM and DAB+ in Europe) that runs on replaceable AA or AAA cells, or on a rechargeable cell with a hand crank. Spare cells stored beside it, not in it; local news frequencies written on the case. Crank models of the FosPower A1 or Midland ER310 class add a small torch and a 2,000-2,600 mAh USB output.

price.basis: GearJunkie's guide, updated 10 Nov 2026, lists a RadioShack two-D-cell multi-band radio at $30, the Kaito KA500 at $60 and the Midland ER310PRO at $100 (https://gearjunkie.com/technology/best-emergency-radio); step 2 found the FosPower A1 at $28.46. The $15 low end, for a plain AM/FM pocket set, is my estimate.

lifeYears.basis: Simple receivers last decades; the rechargeable cell in a crank model fades in 5-8 years. No source.

setupHours.basis: Choose, buy, find the local news stations, write down the frequencies and test.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: One test a year and a recharge or a check of the spare cells.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: A set of alkaline cells every five years or so; nothing for a crank model.

everydayShare.basis: A few owners use it in the garden or when camping; most leave it in a drawer.

reliability.basis: Losses are flat or leaked cells, not finding it, and not knowing which station to tune. In a 2007 Australian storm 42% of households had a battery radio with working batteries and 44% of those who lost power used one (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2443139/).

adherence.basis: An owner with no other news will switch it on; some will not think to. In the Australian survey about as many households that lost power used a battery radio (44%) as owned a working one (42%) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2443139/).

fraction.basis: A radio at hand lifts the share of news value recovered from 0.62 (car radio, neighbours) to about 0.9, the chance a useful station is on air: 0.28 x $11.25 = $3.2 of the $15 baseline day. Broadcast outlasts mobile in every event I checked, e.g. Puerto Rico on day 28 had 60% of AM stations on air against 29% of cell sites (https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-347308A1.txt).

adherence.basis: An owner with no other news will switch it on; some will not think to. In the Australian survey about as many households that lost power used a battery radio (44%) as owned a working one (42%) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2443139/).

fraction.basis: comms.json, battery-radio: at most a fifth of the 0.2 applies to mortality.

adherence.basis: The household must think of the radio, find a station that is broadcasting, and act on what it hears.

fraction.basis: A radio is the likely way to hear 'get inside, stay inside' and, later, when and which way to leave; FEMA hardens 77 stations reaching over 90% of the US population for this purpose (https://www.fema.gov/press-release/20220628/fema-and-audacys-wwl-radio-unveil-new-emergency-broadcast-studio). The size of the effect is my guess, net of a car radio, and the fallout channel belongs to another researcher.

items.name: Phone alert and satellite setup
items.spec: On every phone in the household: confirm government emergency alerts are switched on; register the mobile numbers and home address with the county or city opt-in notification system; install one official or hazard app with push alerts for the home area (in wildfire country, a fire-tracking app); run the satellite SOS or satellite texting demo if the phone has one; fill in the emergency contact and medical ID screen.
items.units: one-off setup of all the household's phones

price.basis: No purchase: the alert settings are part of the phone's operating system and county registration and the apps are free. The cost is the setup time.

lifeYears.basis: Lasts until the household moves or a phone is replaced without its settings; most settings carry over.

setupHours.basis: A few minutes per phone plus finding and completing the local registration form.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: A yearly check after system updates.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Nothing to pay. Apple extended free satellite access for iPhone 14 to 16 for another year in September 2026 (search result only, not opened); a later charge is possible.

everydayShare.basis: Little everyday use beyond routine weather alerts.

reliability.basis: 90.9% of US adults with a working phone reported receiving the October 2023 national test alert (https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/research_reports/RRA2400/RRA2451-1/RAND_RRA2451-1.pdf). Does not cover the network failing before the alert is sent, which is inside fractionRemoved.

adherence.basis: Registration stays valid until the household moves or changes number; the phone must be on and heard.

fraction.basis: In the Camp Fire fewer than 40% of residents had registered for the opt-in calls and at most 17% of the population was reached directly (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/TechnicalNotes/NIST.TN.2252.pdf). I assume registration cuts the chance of learning too late by a third and that 20-50% of deaths turn on late awareness, the rest on immobility or choice: about 0.07-0.17.

adherence.basis: Same as above.

fraction.basis: Government alerts are on by default and only 7.2% of adults have switched off imminent-threat alerts (https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/research_reports/RRA2400/RRA2451-1/RAND_RRA2451-1.pdf), so the action changes little for most. Tornado warnings cut injuries by over 40% at some lead times (https://mercatus.org/students/research/journal-articles/tornado-warnings-lead-times-and-tornado-casualties-empirical): 0.07 x 0.4 = 0.03, with local sign-ups adding a little.

adherence.basis: Needs a charged phone and open sky.

fraction.basis: For the roughly 60% of US households with a satellite-capable phone, having tried the feature lifts the chance of using it from about 0.7 to 0.9: 0.6 x 0.2 x 0.7 x $10.50 = $0.9 of the $15 baseline day. All four inputs are guesses.

items.name: Paper contact list
items.spec: A card in each adult's wallet and one at home: mobile numbers of household members, two relatives or friends (one outside the region), doctor, pharmacy, insurer, utility fault lines and the local news radio frequencies. Reviewed yearly.
items.units: set of cards for the household

price.basis: Paper and a pen; $2 if printed and laminated.

lifeYears.basis: Numbers change; a list older than a few years is partly wrong.

setupHours.basis: Copying ten to fifteen numbers and making copies.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: A yearly check.

everydayShare.basis: Also useful whenever a phone is lost, stolen, broken or flat.

reliability.basis: Fails when out of date or not on the person.

adherence.basis: If it is to hand it will be used.

fraction.basis: Matters only when the household's own phones are dead or lost (about 0.25 of comms-window days), someone else's working line or satellite device is within reach (0.2) and the number is not known by heart (0.6): 0.25 x 0.2 x 0.6 x $10.50 = $0.3 of the $15 day. Fewer than half of Americans can recall their partner's number (https://www.pandasecurity.com/en/mediacenter/digital-amnesia-survey/).

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: When the phone is flat but networks work, a borrowed phone is usually available (0.6); the list supplies the number (0.6); contact is about half of what a flat phone costs and a borrowed call does about a third of the job: 0.6 x 0.6 x 0.5 x 0.3 = 0.05.

items.name: Pair of two-way radios
items.spec: Two licence-free handheld radios (FRS in the US, 0.5-2 W; PMR446 in Europe), kept charged or with spare cells, with an agreed channel and check-in times. No amateur-radio set: that needs a licence and practice.

price.basis: Step 2 took $45 for a Retevis RT22 pair from OutdoorGearLab's 2026 list; the manufacturer page returned 404 for me. The range is my estimate of the market.

lifeYears.basis: Limited by the rechargeable cells.

setupHours.basis: Buy, charge, agree a channel, test the range around home.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Recharge every three to six months.

everydayShare.basis: Some use on hikes, ski trips and with children.

reliability.basis: Self-discharged cells are the usual failure; both people must also be carrying one.

adherence.basis: Both parties must carry a charged set and keep the agreed channel.

fraction.basis: They link only people within about 0.5-1 mile in a city or 1-2 miles in a suburb (vendor table, https://support.cobra.com/support/solutions/articles/47001184443), so they serve only contact between household members who have split up nearby: about 12% of the contact value x 0.5 chance of being in range x $10.50 = $0.6 of the $15 day.

items.name: Satellite messenger
items.spec: A dedicated two-way satellite messenger with an SOS button (Garmin inReach Messenger class) on the cheapest plan that keeps SOS and pay-per-message texting active, kept charged. Households with an iPhone 14 or later, a Pixel 9 or later or a similar phone already have much of this in the phone.

price.basis: Device about $300 (step 2, from OutdoorGearLab; REI and Best Buy refused my fetch) plus a $39.99 activation fee (https://hikingguy.com/hiking-gear/garmin-inreach-subscription-cost-breakdown, reviewed October 2026).

lifeYears.basis: Battery ageing and network or plan changes.

setupHours.basis: Choose device and plan, activate, pair with phones, load contacts, send a test message.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Quarterly charge, firmware update and test message.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Garmin's Enabled plan is $7.99 a month and Essential $14.99 (https://hikingguy.com/hiking-gear/garmin-inreach-subscription-cost-breakdown); 12 x 7.99 = $96. The low end assumes the plan is suspended for part of the year, which Garmin allows at no charge.

everydayShare.basis: High for people who hike, sail or drive in areas with no coverage; near zero otherwise.

reliability.basis: Must be charged, on an active plan, and understood; needs open sky.

adherence.basis: An owner cut off from family will use it.

fraction.basis: It restores about 85% of the contact value. With no satellite-capable phone that is 0.85 x $10.50 = $8.9 of an $18 day (0.49); with one it adds (0.85 - 0.49) x $10.50 = $3.8 to a $13 day (0.29). Weighting 40:60 gives $5.8 of the $15 average day, 0.39, shaded to 0.35 because rescue services are themselves stretched in a disaster.

items.name: Offline and paper maps
items.spec: Offline map regions downloaded in each phone's map app for the home area and the routes to two places the household could go, refreshed yearly; one paper state or regional road map kept in the car or go-bag.

price.basis: Downloads are free. Step 2 found a Rand McNally map at $9.99 on NBC Select; I did not re-check it.

lifeYears.basis: Roads change slowly; downloads expire unless refreshed.

setupHours.basis: Pick regions, download on each phone, buy the map.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Yearly refresh of the downloads.

everydayShare.basis: Offline maps also help on ordinary trips through areas with poor coverage.

reliability.basis: The download must cover where the household ends up going; the phone must be charged or the paper map in the car.

adherence.basis: Used when needed if the download is current.

fraction.basis: Restores navigation, which I put at about a third of the $3.25 ordinary-use share, on the minority of comms-window days when the household travels somewhere unfamiliar: about $0.4 of the $15 day.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Leaving is a little quicker and less stressful when routes can be found without a network. No evidence found; in the Camp Fire the roads failed through gridlock, not navigation (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/TechnicalNotes/NIST.TN.2252.pdf).

items.name: Whistle
items.spec: One pealess safety whistle per person, on a keyring or fixed by the bed.

price.basis: Step 2 found two for $5.99 on NBC Select; I did not re-check it.

lifeYears.basis: Nothing to wear out.

setupHours.basis: Buy and attach.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: None.

everydayShare.basis: Some use outdoors or for personal safety.

reliability.basis: It works if it is there; being within reach is counted in adherence.

adherence.basis: The chance it is within reach of a trapped person.

fraction.basis: Helps only a person trapped alive who would otherwise not be heard. Time to extrication strongly predicts death (a 21-hour cut-off in one 2023 Turkish cohort, search result only), but no study measures what a whistle adds, and few deaths in US housing involve prolonged entrapment.

items.name: Shielded bag for the radio
items.spec: A radio-frequency shielding pouch, or a steel ammunition tin lined with cardboard, in which the battery radio and a spare power bank are stored.

price.basis: Step 2's unverified estimate of $15-40; I found no page to check.

lifeYears.basis: Fabric pouches wear at the fold; a tin lasts indefinitely.

setupHours.basis: Buy and pack.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: None beyond the radio's own yearly test.

everydayShare.basis: No everyday use.

reliability.basis: Cheap pouches vary in how well they shield and must be fully closed. No test data read.

adherence.basis: The radio must be in the bag when the pulse comes.

fraction.basis: It protects only the radio's contribution (0.2 of the day) in the cases where an unshielded, switched-off battery radio would have been destroyed, which I put at about 15%: 0.2 x 0.15 = 0.03. I could not open the EMP Commission's 2008 test results to check the 15%.

items.name: Books, games and downloaded media
items.spec: A deck of cards, one board or travel game, two or three unread paperbacks, and a refreshed download of films, music, podcasts and e-books on a phone or tablet. Most homes already have some of this.

price.basis: My estimate: cards about $3, a game $10-25, second-hand books; downloads free with existing subscriptions.

lifeYears.basis: Durable; downloads need refreshing.

setupHours.basis: Buy and set downloads going.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Refreshing the downloads.

everydayShare.basis: Books and games are used anyway.

reliability.basis: Little to go wrong; downloaded media need a charged device.

adherence.basis: Used if the outage is long enough to be boring.

fraction.basis: Recovers about a quarter of the $3.25 ordinary-use share of a day without internet, beyond what a typical home's books and toys already do: $0.8 of the $15 day. No evidence found.

items.name: Deeper pantry: ready-to-eat food
items.spec: Extra stock of ordinary shelf-stable food the household already eats that needs no cooking, chilling or added water: canned beans, chili, soup, fish, meat and fruit, peanut butter, crackers, cereal, nuts, dried fruit, long-life milk. Bought once on top of the usual shop, then eaten and replaced oldest-first. Units are person-days beyond what the household holds now.

price.basis: Basket for 2,235 kcal: peanut butter 60 g $0.36 (Jif at $2.69/lb, https://www.webstaurantstore.com/search/peanut-butter.html), crackers 100 g $0.45, one can of chili $2.00, one can of beans $1.00, cereal 60 g $0.40, nuts 30 g $0.30, canned fruit or long-life milk $1.00: $5.51, or $5.20 per 2,100 kcal; rounded up for tinned fish and variety. Only the peanut butter price was read on a retailer page; the rest are recalled shelf prices.

lifeYears.basis: This is the rotation cycle, not spoilage. Extension services quoting USDA give best quality of 2 to 5 years for low-acid cans and 12 to 18 months for high-acid ones (search snippet; the USDA page refused the fetch); crackers, cereal and nuts keep 6 to 12 months.

setupHours.basis: Deciding what to stock, one or two larger shops, shelving and dating. My estimate.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Checking dates twice a year and keeping the oldest-first habit. My estimate; it grows with depth.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Waste is carried by everydayShare, so no separate money upkeep.

everydayShare.basis: The food is eaten in the normal course, so the cost is capital, time, space and waste. I assume 10% of each cycle's stock expires uneaten or is eaten grudgingly, about 5% of the stock a year on a two-year cycle. No measurement found; the share falls as the stock gets deeper.

reliability.basis: Main failure is having eaten the stock down without replacing it. My estimate.

adherence.basis: Half of households holding the stock would isolate; half of those could not have done so without it. Both guesses.

items.name: Deeper pantry: food that needs cooking
items.spec: Extra stock of ordinary dry staples the household already cooks: rice, pasta, oats, lentils, dried beans, flour, with oil, salt and seasoning. Rotated like the ready-to-eat pantry. Needs a working way to cook and about 1.5 litres of water per person-day on top of drinking water.

price.basis: BLS average city prices, October 2026: white rice $1.101/lb, spaghetti and macaroni $1.384/lb, dried beans $1.680/lb (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/APU0000701312, APU0000701322, APU0000714233). 2,100 kcal as 45% rice (0.571 lb, $0.63), 30% pasta (0.374 lb, $0.52), 25% beans (0.340 lb, $0.57) costs $1.72; I add $0.50 for oil, salt and seasoning.

lifeYears.basis: Rotation cycle. White rice, pasta and dried beans keep for years in shop packaging if dry and pest-free; whole-grain flour and oil are the short-lived parts. Not checked against a source.

setupHours.basis: One bulk shop plus pest-proof containers. My estimate.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Date and pest checks, oldest-first habit. My estimate.

everydayShare.basis: As for the ready-to-eat pantry: 10% of each cycle lost to expiry, pests or being eaten grudgingly. No measurement found. Lower for households that seldom cook from scratch.

reliability.basis: Given that cooking and water are available. Failures are pests, damp and having eaten it down. My estimate.

adherence.basis: Half of households holding the stock would isolate; half of those could not have done so without it. Both guesses.

items.name: Freeze-dried meal kit (30-year)
items.spec: Freeze-dried pouches of the Mountain House Just In Case class, kept sealed and not rotated. Prepared by adding water to the pouch; hot water is quicker but room-temperature water works in twice the time. The 14-day kit gives about 1,720 kcal a day, so it is 11.5 person-days at 2,100 kcal.

price.basis: $449.00 for the 14-day kit at about 1,720 kcal a day (https://www.firesupplydepot.com/mountain-house-just-in-case-14-day-emergency-food-kit.html): 449 / (14 x 1,720) x 2,100 = $39.16. Low end allows for sale prices near $390 and cheaper large cans; high end for pouches bought singly.

lifeYears.basis: Maker's 30-year taste guarantee, as stated on https://www.firesupplydepot.com/mountain-house-just-in-case-14-day-emergency-food-kit.html. Low end allows for hot storage.

setupHours.basis: Choose, order, shelve. My estimate.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: A glance a year to see it is still there and dry. My estimate.

everydayShare.basis: Some owners eat it on camping trips; most never open it. My estimate.

reliability.basis: Nobody eats it down, so it is there when wanted. My estimate.

items.name: Bulk staples sealed for decades
items.spec: White rice and dried beans (about 60:40 by calories; oats or wheat may replace part) sealed in mylar bags with oxygen absorbers inside lidded buckets, or bought ready-sealed in large cans, and left unopened. Full ration of 2,100 kcal needs about 480 lb per person-year. Needs a way to cook, about 1.7 litres of cooking water and about 0.5 hours of stove burn per person-day.

price.basis: BLS October 2026 prices (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/APU0000701312 and APU0000714233): 1,260 kcal of rice is 0.761 lb x $1.101 = $0.84 and 840 kcal of beans is 0.545 lb x $1.680 = $0.92, so $1.76 of food. Packaging is my estimate: $11 per bucket, lid, bag and absorber holding 33 lb, about 25 person-days, so $0.44. Low end is 25 to 50 lb sacks at warehouse prices; high end is ready-sealed cans.

lifeYears.basis: The Church of Jesus Christ store describes its canned white rice as keeping about 25 years cool and dry (search snippet; the store page redirected and could not be read). Home packing is less sure, and old beans cook slowly.

setupHours.basis: Sourcing sacks, buckets and bags and sealing several months' worth. My estimate; near 1 hour if bought ready-sealed.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Yearly look for damp, pests and rodents. My estimate.

everydayShare.basis: Sealed stock is not rotated, so little of it is ever eaten in normal times. My estimate.

reliability.basis: Home sealing can fail, the household may never have cooked from it, and it is useless without fuel and water. My estimate.

adherence.basis: Half of households holding the stock would isolate; half of those could not have done so without it. Both guesses.

items.name: Emergency ration bars
items.spec: Sealed 3,600 kcal lifeboat ration (Datrex, SOS or Mainstay): 18 wafers of 200 kcal, five-year shelf life, eaten as is with no water or heat. One pack is 1.7 person-days.

price.basis: $7.50 regular, $6.50 on sale at https://www.sosproducts.com/Datrex-Food-Bar-3600-Calorie-Each-p/35025.htm. Other shops list the same pack at $14 to $19 (search snippets).

lifeYears.basis: Five years from manufacture, per https://www.sosproducts.com/Datrex-Food-Bar-3600-Calorie-Each-p/35025.htm. High end assumes owners keep them past the date.

setupHours.basis: Order and put away. My estimate.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Note the expiry date; replace every five years. My estimate.

everydayShare.basis: Nobody eats these by choice.

reliability.basis: Risk is being forgotten past expiry or left in a hot car. My estimate.

items.name: Camping stove with starter fuel
items.spec: Single-burner tabletop butane stove (8,000 BTU/h; Gas One GS-3400P or Choice equivalent) with four 8 oz canisters and two lighters. Boils a litre in about 5 minutes out of the wind. For use with ventilation or outdoors.

price.basis: $19.50 for the Choice 8,000 BTU butane stove (https://www.webstaurantstore.com/search/butane-stove.html) plus four canisters at $1.79 and about $3 of lighters: $29.66. The dual-fuel Gas One GS-3400P lists at $30 without fuel (https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/reviews/camping-and-hiking/camping-stove/gas-one-gs-3400p).

lifeYears.basis: Simple device with a regulator and a piezo igniter that wear. My estimate.

setupHours.basis: Buy, read the instructions and cook one meal on it. My estimate.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Light it once a year. My estimate.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: A canister now and then for testing.

everydayShare.basis: Some owners use it for camping or table cooking; most would not. My estimate.

reliability.basis: Can be mislaid, never tried, or out of fuel. Butane works poorly near freezing, so in an unheated home in a winter storm take the low end unless the stove also takes propane.

micromortsPerDay.basis: CPSC: about 6 deaths a year from propane grills and camp stoves, mostly in tents and campers, against tens of millions of uses; no denominator exists. https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/Non-Fire-Carbon-Monoxide-Deaths-Associated-with-the-Use-of-Consumer-Products-2022-Annual-Estimates.pdf

items.name: Extra stove fuel
items.spec: 8 oz (227 g) butane canisters for the camping stove, bought in packs of twelve and stored cool, beyond the four in the stove kit.

price.basis: $21.49 per pack of twelve, $1.79 each, at https://www.webstaurantstore.com/choice-butane-fuel-refill-8-oz-canister-pack/174BUTANE12.html. Home Depot lists a Gas One twelve-pack at $36.78 (search snippet).

lifeYears.basis: Sealed canisters keep for years; seals and rust set the limit. Not checked against a maker's figure.

setupHours.basis: Order and find a cool place away from heat. My estimate.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Check for rust. My estimate.

everydayShare.basis: Used up in normal life only by owners who camp or cook at the table. My estimate.

reliability.basis: Little to go wrong. My estimate.

items.name: Outdoor grill with spare fuel
items.spec: 22-inch charcoal kettle grill with two 16 lb bags of briquettes kept in reserve, used outdoors only. A household that already owns a grill needs only the spare fuel (about $22, or a spare propane cylinder).

price.basis: Weber Original Kettle 22-inch $149.00 on weber.com plus two 16 lb bags of Kingsford at $10.92 (both search snippets; weber.com and the grocers refused the fetch): $170.84. Low end is spare fuel alone for a household that owns a grill.

lifeYears.basis: Enamelled steel kettle kept outdoors. My estimate.

setupHours.basis: Buy, assemble, cook once. My estimate.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Keep the reserve bags dry and unused. My estimate.

everydayShare.basis: Seven households in ten own a grill for ordinary cooking, so most of the cost is justified by everyday use. The reserve fuel is the preparedness part.

reliability.basis: Needs dry fuel and weather that allows cooking outside; unusable in high wind, heavy rain or under a burn ban. My estimate.

items.name: Infant formula buffer

items.name: Fallout shelter plan
items.spec: A one-page household rule for a nuclear detonation, agreed in advance: the best-shielded spot at home (a basement corner away from windows, or the windowless core of a middle floor in a large building); the nearest better building if home is a light-frame house without a basement or a mobile home; the same for work and school; everyone shelters where they are and nobody drives to collect anyone for 24 hours; stay inside at least 24 hours and for 3 to 14 days unless told it is safe; shut windows and ventilation; on coming in from outside, bag outer clothes and wash; keep a battery radio on. About two hours to read official guidance, walk the building and agree the rule.

price.basis: No purchase; at most printing a card.

lifeYears.basis: Needs redoing when the household moves or changes workplace or school.

setupHours.basis: Read FEMA or Ready.gov guidance, pick the spots at home, work and school, agree the no-pickup rule, write the card.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: A yearly reminder to the household.

everydayShare.basis: The same rule serves a chemical shelter-in-place order or a tornado warning, which are rare.

reliability.basis: Chance the rule is still remembered or the card found; behaviour under stress is in adherence.

adherence.basis: Full cooperation with a stay-inside order rises from 59% to 74% when people know their family is somewhere prepared (2004 survey, n=2,545); experts expect preparation to add 20-30 points to 60-70% compliance. https://webharvest.gov/peth04/20041015115419/http://www.cacsh.org/pdf/RedefiningReadinessStudy.pdf

fraction.basis: Dose share falls from the unprepared mix (0.22 light house with basement, 0.13 masonry house, 0.10 large apartment block) to 1/PF of the best spot (0.05, 0.033, 0.02): 77%, 75%, 81% removed; only 11-38% in a light house without a basement. Weighted 70:30 by the LLNL 2022 share of homes with adequate shelter. https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1880931
