items.name: Pre-set trigger to leave before a nuclear war
items.spec: A written rule, agreed in advance, to leave for a named destination well away from targets (a rural area several hours away, or abroad, ideally the Southern Hemisphere) when a stated tripwire is crossed, such as nuclear use anywhere in a conflict involving the home country or an aggregate forecast above a set level. Includes valid passports, a way to pay for tickets at short notice, somewhere to stay for three to four weeks, and an arrangement to work remotely or take leave. One unit covers one household member.
items.note: Most of what leaving early buys is surviving the first hour, which the model leaves out; the ranking understates this entry.

price.basis: No purchase beyond a valid passport, which the documents entry owns; the cost is the trips, counted under upkeep.

lifeYears.basis: Destinations, jobs and the geopolitical tripwires change.

setupHours.basis: Choose tripwires and destination, check entry rules, agree with employer and household. Per household, not per person.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Watching the tripwires and keeping the arrangement current. Per household.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Chance the trigger fires in a year, 2% (0.5-8%: one to three crises since 1945 would have fired a sensible tripwire, and risk is thought higher now), times $4,000 per person per trip (1,500-12,000: fares, three to four weeks' lodging, lost earnings and disruption). Nearly all firings are false alarms.

everydayShare.basis: A false-alarm trip has some holiday value and remote work continues for some.

reliability.basis: Chance travel is still possible when the trigger fires: flights not sold out, borders open.

adherence.basis: Share of households that would actually go when their own rule says so, given jobs, schools and relatives.

fraction.basis: Share of nuclear wars preceded by a public escalation that crosses the tripwire at least a day or two before the home region is struck. Samotsvety (2022) gave an attentive Londoner a 75% chance of getting out in time during a crisis already under way; a surprise attack gives none. https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/KRFXjCqqfGQAYirm5

items.name: Packed go-bag
items.spec: One 25-35 litre backpack per adult, kept by the door or in the car: filled 1 litre bottle and about 2,400 kcal of bars; headlamp; power bank with cable and plug; small first-aid kit; three N95 masks; poncho and foil blanket; toiletries, toilet paper and wipes; socks, underwear, a warm layer and an old pair of closed shoes (already owned); lighter, whistle, pocket knife, tape, notepad, zip bags; copies of ID, insurance and prescriptions in a pouch and on a USB stick; spare house and car key; paper list of phone numbers. A card on top lists what to grab last: medication, glasses, phone, wallet, passport, laptop. Children share an adult's bag with a few extras. Cash and spare medication are separate entries.
items.units: bag per household member (a child's share is smaller)

price.basis: Built up from typical prices: backpack $30, bottle and bars $20, headlamp $20, power bank and cable $30, first-aid pouch $15, masks $6, poncho and blanket $8, toiletries $10, sundries $10, pouch, USB stick and key copies $15, knife $20: about $185 for an adult, less if the backpack is an old one, and about $50 for a child's share; $130 averages a household. Bounded by two prices read on 19 Nov 2026: a premade one-person kit at $39.99 (https://www.quill.com/ready-america-grab-n-go-1-person-3-days-backpack-emergency-kit-70180/cbs/421760.html) and The Prepared's level-1 list at $400-1,100 (https://theprepared.com/bug-out-bags/guides/bug-out-bag-list/).

lifeYears.basis: Bag and hardware outlast ten years; bars, batteries and masks last about five.

setupHours.basis: Choosing, buying, copying documents and packing for a household.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Two checks a year: recharge the power bank, swap clothes for the season and for growing children, rotate food.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Replacing bars, batteries and masks for a household every five years or so.

everydayShare.basis: The bag only works if it stays packed, so little of it earns its keep day to day; the power bank and headlamp are borrowed for trips.

reliability.basis: Chance the bag is where it should be, complete and current when the household has to leave.

adherence.basis: Share of departures in which the bag is in fact taken.

fraction.basis: A household that leaves with no notice goes without chargers, toiletries, spare clothes, papers and sometimes glasses or medication; replacing them and doing without costs perhaps $50 (20-130) a person, about 15% of the first three days' $330 hardship and nothing after. The first three days are a tenth of displacement harm on Household Pulse durations and up to four tenths in hazards with short evacuations, so 0.15 x 0.1-0.4 gives 0.015-0.06.

adherence.basis: Owners still stop to gather pets, valuables and relatives.

fraction.basis: Marshall Fire evacuees spent a mean 64 minutes preparing after deciding to go, and each minute of preparation added 0.7 minutes to departure (https://mro.massey.ac.nz/server/api/core/bitstreams/5f9e7234-160d-47cf-8ee0-3261de5524c8/content). If packing is a third of that and the bag halves it, departure comes about 8 minutes sooner, under a tenth of the usual 90-140 minutes from awareness to leaving. Late evacuation accounts for 48% of Australian bushfire deaths (https://www.csiro.au/en/news/All/Articles/2016/December/bushfire-loss-data), so a small gain in time is taken to remove a few percent of deaths. The low end is zero because no study shows packed bags speed departure, and prepared households in both US regressions left no sooner.

items.name: Evacuation plan with a pre-arranged place to stay
items.spec: One evening's work, written on one page and known to everyone in the home: (1) a named friend or relative one to three hours away who has agreed in advance to take the household in, and a fallback town with hotels; (2) two routes out, saved offline; (3) personal triggers stricter than an official order (leave at 'warning' or 'voluntary', or on seeing smoke, flames or rising water; know your hurricane zone); (4) who fetches children, pets and anyone who cannot drive, a meeting point and an out-of-area contact; (5) a five-minute grab list. Sign up for local emergency alerts. Review once a year.

price.basis: No purchase needed; the cost is time.

lifeYears.basis: Goes stale as jobs, schools, cars and the host's circumstances change.

setupHours.basis: Look up zone and routes, call the host, agree triggers with the household, write it down.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Yearly review and a call to confirm the host.

everydayShare.basis: No everyday use.

reliability.basis: Chance the plan is remembered and the host still available when needed.

adherence.basis: Share of displacements in which the arranged host is in fact used and not also displaced.

fraction.basis: Most evacuees stay with friends or family without any plan (median 62% across hurricane studies; 62% in Texas 2021), so the gain is only among the 27% (13% in Texas) who pay for rooms. If a standing invitation moves a third of them, 9% of households save about $65 of the $90 daily hardship: 6.5%, plus perhaps 2% for everyone from knowing where to go. That 8% holds for the first month, which is 35-70% of displacement harm, giving 0.03-0.055.

adherence.basis: Plans to leave early are often abandoned for wait-and-see on the day.

fraction.basis: Two routes by which a plan could save lives, neither measured. Leaving sooner: deciding takes longer than packing (Marshall Fire delay 137 minutes against 64 of preparation), and agreed triggers attack the deciding. Leaving at all: 31% of coastal residents said they would not evacuate if told to, but the reasons a plan addresses are the minority ones (roads too crowded 56%, pets 27%; cost named by 14% of Irma non-evacuees in a search snippet). Against this, plan-holders left no sooner in the Camp Fire, were no likelier to leave in the Marshall Fire, and fared no better after Sandy.

feasible.basis: mobility.json, evacuation-plan.

items.name: Keep the tank at least half full
items.spec: Refuel the household's main vehicle when it reaches half a tank, which keeps about seven US gallons, 150-200 miles, in hand; for an electric car, charge nightly and do not let it sit below half. Fill up whenever a hurricane, fire-weather or winter-storm watch is issued.

price.basis: Refuelling at half instead of a quarter raises the average level of a 14-gallon tank by an eighth, 1.75 gallons, about $5 of fuel held; it is burned later, so only the interest is a cost. Pump price assumed near $3 a gallon, not checked.

lifeYears.basis: A habit has no service life; the figure only spreads a trivial set-up cost.

setupHours.basis: Deciding to do it.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: About 11,500 miles a year at 25 mpg is 460 gallons: 44 fills of 10.5 gallons (refuelling at a quarter) or 66 fills of 7 gallons (at a half). Twenty-two extra stops at about 4 minutes of fixed time each is 1.5 hours; less for the many drivers who already refuel early, nil for an electric car charged at home. Inputs are round figures from memory.

everydayShare.basis: The fuel is used anyway.

reliability.basis: Share of the time the tank is in fact above half once the habit is adopted.

adherence.basis: A full tank is used automatically; lapses are in reliability.

fraction.basis: A driver who refuels at a quarter is below half a third of the time. In a mass evacuation perhaps 40% of them meet dry pumps or long queues (37-60% of stations in Florida metro areas were out of fuel around Irma), so 13% of households lose one to three hours, worth $20-60 a person: about $5 on a $330 three-day evacuation, 1.5%, and less over longer displacements.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Fuel decides the outcome only for the few percent of households that would otherwise not leave, leave hours late, or run dry in a jam; in the Rita evacuation, 12-36 hours on the road, cars ran out of fuel in 100-mile queues in great heat. Unmeasured.

feasible.basis: mobility.json, half-tank-habit.

items.name: Car emergency kit
items.spec: In the boot of the main car: jump leads or a lithium jump starter, 12-volt tyre inflator and plug kit (and a checked spare), two warning triangles, headlamp, work gloves, 2 litres of water, a blanket and a phone cable. In cold-winter areas add an ice scraper, a folding shovel and a bag of sand or cat litter.

price.basis: Leads $20-30, inflator $30-40, plug kit $10, triangles $15-20, gloves and water $10; about $100 more if a lithium jump starter replaces the leads (NOCO GB40 at $99.95 in Best Buy and Walmart search snippets; no retailer page loaded). Premade kits ran $18-78 in Walmart snippets.

lifeYears.basis: Leads and triangles last decades; inflators and lithium packs five to eight years.

setupHours.basis: Buy, stow, and learn to use the jump starter and plug kit.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Recharge the jump starter twice a year, check the spare tyre's pressure, swap the water.

everydayShare.basis: AAA took over 27 million roadside calls in 2024, about 7 million for batteries (https://newsroom.aaa.com/2025/04/aaa-urges-drivers-to-stay-proactive-on-auto-repair-and-maintenance/). With about 60 million members (from memory) that is a call every two to three years and a battery or slow-puncture call every five or so. Fixing those oneself saves about an hour's wait, or a $75-125 call-out for a non-member: $4-15 a year against a kit costing about $25 a year, so 0.15 to 0.6; higher for a driver without roadside cover.

reliability.basis: Jump starter charged, spare inflated, owner able to use them.

adherence.basis: Share of curable breakdowns the owner in fact cures.

fraction.basis: 27 million AAA calls over roughly 0.7 trillion member-miles is one breakdown per 26,000 miles: 0.6% on a 150-mile evacuation, perhaps 2% in heat, queues and debris. The kit cures about 40% of those (battery, slow puncture), so under 1% of evacuations are saved from a stall of several hours, and few stalls are fatal.

items.name: Small tent or tarp for outdoor shelter
items.spec: A freestanding two- or three-person tent with flysheet, or at least a 3 by 4 metre tarp with cord and pegs, used with the sleeping bags and mats of the warmth entry: for sleeping in the garden, at a relative's or at a campsite when the house is unsafe and rooms are full or far away.
items.units: tent for up to three people

price.basis: Kelty Discovery Trail 2-Person Tent $129.95, read on the retailer's page on 19 Nov 2026 (https://www.kitterytradingpost.com/kelty-discovery-trail-2-person-tent/). Budget dome tents and tarps cost less (not checked), so the middle is set below the price read.

lifeYears.basis: Stored dry and rarely used.

setupHours.basis: Buy it and pitch it once.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Check it now and then.

everydayShare.basis: High for households that camp, near zero for the rest.

reliability.basis: Complete, findable and usable in the weather on the day.

adherence.basis: Weather, security and willingness to camp.

fraction.basis: After a damaging earthquake many households whose homes still stand sleep outside nearby for days (from memory of Northridge and Christchurch; no source opened). For those with no host close by, perhaps a fifth, a tent replaces a hotel or a long drive: it saves most of the $50 money cost and adds discomfort, a net $30 of the $90 day. 0.2 x 0.33 is about 6% for the first week or two in mild weather.

adherence.basis: Most people who can reach a bed will not camp.

fraction.basis: Campgrounds and vacation homes took 8% of San Diego's 2007 fire evacuees, mostly people with caravans or cabins; a tent adds a cheap option for a few households when rooms are sold out.

items.name: Cash at home in small notes
items.spec: US currency in $5, $10 and $20 notes kept hidden at home; one unit is $100. Elsewhere the local equivalent: euros in Western Europe; in Buenos Aires no more than a week of pesos, the rest in US dollar notes.

price.basis: Face value; there is no purchase price.

lifeYears.basis: US notes are never demonetised; some European series have been withdrawn but stay exchangeable. Irrelevant to cost when everydayShare is 1.

setupHours.basis: One bank or ATM visit and asking for small notes.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Checking it is still there and topping up after use.

upkeepUsdPerUnitYear.basis: Per $100: inflation $3.2 (CPI +3.7% in the 12 months to September 2026, https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/cpi_11102026.htm; I use a longer-run 3.2) minus the $0.39 an average savings account would pay (https://www.fdic.gov/national-rates-and-rate-caps) plus theft and loss $0.8 (burglary 1.3% of households a year x 40% found, fire claims 0.21% x 25%, misplaced 0.25%; the three shares are guesses). The low end is theft and loss alone, for money that would otherwise sit in an account paying about inflation or for a reader who counts only what a current account pays; the high end is the 4.1-4.35% a top savings account pays plus high theft.

everydayShare.basis: Set as the assignment instructs: the money remains the household's, so the cost is the carrying cost in upkeepUsdPerYear.

reliability.basis: Spent beforehand, stolen, forgotten, or in $100 notes a cash-only shop cannot change: three quarters of the value of cash Americans store is in $100s (Fed Diary 2026).

items.name: Second bank and second card network
items.spec: A current account at a second, unrelated bank with its own debit card, plus a credit card on the other network (one Visa, one Mastercard); physical cards with PINs known; about a month of spending kept in the second account.
items.units: second account and card, set up once

price.basis: Free current accounts and no-fee credit cards are widely offered; not priced on a fetched page.

lifeYears.basis: Lasts until the bank closes the account or the household lets it lapse.

setupHours.basis: Opening an account and a card online and funding it.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Keeping both active and watching a second statement.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Zero if the fee-waiver conditions are met; monthly fees otherwise.

everydayShare.basis: Most of its use is everyday: a card blocked for fraud, a lost wallet, one bank's IT failure. 1 in 7 UK adults had a card made unusable by a glitch in 2018 (Which? survey, search snippet).

reliability.basis: The second card is at home, active and its PIN remembered.

adherence.basis: Share of owners who keep a usable balance in the second account.

fraction.basis: Greece's 2015 cap was 60 euros per depositor per credit institution per day (legal act quoted in search snippets), so a second bank doubled it, and a second bank survives the resolution of the first (Laiki in Cyprus). It does nothing on days when every bank and ATM is shut.

items.name: Account in another country
items.spec: A bank, brokerage or e-money account in another jurisdiction and currency, funded in advance, with a debit card issued there: a US or Uruguayan account for residents of Argentina, an account in another member state or outside the euro for euro-area residents. One unit is the account; the balance is the reader's choice.
items.note: Ranked only for keeping payments working. What it does for savings in a freeze is described in the text, not ranked.

price.basis: Opening is usually free; some banks require a visit or a minimum deposit. Not priced on a fetched page.

lifeYears.basis: Until the provider closes non-resident accounts or rules change.

setupHours.basis: Identity checks, funding, learning the tax reporting.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Foreign-account tax reporting and keeping the account active.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Account fees and a 0.4-2% currency cost on each transfer; the balance itself can earn dollar money-market rates, so it has no carrying cost beyond the engine's.

everydayShare.basis: Also used for travel, cheaper currency exchange and investing.

reliability.basis: Non-resident accounts get closed, compliance freezes happen, and controls can block topping it up; the card needs working ATMs and terminals.

adherence.basis: Share of owners with a useful balance abroad and the card at hand when controls arrive.

fraction.basis: In Greece in 2015 cards issued abroad were exempt from the 60-euro limit as long as ATMs held cash (Greek foreign ministry notice, seen in a search snippet only). It fails when ATMs are empty or merchants refuse cards.

items.name: Copies of documents and a home inventory
items.spec: Photos or scans of IDs, insurance policies, deed or lease, medical and bank details, and a ten-minute phone video of every room as an inventory; kept encrypted in the cloud and on a USB stick, with paper copies in a waterproof pouch.
items.units: set of copies for the household

price.basis: Waterproof pouch and USB stick; the longlist's estimate of $10-20, not checked on a retailer page.

lifeYears.basis: Until documents expire or policies change enough that the set must be redone.

setupHours.basis: Gathering, scanning, filming and filing.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Yearly refresh, as Ready.gov and the Red Cross advise.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Fits in free cloud storage; a paid tier otherwise.

everydayShare.basis: Also used after a lost wallet and for loan, visa and tax paperwork.

reliability.basis: Out of date, password forgotten, or the cloud unreachable while communications are down.

adherence.basis: Share of owners whose copies are current and retrievable when needed.

fraction.basis: An inventory raises the contents payout and proof of ownership unlocks aid. Only 10% (six months) to 23% (twelve months) of Los Angeles total-loss claimants got their full contents limit without an itemised inventory, and FEMA declared about 60% of Hurricane Maria applications ineligible, many for lack of ownership papers (search snippets). The size of the gain is my guess.

adherence.basis: Share of owners whose copies are current and retrievable when needed.

fraction.basis: An inventory raises the contents payout and proof of ownership unlocks aid. Only 10% (six months) to 23% (twelve months) of Los Angeles total-loss claimants got their full contents limit without an itemised inventory, and FEMA declared about 60% of Hurricane Maria applications ineligible, many for lack of ownership papers (search snippets). The size of the gain is my guess.

adherence.basis: Same as above.

fraction.basis: Hours not spent proving identity and re-creating policy and account details while displaced; perhaps 5-15 hours over a displacement of weeks.

items.name: Fire-resistant document chest
items.spec: SentrySafe 1200 fire chest, 0.18 cubic feet, UL classified for 30 minutes at 1,550 F, key lock, not waterproof; holds passports, certificates, titles and the cash reserve.

price.basis: Manufacturer page lists the model in a $20-$50 band (https://www.sentrysafe.com/product/1200); $29.99 on the manufacturer's store and $25-31 at Walmart are from search snippets.

lifeYears.basis: No moving parts beyond the lock.

setupHours.basis: Buying it and gathering the originals.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Returning documents after use.

everydayShare.basis: A fixed place for important papers has some everyday use.

reliability.basis: The originals are in it, the fire stays within the 30-minute rating, and hose water does not ruin the contents (this model is not waterproof).

adherence.basis: Share of owners who actually keep the originals in it.

fraction.basis: Replacing passports, birth certificates and titles costs perhaps $300-600 in fees plus 10-20 hours, about $700, against an average fire claim of $101,092 (III): under 1% of the loss.

adherence.basis: Share of owners who actually keep the originals in it.

fraction.basis: Replacing passports, birth certificates and titles costs perhaps $300-600 in fees plus 10-20 hours, about $700, against an average fire claim of $101,092 (III): under 1% of the loss.

items.name: Automatic data backup
items.spec: Continuous cloud backup of the main computer (Backblaze Personal Backup) and cloud sync of phone photos, plus a 2 TB external drive updated automatically.

price.basis: A 2 TB portable drive, the longlist's $60-80 estimate; not read on a retailer page. Zero if cloud only.

lifeYears.basis: Typical service life of a portable drive.

setupHours.basis: Installing, choosing what to back up, first upload left running.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Checking that backups still run and a test restore.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Backblaze Personal Backup is $99 a year for unlimited data (https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-backup/personal/pricing); the low end is a 50 GB phone-photo plan at about $1 a month (recalled).

everydayShare.basis: Disasters destroy devices far less often than everyday causes: fire claims 0.21% and burglary 1.3% of households a year against roughly 5% a year for drive failure, loss, theft and accidents per device (recalled).

reliability.basis: Backups that silently stopped, lost passwords, files excluded.

adherence.basis: Share of set-ups still working when the loss happens.

fraction.basis: Assumes a household values its photos and records at about $3,000 ($500-10,000), against an average fire claim of $101,092. The valuation is a guess; the loss is not a market loss.

adherence.basis: Share of set-ups still working when the loss happens.

fraction.basis: Assumes a household values its photos and records at about $3,000 ($500-10,000), against an average fire claim of $101,092. The valuation is a guess; the loss is not a market loss.

items.name: Offline backup and spare computer
items.spec: A 2 TB portable drive, encrypted (BitLocker, FileVault or the drive's own password), holding the household's essential files and refreshed monthly, then unplugged and kept in the go-bag or away from home; plus a spare laptop, either an old one kept charged and updated or a cheap new one, holding the same essentials, a password-manager emergency kit, and offline copies of the tools needed to work (an office suite, a PDF reader, installers, any cloud-only documents exported to files). Both are tested twice a year by opening a few files on the spare machine with the network off.
items.units: backup drive and spare laptop for the household

price.basis: Read on retailer pages on 20 November 2026, when storage prices were two to three times their 2024-25 level. Drive: Seagate Expansion 2 TB $95.99 (Staples, out of stock), WD Elements 2 TB $169.99 on sale (Target), Seagate One Touch 2 TB with password $163.99 (Zones); software encryption (FileVault, BitLocker, VeraCrypt) is free. Spare laptop: refurbished Lenovo ThinkPad T490 $209.99 or T14 Gen 1 $304.99, new HP 14 (N150, 4 GB) $299.99, Acer Aspire Go 15 $459.99 (all Target). Lo: drive only, the old laptop serving as the spare. Mid: a $170 drive and a refurbished business laptop or a cheap new one, about $230 more. Hi: a 2 TB portable SSD ($458-575, SanDisk Extreme or Samsung T7 Shield) and a $300 laptop.

lifeYears.basis: A portable drive and a cheap laptop each last about five years; an old laptop kept as the spare is already part-way through its life, and its operating system may stop receiving updates.

setupHours.basis: Choosing what is essential, exporting cloud-only documents, encrypting the drive, setting up the spare laptop and writing down the passwords needed to open both.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: About five minutes a month to refresh the drive and twenty minutes a quarter to update and charge the spare laptop, plus two short restore tests.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: None beyond electricity; hi allows for a paid backup utility.

everydayShare.basis: An offline copy and a second computer protect against drive failure, theft, breakage and ransomware, which happen far more often than any regional event: about 5% of devices a year fail or are lost (money-docs.json, data-backup, recalled), and about 6% of adults a year have an account taken over (Security.org). Lower than data-backup's 0.95 because the spare laptop and the monthly unplugging are bought for resilience, not convenience.

reliability.basis: Failures: a copy months out of date, a forgotten encryption password, a spare laptop with a flat battery or an expired operating system, essentials that were never copied.

adherence.basis: The household remembers the copy and the outage lasts long enough to fetch it.

fraction.basis: With the network down, a household that would otherwise improvise with its phone and whatever synced folders hold can open its cloud-only documents, records and photos and do offline work (writing, spreadsheets, accounts). Work that needs the network is not restored.

adherence.basis: A household locked out has every reason to use it.

fraction.basis: After ransomware, a wiped device or a locked account, an unplugged copy and a second computer restore the files and a working machine at once; what remains is the locked account itself (its email, its online services).

adherence.basis: The drive was where the plan said when the household left.

fraction.basis: Only if the drive is in the go-bag or away from home; the spare laptop is usually left behind or lost with the main one. With the drive, any borrowed or new computer has the files the same day instead of after a cloud restore.

items.name: Offline reference library
items.spec: Kiwix (free) on a laptop with the full English Wikipedia (119 GB) and on each phone with the 'mini' edition (13 GB) or the edition without pictures (49 GB); Wikipedia's medicine collection (WikiMed, 1.7 GB); iFixit repair guides (3.3 GB), Wikivoyage (1 GB) and Stack Exchange's DIY, cooking and gardening sites (about 3 GB); and a handful of practical books in PDF. Refreshed once a year. Plus two paper books for when the battery is flat: the SAS Survival Handbook and a home-repair manual (Black & Decker's Book of Home How-To). The paper first-aid manual and lay medical handbook are a separate entry (reference-books).

price.basis: Kiwix and its collections are free on Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS (https://get.kiwix.org/en/solutions/applications/kiwix-reader/). Paperbacks at Barnes & Noble, 20 November 2026: SAS Survival Handbook $25.99, Black & Decker The Book of Home How-To $40.00, The Encyclopedia of Country Living $29.95. Lo: one book, downloads on storage the household has. Mid: two books. Hi: three books and a 256 GB microSD card for a phone too full for Wikipedia (SanDisk Ultra $62.99 at Target).

lifeYears.basis: The downloads are refreshed yearly at no cost; the card and the paper books last five to twenty years.

setupHours.basis: Installing Kiwix, choosing and downloading collections (large downloads run unattended), buying the books and finding where the medical pages are.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: A yearly refresh of the downloads.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Kiwix and its collections are free.

everydayShare.basis: Looking things up on flights, abroad without data or in places without signal, and reading the books.

reliability.basis: The device must be charged and the files present; the household must remember it has them and find the right page under stress. The paper books cover a flat battery.

adherence.basis: Used when a question comes up and the network is down.

fraction.basis: The information need's $15 day (comms.json) is news and instructions ($11.25), contact ($10.50) and ordinary use ($3.25), of which looking things up is a part. An encyclopedia and how-to library recovers perhaps a sixth of ordinary use ($0.55) plus a little practical guidance in long outages: about 4% of the day, beside offline entertainment's 5% and offline maps' 3%. Nothing for news or contact.

adherence.basis: Consulted and followed.

fraction.basis: As reference-books (0.01): only where care is out of reach for weeks. WikiMed is fuller and searchable but needs a charged screen and is slower to use in an emergency than a paper manual. No study measures the effect of owning either.

items.name: Family verification phrase and call-back habit
items.spec: Agree a phrase that family members will ask for before acting on any urgent request for money, and the habit of hanging up and calling back on a number you already have.
items.note: Recommended by the FBI, the National Cybersecurity Alliance and others. No study of its effectiveness exists, so the fraction is a guess.

setupHours.basis: The model's own guess.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: The model's own guess: a yearly reminder.

reliability.basis: The model's own guess: the chance that the person targeted remembers to use it.

fraction.basis: Imposter scams are most of the expected loss (ai-economy.md); the share a phrase and a call-back would stop is unmeasured.

adherence.basis: The model's own guess.

items.name: Passkeys or hardware keys, credit freeze and port-out PIN
items.spec: Passkeys or hardware keys on email, bank and phone accounts; a credit freeze; a port-out PIN with the mobile carrier; transaction alerts.
items.note: In a 2019 Google study hardware keys blocked every targeted account-takeover attempt; but takeover is the smaller part of the loss, and no study measures a credit freeze or a port-out PIN.

price.basis: Two hardware keys; passkeys alone cost nothing.

setupHours.basis: The model's own guess.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: The model's own guess.

reliability.basis: The model's own guess.

fraction.basis: Account takeover is roughly a tenth of the expected loss (ai-economy.md: about $15 of $130 a year); hardware keys stop nearly all of it.

items.name: Pepper spray
items.spec: One keychain canister of OC spray (about 15 g, 25 short bursts, 3 m range) per adult, kept by the door or bed, with one practice burst outdoors.

price.basis: Step 2 read $9.99 on the maker's page; search snippets from Academy and Tractor Supply show the same. Retailer pages refused my fetches.

lifeYears.basis: Maker's stated four-year shelf life (step 2).

setupHours.basis: Buy, read the instructions, one practice burst.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Check the date.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: None beyond replacement at end of life.

everydayShare.basis: Some owners would carry it outdoors anyway; that use is outside the model.

reliability.basis: In date, within reach, and the user gets the safety off under stress.

adherence.basis: Share of confrontations at home in which the canister is at hand and used.

fraction.basis: Police field data show incapacitation in 156 of 174 uses (90%), but by trained officers with back-up. No civilian outcome study exists. Most burglaries happen with nobody home (72%) and 65% of violent ones are by people the victim knows, so the spray can matter in a minority of cases.

items.name: Firearm with training and locked storage
items.spec: One pump shotgun or handgun, a basic safety and handling course (4-8 hours), a quick-access lock box or cable lock, 100 rounds, and one range session a year.

price.basis: Shotgun $289.99 (Academy, fetched) + lock box about $110 + basic course about $110 (65-150) + 100 rounds about $50; the last three from search snippets. A handgun adds $150-400.

lifeYears.basis: Firearms last decades.

setupHours.basis: Purchase and background check, course, first range session.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: One range session and cleaning.

everydayShare.basis: Zero unless the household shoots for sport.

reliability.basis: A trained adult is home, reaches the locked gun in time and is able to use it.

adherence.basis: Share of home confrontations with a trained adult present and the gun reachable.

fraction.basis: National Crime Victimization Survey 2007-2011: 4.1% of victims were injured after defending themselves with a gun against 4.2% after any protective action; California cohort: no lower risk of being killed by strangers for people living with handgun owners. Property was lost in 38.5% of thefts resisted with a gun, 55.9% with any action, 34.9% with another weapon. So about zero for injury and death and a little for property.

adherence.basis: Household alert and at home.

fraction.basis: With police absent, deterrence may count for more than the everyday data show. No data.

micromortsOwner.basis: plans-skills-security.json: firearm suicide and accident among owners (Studdert et al. 2020).

micromortsOtherAdult.basis: plans-skills-security.json: risk to an adult living with an owner.

items.name: Protective helmet
items.spec: One hard hat or bicycle helmet per person, kept with sturdy shoes by the bed or the go-bag.

price.basis: Step 2 estimate of $20-40; basic hard hats sell for $12-25 (recalled). No retailer page would load.

lifeYears.basis: Makers advise replacing shells after about five years of work use; stored ones last longer.

setupHours.basis: Buy and place.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: None.

everydayShare.basis: Many households already own bicycle helmets, which serve.

reliability.basis: It is found and put on in time.

adherence.basis: Worn when debris is falling.

fraction.basis: Northridge 1994: the 33 deaths in Los Angeles County were mainly from building collapse; hospital admissions were mostly falls and being hit by objects. A helmet cannot be put on during 20 seconds of shaking, so it serves aftershocks, tornado sheltering and clean-up only.

items.name: Entry door reinforcement
items.spec: For the main exterior door (and back door of a house): 75 mm screws through strike plate and hinges into the stud, a steel jamb-and-strike reinforcement kit, a deadbolt if absent, and a motion-sensor light at the entry.

price.basis: Jamb reinforcement kit about $100-145 (marketplace listings in search snippets; maker's page refused the fetch) plus a $25 sensor light; screws alone cost under $15.

lifeYears.basis: Steel hardware; lasts as long as the door frame.

setupHours.basis: A drill-and-screw job.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: None.

everydayShare.basis: All of its benefit is the everyday burglary risk, which the model counts through the violence channel; a positive share here would count it twice.

reliability.basis: Fixed hardware.

adherence.basis: The door has to be locked: about 40% of unlawful entries to unoccupied homes were through an unlocked door or window (BJS).

fraction.basis: Dutch building code of 1999 requiring certified burglar-resistant doors and windows cut burglary of new homes by 26% (1.1% to 0.8% a year). Doors alone address less: forcible entry is 55.7% of US burglaries (FBI 2019, snippet); if half of forced entries are through a door and reinforcement defeats 45% of those net of burglars switching to a window (both guesses), 0.557 x 0.5 x 0.45 = 0.12. High end: a survey cross-section in England and Wales gives door double locks or deadlocks alone a protection factor of 2.8, inflated by confounding.

items.name: Keeping quiet about supplies
items.spec: Do not advertise stored food, fuel, cash or a generator beyond the neighbours the household has agreed to share with; keep stores out of sight from the street.

price.basis: Free.

lifeYears.basis: A habit; life is immaterial at zero cost.

setupHours.basis: None.

everydayShare.basis: None.

reliability.basis: Neighbours notice deliveries, generator noise and lit windows anyway.

adherence.basis: Share of households that in fact stay unnoticed.

fraction.basis: No data. A household not known to hold supplies is a less likely target once scarcity lasts weeks; in short events there is nothing to reduce.

items.name: Basic digital security
items.spec: A password manager with a unique password per account, two-factor authentication on email, bank and phone-carrier accounts with printed recovery codes, automatic updates on, and a free credit freeze at the three bureaus.

price.basis: Free tiers of password managers and built-in authenticators suffice.

lifeYears.basis: Until accounts and devices have turned over.

setupHours.basis: Moving 50-100 accounts into a manager and enabling two-factor on the important ones.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: New accounts, device changes.

upkeepUsdPerYear.basis: Zero on a free tier; paid family plans run to about $40 a year (recalled).

everydayShare.basis: Nearly all the benefit is against everyday fraud, which the model has no hazard for.

reliability.basis: Kept up, and the user does not approve a fraudulent prompt.

fraction.basis: plans-skills-security.json: removes about 20% of an out-of-pocket loss of $10 to $25 a year, against an expected loss to scams of about $100.

items.name: Basic tools bundle
items.spec: Multitool with pliers, a fixed or locking knife, one roll of duct tape, two pairs of leather work gloves, 30 m of paracord, a box of contractor bags and zip bags, sewing kit, notebook and pencil, in one box.

price.basis: Multitool $50-70 (step 2: Leatherman Wingman $50 list), knife $20, tape $7.16 (step 2), gloves $15, cord $10, bags $20, sundries $5. Maker pages refused my fetches.

lifeYears.basis: Tools last decades; tape and bags get used up.

setupHours.basis: Buy and box.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Replace what was borrowed.

everydayShare.basis: Most households own and use most of this already.

reliability.basis: Still together and findable.

adherence.basis: Household has the materials (sheeting or a tarpaulin) and someone able to do it.

fraction.basis: A patched window or roof keeps some homes habitable a day or two sooner. No data.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Sealing draughts and a broken pane in one room. Overlaps the warm-room plan.

items.name: Hatchet, shovel and folding saw
items.spec: A 35 cm hatchet, a round-point shovel and a 25 cm folding pruning saw, kept where they can be reached from inside (in flood zones, the hatchet in the attic).

price.basis: Search snippets: Fiskars X7 hatchet $33-38, digging shovel $19-49, Corona 10-inch folding saw $20-38.

lifeYears.basis: Hand tools.

setupHours.basis: Buy and store.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Sharpen, oil.

everydayShare.basis: Garden use in a house with trees.

reliability.basis: Simple tools; must be reachable.

adherence.basis: Someone fit enough to use them.

fraction.basis: Regaining access or drainage a day sooner in a minority of events.

adherence.basis: Tool is in the attic and the occupant can cut through.

fraction.basis: Attic entrapment drownings are real (New Orleans 2005, recalled) but a small share of flood deaths, and most are averted by leaving.

items.name: Written household plan
items.spec: One page: phone numbers including a contact outside the region, two meeting points, two ways out of each bedroom, who collects the children, where the shut-offs are, medical ID set on phones; a copy in each wallet and on the fridge; walked through once a year with a fire drill.

price.basis: Printing.

lifeYears.basis: Until the household, its phones or its address change.

setupHours.basis: Write, print, talk it through.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Yearly review and one drill.

everydayShare.basis: The contact sheet helps when a phone is lost.

reliability.basis: Still current and remembered: in one survey 79% said they had an escape plan but over half had never practised it.

adherence.basis: Plan was practised and is followed.

fraction.basis: No study compares fire deaths with and without a practised plan. Mechanism: people delay leaving (an NFPA survey found 8% respond to an alarm by leaving at once; search snippet). The channel owner may override.

adherence.basis: Members remember it.

fraction.basis: Removes part of the distress of not knowing where family members are when phones are down, by fixing a meeting point and an outside contact.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: A quicker and calmer departure. The one outcome study found no benefit.

items.name: Neighbour network
items.spec: Swap phone numbers with four to six nearby households, agree to check on one another in outages, heat and cold, note who has a generator, medical training or a frail member, and keep one shared contact sheet.

price.basis: Free; perhaps a round of coffee.

lifeYears.basis: Until neighbours move.

setupHours.basis: Knocking on doors, one get-together.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Keeping in touch.

everydayShare.basis: Ordinary neighbourly value: parcels, keys, an eye on the house.

reliability.basis: Neighbours are present, able and willing when it counts; in a regional event they are hit too.

adherence.basis: Network is activated.

fraction.basis: Pooling and lending shorten some unmet days. The need curves already assume spontaneous sharing, so this is only what prior arrangement adds.

adherence.basis: Network is activated.

fraction.basis: As for water.

adherence.basis: Someone does check.

fraction.basis: Chicago 1995: living alone OR 2.3 and not leaving home daily OR 6.7 for heat death; social contacts protective. A check-in or a neighbour's cooled room removes part of that excess; for a member who lives alone or is over 75 I would use two to three times this.

adherence.basis: Someone does check.

fraction.basis: Sheltering with a neighbour who has heat; a check that finds someone failing. Same reasoning as cooling, less evidence.

adherence.basis: Neighbours know who is home and look.

fraction.basis: Kobe 1995: most people pulled from rubble were rescued by residents, not services (over 70% in one source). Neighbours also drive people to care when ambulances are delayed.

adherence.basis: Neighbours do keep watch.

fraction.basis: Neighbourhood watch schemes are associated with 16-26% less crime in a meta-analysis of 18 evaluations; an informal arrangement of a few households is weaker than an organised scheme, so about a third to a half of that.

adherence.basis: Network is activated.

fraction.basis: News of where water, fuel and help are travels by word of mouth when phones are down.

items.name: Practice and yearly review
items.spec: Once a year, about three hours: check dates and rotate water, food, drugs and batteries; test alarms, lights, radio, stove and generator under load, outdoors; cook one meal without mains power; walk through the plan.

price.basis: Replacements are already in each item's upkeep.

lifeYears.basis: A yearly action.

setupHours.basis: None beyond the first session.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: One session; government sources ask for one every 6 or 12 months.

everydayShare.basis: None.

reliability.basis: The session is in fact held each year.

adherence.basis: What was practised is done under stress.

fraction.basis: Rehearsing where the generator and stove may run removes part of the misuse behind carbon monoxide deaths: in Texas 2021, 26% of those who stayed heated with a gas oven or hob and 8% used a grill indoors (step 2). No trial of drills.

items.name: Learn local hazards and warning signals
items.spec: Two hours, once: look up the address's flood and evacuation zones and wildfire, earthquake, tsunami and dam maps; learn what the local sirens and alert levels mean and where the nearest shelter and cooling centre are; write the answers on the household plan.

price.basis: Free public maps.

lifeYears.basis: Until the household moves or forgets.

setupHours.basis: Reading maps and local pages.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: A glance at the yearly review.

everydayShare.basis: None.

reliability.basis: Remembered or written down.

adherence.basis: Household acts on what it knows.

fraction.basis: Tornado warnings cut expected injuries by about 32%, and that is the value of the warning reaching people who act on it. Knowing in advance what the warning means and where to go is a part of that; I take a sixth.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Leaving in time and to the right place; not leaving when outside the zone.

items.name: Reference books
items.spec: A current first-aid manual and a lay medical handbook written for places without doctors, on paper, kept with the first-aid kit.

price.basis: Step 2 estimate $20-40 for one; two books $40. Free PDFs exist but need a charged device. Publisher's shop returned 429.

lifeYears.basis: Paper.

setupHours.basis: Skim so that the layout is familiar.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: None.

everydayShare.basis: Occasional household use.

reliability.basis: Found, and the right page reached, under stress.

adherence.basis: Consulted and followed.

fraction.basis: Only where care is out of reach for weeks. A book adds little to a trained person and less to an untrained one.

items.name: Pandemic isolation plan
items.spec: Confirm with each employer that work can be done from home at a day's notice (equipment, access); set up grocery and pharmacy delivery accounts; agree the household's trigger for withdrawing and how a sick member would be kept apart at home; know how many weeks of pay the household can forgo.

price.basis: Free where the employer supplies equipment; a headset or webcam otherwise.

lifeYears.basis: Until jobs change.

setupHours.basis: Conversations with employers, account set-up, a household talk.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Check that it still holds.

everydayShare.basis: Remote-work readiness and delivery accounts have ordinary uses.

reliability.basis: The plan works only if every earner's job can in fact be done remotely or paused; about 37% of US jobs can be done from home (Dingel and Neiman 2020, recalled).

adherence.basis: Household holds to isolation for as long as it matters.

fraction.basis: COVID-19 case-control study: going only to an office or school carried adjusted OR 1.8 against any telework, so telework removes about 44% of a worker's risk ((1.8-1)/1.8). In 2020 most remote-capable workers were sent home within two or three weeks with or without a plan, so the plan earns only the earlier start, the delivery set-up and separation of a sick member: I take a quarter.

adherence.basis: Looser adherence.

fraction.basis: Same mechanism; households isolate less strictly when the disease is milder.

items.name: Strap the water heater and anchor tall furniture
items.spec: Two metal straps on the water heater, anti-tip anchors on bookcases, wardrobes and televisions, latches on high kitchen cabinets; nothing heavy above beds.

price.basis: Recalled: strap kit about $20-25, anchors $10-15 per pack, latches $10-20; three to five packs. Not verified on a retailer page.

lifeYears.basis: Until furniture is rearranged or the heater replaced.

setupHours.basis: Do-it-yourself with a drill and stud finder.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Re-anchor what has moved.

everydayShare.basis: Anti-tip anchors also protect small children.

reliability.basis: Installed into studs, still attached.

adherence.basis: Most heavy items anchored.

fraction.basis: Northridge: deaths were mainly from building collapse, which this does not touch; hospital admissions were mostly falls and being struck by objects, which it does. So a small share of deaths and a larger share of injuries.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Contents and water damage; a small part of total earthquake loss.

items.name: Brace-and-bolt seismic retrofit
items.spec: For a wood-frame house built before about 1980 on a raised foundation: bolt the sill to the foundation and brace the crawl-space walls with plywood, to code.

price.basis: Typical cost $3,000-7,000 according to the PEER brochure for California's programme (search snippet); grants of up to $3,000 exist.

lifeYears.basis: Life of the house.

setupHours.basis: Quotes, permit, supervising.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: None.

everydayShare.basis: Part is recovered in resale value and insurance discounts.

reliability.basis: Permitted structural work.

adherence.basis: Passive once built.

fraction.basis: The PEER-CEA project reports substantial cuts in expected loss for the vulnerable house types, larger for two-storey houses; I could not read the figures.

adherence.basis: Passive.

fraction.basis: A house that stays on its foundation stays habitable.

adherence.basis: Passive.

fraction.basis: Fewer collapses of the house itself; most US earthquake deaths have been in other building types.

items.name: Shutters or panels for windows and garage door
items.spec: Pre-cut plywood or storm panels with fixings for every window and glazed door, and a brace kit for the garage door, stored labelled; at the next re-roofing, a sealed roof deck and stronger nailing.

price.basis: Recalled price bands, not verified: plywood for a dozen openings a few hundred dollars; metal storm panels $1,500-4,000; accordion shutters more.

lifeYears.basis: Panels last; plywood warps.

setupHours.basis: Measure, cut, fit anchors.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Fitting before a storm takes half a day; averaged over years.

everydayShare.basis: Insurance discounts in some states.

reliability.basis: Fitted in time before landfall, by someone able to lift them.

adherence.basis: Panels are up when the storm arrives.

fraction.basis: Hurricane Sally, coastal Alabama: homes built or re-roofed to the FORTIFIED standard had 55-74% fewer claims and 14-40% lower severity than conventional homes (press reports of the state study). Opening protection is one part of that standard and nearly half the claims were fallen trees, so I take about a third.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: A house that keeps its envelope stays habitable; power and water outages displace households regardless.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Fewer injuries from breaking glass for those who stay; fitting the panels has its own fall risk.

items.name: Basic flood-proofing
items.spec: Backwater valve on the sewer line, sump pump with battery backup, boiler, electrical panel and appliances raised above expected water level, valuables off the basement floor, and deployable barriers for doors and vents.

price.basis: Recalled contractor price bands, not verified: backwater valve $1,000-2,500 installed, backup sump pump $500-1,500, raising utilities $1,000 upward.

lifeYears.basis: Pumps 10 years, valves and raised utilities longer.

setupHours.basis: Quotes and supervision.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Test the pump and valve.

everydayShare.basis: A sump pump and valve also handle ordinary heavy rain and sewer backups.

reliability.basis: Pump runs, barriers are placed in time; overtopped in a deep flood.

adherence.basis: Measures in working order when the water comes.

fraction.basis: Household flood measures cut building and contents damage by a fifth to a half in shallow floods and little in deep ones (recalled from studies of the 2002 Elbe flood; step 2's French study says cost-efficiency depends strongly on flood probability).

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: A dry basement with working utilities shortens the time away.

items.name: Wildfire home hardening
items.spec: Ember-resistant vents, a 1.5 m strip around the house with nothing that burns, metal gutter guards, gaps under doors and eaves sealed, and vegetation cleared yearly out to 10 m.

price.basis: Recalled, not verified: vents $50-150 each for 10-20 vents, gravel strip and gutter guards a few hundred to a few thousand dollars; more if siding or roof is replaced.

lifeYears.basis: Hardware lasts; vegetation grows back.

setupHours.basis: Much of it is the owner's labour.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Yearly clearing of leaves, needles and brush.

everydayShare.basis: Insurability and premium discounts in some states.

reliability.basis: Maintained; neighbours' houses close by can still ignite it.

adherence.basis: Perimeter kept clear.

fraction.basis: The US mitigation study gives wildland-urban interface retrofit 2:1 overall and above 6:1 where fire is most likely, which implies a large cut in loss probability; post-fire surveys find homes built to ember-resistant codes surviving at two to three times the rate of older ones (recalled, Camp Fire).

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Evacuation is unchanged; the months of displacement after losing the house are what fall.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Matters to life only for those who cannot leave.

items.name: Home solar with battery backup
items.spec: 8 kW of rooftop solar with one 13.5 kWh battery wired for backup (islanding), with a reserve setting that keeps the battery at least half full.

price.basis: 8,000 W x $2.60 per watt (EnergySage, 2026, before incentives) = $20,800, plus a Tesla Powerwall 3 at $13,473 installed (EnergySage) = $34,300. The federal credit for owner-purchased systems ended in 2025 (search snippet); leases still qualify.

lifeYears.basis: Battery warranty 10 years (EnergySage); panels about 25.

setupHours.basis: Quotes, permits, utility paperwork.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Monitoring.

everydayShare.basis: Solar pays for itself in about 10 years on bills (EnergySage), so about 0.9 of its $20,800; the battery earns little outside time-of-use tariffs, about 0.15 of $13,473 (guess). (18,700 + 2,000) / 34,300 = 0.60.

reliability.basis: Battery charged when the outage starts; panels undamaged and not under snow or smoke.

adherence.basis: System islands correctly.

fraction.basis: Summer sun yields 30-40 kWh a day, enough to cool one or two rooms continuously.

adherence.basis: As above.

fraction.basis: Runs a gas furnace's fan and controls (about 6 kWh a day) for two days from the battery alone and longer with sun; runs a heat pump for hours, not days, in deep cold.

items.name: Rain barrel on a downpipe
items.spec: A 190-litre (50 US gallon) lidded, screened barrel with a downpipe diverter and tap; water is for flushing and washing, and for drinking only after filtering and disinfecting.
items.note: The water needs treating, so it counts toward sanitation only.

price.basis: Home Depot listings in search snippets: $99 to $139 for rigid 50-gallon barrels, $34 collapsible, $190 at the top. Page not opened.

lifeYears.basis: Plastic outdoors.

setupHours.basis: Level base, cut the downpipe, fit the diverter.

upkeepHoursPerYear.basis: Clean, drain before frost, check the screen.

everydayShare.basis: Garden watering.

reliability.basis: The barrel holds water when the event begins: empty in dry spells and drained in freezing winters.

adherence.basis: Household carries the water in.

fraction.basis: A flush takes about 6 litres; one barrel is some 30 flushes when taps are dry but drains work.
